lessons.plain: Before an organization can choose which projects to fund, someone has to find out what it is actually trying to achieve. This means reading written plans such as annual goals, strategy papers and budget documents, then talking to the people who own those goals to check what the words mean in practice. Think of a new navigator who reads the trip plan, then asks the captain where they really want to go before picking a route. The aim is to gather good enough information about direction so that later decisions about which work to keep, pause or start rest on evidence rather than guesswork.
lessons.guessPrompt: A written strategy says the company wants to grow its customer base. Two project managers each propose a new project to support that goal. What single piece of information would you most want before deciding which proposal fits the strategy better, and why?
lessons.teach: A strategic goal is a broad, longer-term result the organization wants, such as entering a new market. A strategic objective is a more specific, measurable step toward that goal, such as signing three regional partners within twelve months. Evaluating goals and objectives means finding out what they are, how they are measured, and how much weight leaders really give them. Portfolio managers do this with three kinds of information gathering. Document review means reading strategy papers, business plans, board minutes and budget documents. Interviews are one-to-one conversations with the executives and managers who own those goals, used to learn what the words mean in practice and what trade-offs they accept. Information gathering is the wider habit of collecting supporting data, such as sales figures or customer surveys, to test what the documents and people say. Why this works: written documents show what was decided, while interviews reveal intent, priorities and disagreements. Each source can be incomplete or out of date on its own, so you compare them. When sources agree, confidence rises; when they conflict, you have found a question to resolve before funding anything. Worked example: a plan lists the goal improve service quality. Step one, you review the annual plan and find an objective to cut complaint resolution time to two days by year end. Step two, you interview the operations director, who says the real priority is the two largest regions, not all of them. Step three, you check complaint data, which shows most delays come from one region. You now record a sharper priority: fix resolution time in that region first. Common mistake: treating the first document as the final word, or writing that a project aligns with strategy without naming the specific goal and its source. Consequence: if a goal is misread, the portfolio funds work that looks busy but moves no measured result, and that work is hard to justify later.

questions.prompt: A software company's strategy deck lists the goal grow recurring revenue and the objective raise annual renewal rate from 82 percent to 88 percent by next fiscal year. The company's board-approved budget paper gives no new money for customer success staff. Step one: the portfolio manager reads the strategy deck and records the objective and its target. Step two: the customer success lead says the real trade-off leaders accept is focusing on mid-market accounts, not enterprise accounts, because enterprise renewals are already stable. Step three: renewal data shows that most lost renewals come from mid-market accounts. The sources now conflict on one point: the budget paper assumes no added staff, but the objective needs more customer success effort. What should the portfolio manager do with this conflict before any funding decision?
choices: Record the conflict as an open question and settle it with the sponsor and the customer success lead before funding.
Count the stable enterprise renewals as progress toward the 88 percent objective.
Drop the renewal objective, since the interview outranks the written strategy deck.
Fund the added staff, because the board-approved budget paper is the final word.
questions.why: When sources conflict, the portfolio manager should record the conflict as a question to resolve before funding, rather than letting any single source decide.

questions.prompt: Which of these statements is a strategic objective rather than a strategic goal?
choices: Expand into a national brand presence with recognized customer loyalty.
Raise on-time departures to 85 percent within 18 months.
Build a reputation as the preferred employer across the entire region over time.
Improve the overall customer experience for travelers at every touchpoint.
questions.why: A strategic objective is a specific, measurable step with a target and timeframe, and only the on-time departures statement has both.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's strategic goal is to cut carbon emissions by 30 percent by 2030. A project manager must justify a proposed fleet upgrade to the portfolio board. Which evidence best ties the project to that specific goal?
choices: The project supports sustainability, which appears in our company values statement and annual report.
Leadership said green projects are popular this year.
It cuts diesel use at the two depots producing most route emissions, toward the 30 percent target.
The vendor's brochure claims the vans are eco-friendly.
questions.why: Naming the specific depots, the fuel reduction, and the 30 percent target links the project to a measurable goal and its source data.

questions.prompt: A portfolio manager decides which projects to fund using only last year's board minutes, which set a priority on store expansion. This year, the budget was reallocated toward online sales, but the manager did not check current documents or interview the executive sponsor. What is the main risk?
choices: Board minutes should never be used as evidence and must be deleted from the file.
The project will run late because formal minutes slow down every reader who reviews them.
It may fund work for a priority leaders have since dropped, since the minutes are out of date.
Charter templates may not fit minutes' formatting neatly.
questions.why: Relying on one outdated document without checking current sources can fund work tied to a priority that leaders have already dropped.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would evaluate an organization's strategic goals before proposing which portfolio components to fund. Name one limit or trade-off of the approach you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the written strategy and annual plan to list the stated goals and the objectives under each, noting how each is measured. Then I would interview the owners of those goals to learn which ones they really prioritize and where they disagree. Finally I would check a few supporting data sources, such as financial or performance figures, to see whether the documents and interviews match what is happening. Only then would I tie each proposed component to a named goal and source. The main limit is time: interviews take effort, and some stakeholders may be vague or guarded, so my picture of priorities could still be partial. I would record my assumptions and flag them to governance so the decision can be revisited if the evidence changes.
rubricPoints: Names the sources used: documents, interviews and supporting data
Explains that sources are compared so that conflicts are surfaced
Ties proposed components to a specific named goal or objective
States a real limit or trade-off, such as time cost or incomplete information

suggested.rationale: Explaining how goals are read and checked against sources is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine practises document review or stakeholder interviews.

lessons.plain: A prioritization criterion is a yardstick a portfolio manager uses to decide which projects get money, people, and attention first. Think of a household deciding which bills to pay when cash is short: legal obligations come first, then bills that unlock other bills, then what saves or earns the most, what the people affected expect, and what fits the family's goals. In a portfolio, the same kinds of yardsticks help a team explain why one initiative goes ahead and another waits. The skill is naming which criterion is driving each decision, instead of saying it just seemed important.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has two projects competing for the same budget. One is a project the government requires by a fixed date, and the other promises a higher financial return. Which one would you fund first, and what single reason would you give for your choice?
lessons.teach:
A portfolio is a group of projects, programs, and ongoing work that an organization manages together so the money and people are spent on what matters most. A prioritization criterion is a stated test used to rank items in that portfolio. This objective covers five common criteria. A legislative or regulatory driver is a requirement imposed by law or regulation, usually with a fixed deadline and little room to negotiate. A dependency is a link where one item must finish or start before another can proceed. Return on investment (ROI) is the benefit an item produces divided by its cost, usually measured over a stated period. Stakeholder expectations are the needs and promises made to the people who have a stake in the outcome. Strategic fit is how directly an item supports a specific, written organizational goal.

These criteria work because they make decisions traceable and comparable across very different items. Worked example: a fleet operator has three candidates. Item A is a reporting module a regulator requires by March 1. Item B is a telematics upgrade that a second project cannot start without. Item C is a driver app redesign with an ROI of 1.4 and strong executive interest, but it does not serve the stated goal of reducing vehicle downtime. Step one: A carries a legislative driver with a hard deadline, so it is non-negotiable and goes first. Step two: B is a dependency, so it is sequenced next to unblock other work. Step three: C has a good ROI, but its strategic fit is weak, so it waits even though it looks attractive.

The common mistake is letting one criterion, often ROI or the loudest stakeholder, decide everything, or ranking a legally mandated item by its ROI as if the law were optional. In a running operation, deprioritizing a mandatory reporting module can lead to fines or forced suspension of service, which is why legal drivers are checked first.

questions.prompt: A regional credit union is ranking three portfolio items. Item P is a data-protection update that a state banking regulator requires by 30 June. Item Q is a loan-origination upgrade that a new savings-product launch cannot start without. Item R is a branch-signage refresh with an ROI of 2.2, enthusiastic personal backing from one board member, and no link to the written goal of growing digital account openings. Step one: P carries a legislative driver with a fixed date, so it goes first. Step two: Q is a dependency, so it is sequenced next to unblock the launch. Step three: ____
choices: Because R has a board member's backing, it should be ranked ahead of Q, since stakeholder expectations always outrank dependencies in a ranking.
R waits, because its weak strategic fit with the digital-accounts goal outweighs its ROI and sponsor interest.
R is removed from the portfolio entirely, because a good ROI cannot be used as a criterion when a stakeholder is not also a regulator.
R has the highest ROI of the three, so it should be ranked second because ROI is the most reliable criterion for any decision in the portfolio.
questions.why: Strategic fit measures how directly an item supports a specific written goal, and R has weak fit, so it is deferred even though its ROI and sponsor interest look attractive.

questions.prompt: In portfolio prioritization, what does a dependency mean as a criterion?
choices: A requirement set by law that has a fixed deadline and cannot be negotiated away.
The needs and promises made to people who have a stake in the outcome.
A benefit-to-cost measure calculated over a stated period of time.
A link where one item must finish or start before another item can proceed.
questions.why: A dependency is a sequencing link where one item has to finish or start before another can move forward, which is the meaning given in the teaching text in plain words.

questions.prompt: A retail chain is comparing a warehouse scanner upgrade that costs 180,000 and is expected to produce benefits of 270,000 over two years. What ROI does this item carry under the definition used in portfolio prioritization?
choices: 90,000, found by subtracting cost from benefit.
0.67, found by dividing cost by benefit.
1.5, found by dividing benefit by cost over the stated period.
2.7, found by dividing benefit by the number of years.
questions.why: ROI is the benefit an item produces divided by its cost over a stated period, so 270,000 divided by 180,000 gives 1.5.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm ranks a mandated accessibility fix last because its ROI is low, and the fix misses its legal deadline. What is the core error in this decision?
choices: The firm should have ranked the fix first because dependencies always come before ROI in every case.
The firm ranked by ROI correctly, but should have used a longer measurement period for the benefit.
The firm used strategic fit instead of stakeholder expectations to rank the fix.
The firm treated a legally required item as optional and judged it by ROI when a legal driver should be checked first.
questions.why: A legislative driver is a fixed requirement that must be checked before other criteria like ROI, so ranking a mandated fix by ROI as if it were optional is the mistake that leads to missed deadlines and penalties.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to portfolio work how you would use prioritization criteria to choose between two candidate projects when the budget covers only one. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first check for a legislative or regulatory driver, since a legal deadline usually overrides everything else. If neither project is mandated, I would look at dependencies to see whether one unblocks other work, then compare ROI and strategic fit against the goal we have written down. I would also record stakeholder expectations so the decision is visible to them. The main limit is that these criteria can conflict, for example a high-ROI project with weak strategic fit, so I would present the tradeoff to governance rather than hide it in a single score. Scoring also depends on estimates that may be wrong, so I would note the assumptions behind each ranking.
rubricPoints: Names legislative or regulatory drivers as a first check because they are typically non-negotiable
Explains that dependencies, ROI, stakeholder expectations, and strategic fit are applied in a stated order or weighting
Ties the choice to a specific written strategic goal rather than a general alignment claim
States a concrete limit, such as criteria conflicting or ROI relying on uncertain estimates

suggested.rationale: No listed mission covers portfolio prioritization, and reasoning through an exam-style scenario that ranks competing items against these criteria adds the most value.

lessons.plain: When a company has more good ideas than money or people, it has to decide which ones go first. Ranking strategic priorities means putting the goals and the proposed projects in order of importance, using rules agreed in advance and the views of the people who will be affected. Qualitative analysis judges things in words, such as whether a project fits the company's direction. Quantitative analysis puts numbers on things, such as cost or expected return. Good ranking uses both, and the people who care about the outcome take part, so the order is one they can accept and defend later.
lessons.guessPrompt: Three projects compete for one budget. Project X clearly supports the company's main goal but is expensive. Project Y is cheap and pleases the finance director but does little for that goal. Project Z is moderately useful to both. Which would you fund first, and what would you need to know before deciding?
lessons.teach:
A strategic priority is an organisation goal that leaders have chosen to put ahead of others, such as growing in a new region or cutting service outage time. A stakeholder is any person or group who is affected by a decision or can influence it, such as a sponsor, a finance lead or an operations manager. Ranking means putting candidate initiatives in order, and it works best when the criteria are agreed before anyone looks at the scores.

Qualitative analysis judges things by description and reasoned argument, for example whether an initiative supports a named goal or how risky a dependency looks. Quantitative analysis puts numbers on similar things, such as expected return, cost, or the share of users affected. A weighted scoring model combines both. Each criterion gets a weight that reflects its importance, each initiative gets a score from 1 to 5 on each criterion, and the weighted total gives the rank.

Worked example. Criteria and weights: strategic fit 40 percent, return on investment 30 percent, stakeholder support 20 percent, dependency risk 10 percent. Initiative C scores 4, 4, 5 and 3. Its total is 0.4 x 4 + 0.3 x 4 + 0.2 x 5 + 0.1 x 3, which is 1.6 + 1.2 + 1.0 + 0.3 = 4.1. Initiative A scores 5, 3, 4 and 2, giving 3.9. Initiative B scores 3, 5, 2 and 4, giving 3.5. The order is C, then A, then B.

Common mistake: letting the most senior or loudest stakeholder set the weights after seeing the scores. That turns the ranking into a justification of a preferred answer rather than a decision. The total is also an input to the decision, not the decision itself; a regulatory requirement still applies even if its score is low.

In a running portfolio, a ranking that is not recorded with its weights and scores cannot be re-run when goals change, so funding moves become hard to explain to governance.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital network ranks three candidate initiatives using four agreed criteria with weights: patient safety 50 percent, cost savings 25 percent, staff readiness 15 percent, and vendor lock-in risk 10 percent (a low score means more lock-in risk). Initiative X scores 3, 5, 4 and 2, so its total is 0.50 times 3, plus 0.25 times 5, plus 0.15 times 4, plus 0.10 times 2, which equals 3.55. Initiative Y scores 4, 2, 3 and 5, so its total is 3.45. Initiative Z scores 2, 4, 5 and 3 on the same four criteria, in the same order. Step still missing: calculate Z's weighted total and state where Z ranks among X, Y and Z.
choices: 3.05, ranks third behind X and Y
3.05, ranks first because readiness carries a high score
3.75, ranks second ahead of Y
2.95, ranks third behind X and Y
questions.why: Z's total is 0.50 times 2 plus 0.25 times 4 plus 0.15 times 5 plus 0.10 times 3, which is 1.00 plus 1.00 plus 0.75 plus 0.30, giving 3.05, and 3.05 is below X's 3.55 and Y's 3.45, so Z ranks third.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines a stakeholder in portfolio work?
choices: Anyone affected by or able to influence a decision
Any outside vendor supplying a product used in the project
Only people who report directly to the portfolio manager
Only the executive who approves the funding for a portfolio
questions.why: A stakeholder is any person or group affected by a decision or able to influence it, which is broader than funders, direct reports, or vendors alone.

questions.prompt: A school district compares a proposed app by having a panel write a reasoned account of how well it supports the stated goal of improving reading levels, without assigning any numbers. Which kind of analysis is this?
choices: Quantitative, because the panel is rating the app
Qualitative, since it rests on reasoned description
Neither, because judgements without numbers cannot be analysed
Quantitative, because it belongs to a weighted scoring model
questions.why: Qualitative analysis judges things through description and reasoned argument, which is what the panel's written account does, while quantitative analysis would need numbers placed on the items.

questions.prompt: After a weighted ranking is drafted, a sponsor asks the team to raise the weight on cost savings after seeing that their preferred initiative scores lower, so it moves to the top. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The lowest-scoring initiative is removed from the portfolio automatically
The ranking becomes a justification of a preferred answer and cannot be defended to governance
Nothing changes, because weights are only inputs and can be adjusted freely at any point
The ranking becomes more accurate because the sponsor understands the costs better
questions.why: Setting weights after seeing scores turns the ranking into a justification of a preferred outcome, which undermines its credibility, because criteria and weights should be agreed before scores are examined.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never run a prioritisation exercise how a weighted scoring model ranks strategic priorities, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on the resulting numbers.
lessons.modelAnswer: A weighted scoring model first agrees the criteria with stakeholders, such as strategic fit, return and stakeholder support, and gives each a weight that shows how much it matters. Each candidate initiative is then scored, usually from 1 to 5, on each criterion. Multiplying each score by its weight and adding them gives a total, and the totals give the ranking. It combines qualitative judgement, which decides what the criteria are and what each score means, with quantitative arithmetic, which keeps the comparison consistent. The main limit is that the output is only as good as the weights and scores. Two reasonable groups can pick different weights and get different orders, and a number can make a close call look more certain than it is. So the ranking should be recorded with its weights, tested by changing them, and checked against any hard constraints such as a regulatory requirement that a low score cannot override.
rubricPoints: Describes agreeing criteria and weights with stakeholders before scoring
Explains scoring each initiative on each criterion and combining weighted scores into a rank
Distinguishes qualitative judgement from quantitative arithmetic
Names a limit such as sensitivity to weights or false precision, and a remedy such as recording and testing the weights

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine teaches stakeholder-weighted prioritisation, so an exam-style situation to reason through is the best fit.

lessons.plain: A portfolio is the full set of projects, programs and ongoing work an organization chooses to fund at the same time. A component is one item in that set. This objective is about reading the business plans and proposals that arrive and sorting out two things: what is already running or committed, which is existing, and what might be started, which is potential. Those pieces are then combined into a few alternative portfolio scenarios, each a different possible mix, so leaders can compare them. Think of a household budget: you list the bills you already pay and the purchases you are considering before you decide what to do.
lessons.guessPrompt: A regional transport company has a plan to replace its dispatch software, a proposal to add electric vehicle charging at two depots, and a signed contract to maintain its radio network. Which of these would you list as existing portfolio components and which as potential ones, and why might that distinction matter before any funding decision?
lessons.teach:
A portfolio is the collection of projects, programs and operational work that an organization groups together so it can be funded, staffed and reviewed as one set. A component is a single item inside that collection. An existing component is one already approved, funded, and under way or under contract. A potential component is one that has been proposed or implied by a plan but not yet approved. A business plan is a document describing where an organization intends to go and what it will do to get there. A proposal is a document asking for resources to pursue one specific item. A scenario is one possible version of the portfolio, a particular mix of components that can be compared against other mixes. A baseline is the agreed starting point of what is already committed.

Why it works: the documents are your raw material. Read each plan and proposal, write down every initiative it names, then mark each as existing or potential by checking the evidence: an approved budget, a signed contract, or a named team. Only after that do you combine items into scenarios, because every scenario needs a clear baseline to be measured against.

Worked example: a water utility has three documents. The strategic plan names a leak-reduction program. A billing upgrade charter is already approved and funded. A vendor proposal offers a new customer portal. Step 1: list leak reduction as a potential component, since it is in the plan with no approved funding. Step 2: list the billing upgrade as existing, because it is approved and funded. Step 3: list the customer portal as potential, because it is only a proposal. Step 4: build two scenarios on the billing baseline, one adding leak reduction and one adding the portal, and compare them.

Common mistake: counting a proposal as existing, or listing the same initiative twice because two documents describe it. Both inflate the baseline and make scenarios look cheaper or more complete than they are.

Consequence: if the baseline is wrong, every scenario built on it overstates available money and staff, and leadership can approve a mix the organization cannot actually deliver.

questions.prompt: A regional library system has three inputs. Its board approved a van replacement last year and the purchase order is signed, so the van is an existing component. Its strategic plan names a digital lending expansion, but no budget has been approved for it, so it is a potential component. A memo from the branch managers describes the same digital lending expansion in different words, and the team must handle this before building scenarios. Step 3 is the missing step: the team deals with the duplicate. Step 4: the team builds scenarios on a baseline that includes the signed van purchase. Which action fills step 3?
choices: Merge the two descriptions into one potential component so the expansion is counted once before any scenario is built.
Add the memo's digital lending item as a second potential component so the scenario carries more weight.
Build the scenarios first and reconcile the duplicate afterward if the totals look wrong.
Reclassify the digital lending expansion as existing because the branch managers support it.
questions.why: The same initiative described in two documents must be counted once, and because it has no approved funding it stays a potential component, so merging the descriptions before scenario building keeps the baseline honest.

questions.prompt: In this framework, what separates a potential component from an existing one?
choices: A component is potential if a plan or proposal implies it but no approval exists yet; existing components are approved and funded.
A component is potential if it appears in any business plan, whereas existing components appear in approved proposals.
A component is potential if its team has been named but no budget has been approved yet, whereas existing components have a budget.
A component is potential if it has a signed contract that has not yet started, whereas existing components are already under way.
questions.why: A potential component has been proposed or implied but not approved, while an existing one is approved, funded, and under way or under contract.

questions.prompt: A charity lists a community garden project in its strategic plan, a vendor proposal for a food truck, and a roof repair that is approved, funded, and has a named contractor. Which classification is correct for building the baseline?
choices: Roof repair as existing, food truck and garden as potential.
Roof repair, food truck and garden all as existing because all three were discussed.
Garden as existing because it is in the plan, roof as potential because the contractor is not yet paid.
Roof repair and food truck as existing, garden as potential.
questions.why: The roof repair has approved funding and a named team, so it is existing, while the food truck is only a proposal and the garden has no approved funding, so both are potential.

questions.prompt: A team counts an unsigned vendor quote as an existing component and builds a scenario on that baseline. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The scenario is still valid because quotes are a form of commitment, and only the cost estimate needs updating later.
Leadership will notice the error at the next review and reduce the scope of the scenario automatically.
The baseline is correct, but the scenario will simply take longer to compare against other mixes.
The scenario overstates the money and staff available, so leadership may approve a mix the organization cannot deliver.
questions.why: An unsigned quote is only a proposal, so counting it as existing inflates the baseline, which makes every scenario built on it appear more affordable and complete than it is.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would turn a folder of business plans and proposals into two or three portfolio scenarios. Name one limit or tradeoff in how you decided which items count as existing and which as potential.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing every initiative named in the plans and proposals, one line each, with its source document. Then I would mark each as existing or potential by checking evidence: an approved budget, a signed contract, or a named team means existing; a proposal or a plan line without funding means potential. Duplicates across documents get merged into one component. Once the list is clean, I set the existing components as the baseline and build two or three scenarios by adding different potential components to it, noting the cost and staff each adds. The main tradeoff is that some items are half approved, such as a funded study that leads to an unfunded build. Treating those as existing overstates the baseline, while treating them as potential understates the commitment, so I flag them explicitly for the governance group to decide.
rubricPoints: Defines existing components as approved or committed and potential components as proposed but not yet approved
Lists initiatives from each document and merges duplicates before building scenarios
Sets the existing components as the baseline before comparing scenarios
Names a real limit, such as partially approved items or weak evidence, and how to handle it

suggested.rationale: Sorting real-looking documents into existing and potential components and then comparing scenarios is an exam-style reasoning task, and no listed mission or engine covers portfolio work directly.

lessons.plain: A what-if scenario is a made-up version of your portfolio, built to test a choice before you commit money and people to it. Suppose leadership asks what happens if the budget is cut by a fifth, or a new regulation arrives next year. You build two or three alternative sets of projects and compare them on cost, risk, and how well each still serves the organisation's goals. Options analysis, risk analysis, SWOT and financial analysis are the common tools for making that comparison fair. The aim is to see the trade-offs before the decision is made, not after.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has budget for either a new customer portal or a warehouse automation project, but not both. Before any analysis, which would you compare first, and what single piece of information would most change your mind?
lessons.teach:
A portfolio is the full set of projects, programmes and ongoing operations an organisation funds to reach its goals. A scenario is one complete alternative version of that set, with its own assumptions. Options analysis means listing realistic alternatives, including doing nothing, and scoring each one against the same criteria. Risk analysis asks what could go wrong in each scenario, how likely it is, how costly, and what happens if an assumption fails. SWOT sorts the factors for each scenario into strengths and weaknesses (inside the organisation) and opportunities and threats (outside it). Financial analysis compares cost with expected benefit over time; net present value (NPV) is the total of future money discounted back to today's value, so that later money counts for less.

Why it works: putting scenarios side by side on the same criteria stops the team from choosing whichever option sounds most exciting.

Worked example, using illustrative figures. Both options cost 1.2 million. Option A, the portal, is expected to return 1.8 million over three years and supports the goal of growing online sales. Option B, automation, is expected to return 1.5 million, and its supplier may delay delivery. Step 1: hold the budget constant. Step 2: subtract cost from benefit, giving A a net of 0.6 million and B a net of 0.3 million. Step 3: rerun B with a six-month delay, which pushes some benefit past year three and lowers its value further. Step 4: note the SWOT weakness that the organisation has no in-house automation skills. Step 5: conclude that A is stronger, unless the stated goal is cost reduction.

Common mistake: testing only the preferred option, or changing one assumption without rerunning every scenario, so the comparison confirms what the team already wanted.

Consequence: if the chosen scenario relies on a shared platform that is not funded, the dependent projects stall partway through the year and the portfolio misses its benefits.

questions.prompt: A regional library system has 0.9 million to spend and is comparing two scenarios. Scenario 1 is a self-checkout kiosk rollout, expected to return 1.4 million over three years. Scenario 2 is a mobile lending app, expected to return 1.2 million over three years, but its vendor may delay launch by six months. Step 1: hold the budget constant at 0.9 million for both scenarios. Step 2: subtract cost from expected benefit, giving Scenario 1 a net of 0.5 million and Scenario 2 a net of 0.3 million. Step 3: rerun Scenario 2 with the six-month delay, which pushes part of its benefit past year three and lowers its value. Step 4 (missing from this analysis): ___. Which step correctly completes the analysis?
choices: Remove the do-nothing option from the comparison, because it has no cost to subtract.
Add a SWOT for Scenario 1 only, so the comparison has balanced detail.
Stop after Step 3 and choose Scenario 1, since it already has the higher net value.
Rerun Scenario 1 under the same delay assumption, so every scenario is tested against the same stress before comparing them.
questions.why: Changing an assumption for one scenario means every scenario must be rerun under that same assumption, or the comparison favours whichever option was not stressed.

questions.prompt: A committee compares two scenarios that each return 2.0 million in total. Scenario X returns 1.0 million in year one and 1.0 million in year two. Scenario Y returns 0.4 million in year one and 1.6 million in year three. Which statement about comparing them with net present value is correct?
choices: Scenario Y is worth more because its larger payment comes in year three, which gives the project a longer period to earn.
The two scenarios are equal in value because both return the same total of 2.0 million.
Scenario X is worth more today, because its money arrives sooner and later money counts for less.
Timing does not matter once cost is subtracted, so the two scenarios are equal in value.
questions.why: Net present value discounts future money back to today's value, so money received earlier is worth more than the same amount received later.

questions.prompt: In a SWOT analysis for a credit union's proposed online loan-approval scenario, which factor belongs under opportunities?
choices: Staff have no experience running the approval software.
A regulator is considering new lending rules that could cut the union's margins.
The union owns its headquarters building outright.
A competitor has just stopped offering local business loans.
questions.why: Opportunities are external factors the scenario could use, and a competitor leaving the local market is outside the union and could be exploited, whereas the other three are internal or threats.

questions.prompt: A hospital team runs a risk analysis on a new scheduling system, but it only tests the option the sponsor prefers and then reports that option as the strongest. What is the main flaw in this analysis?
choices: Scoring only the preferred option means the result confirms the existing preference rather than testing it against alternatives.
The team should have converted the scheduling system's benefits to present value before running the risk analysis.
The sponsor's preference should have been removed from the criteria entirely before testing began.
The team used too few risk categories, and adding more categories would fix the result.
questions.why: A comparison only shows which option is strongest when every realistic alternative, including doing nothing, is scored against the same criteria.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would build and compare two what-if portfolio scenarios after a budget cut, and name one limit of the financial numbers you would rely on.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by writing down the budget ceiling and the strategic goals both scenarios must serve, then build two realistic sets of projects that fit under that ceiling. For each set I would score cost, expected benefit, and a simple net present value, using the same discount rate for both. Next I would run a risk pass and a SWOT on each scenario, asking what happens if a key assumption, such as a supplier date, slips. The main limit is that the financial figures are estimates made before the work starts, so a small change in benefit timing can reverse the ranking. I would therefore present the sensitivity results alongside the headline numbers, so governance sees how fragile the recommendation is.
rubricPoints: Builds each scenario within the same stated budget and goals, so the comparison is fair
Uses financial measures such as net benefit or NPV with a consistent basis
Tests risks and assumptions by rerunning scenarios, not just the preferred one
Names a real limit of the forecasts, such as sensitivity to timing or estimates

suggested.rationale: Choosing between scenarios under a budget constraint is an exam-style reasoning task, and no listed mission models portfolio decisions, so reasoning through a situation adds the most.

lessons.plain: A portfolio is the full set of projects, programs and ongoing work an organization funds at once. A portfolio scenario is one possible version of that set: a particular mix of initiatives with a particular budget and timing. Recommending a scenario means choosing one option from several and telling a governance group, the people who approve funding and direction, which components to fund, in what order, and why. The why is the rationale: a short, evidence-based argument that links each choice to a stated strategic goal or ranking criterion. A recommendation with no link back to the goal is just an opinion, and governance groups tend to reject it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team can fund two of three candidate projects this year. One has the highest expected return but does not support the company's top stated goal. Which two do you recommend, and what single sentence would you use to justify that choice to the investment board?
lessons.teach: A portfolio component is any single item inside a portfolio, such as a project, a program (a group of related projects managed together), or an ongoing operational service. A scenario is a costed, timed combination of components that could be chosen. Governance is the body, often called a steering committee or investment board, that approves scenarios and oversees the funding. Rationale is the chain of reasoning that runs from a strategic goal, through the criteria used to rank options, to the specific components recommended. Governance decides under limited money and people, so a recommendation that names the goal it serves and the trade-off it accepts lets the board decide quickly. Worked example: the strategic goal is to grow recurring subscription revenue by 15 percent within 18 months. Candidates are A, a self-serve billing portal (strong fit, 6 months); B, a partner integration program (moderate fit, 12 months, and it needs A's interface to exist first); and C, a legacy report rewrite (good return, but no link to the goal). Budget covers two. Step 1: score each candidate against the goal. Step 2: check dependencies, which shows B cannot run without A. Step 3: build scenarios: A plus C, A then B, or all three, which is over budget. Step 4: recommend A then B, stating that both map directly to the goal and that C is deferred, with the trade-off that legacy reporting stays slow. A common mistake is recommending the scenario with the most projects or the highest total return without naming the goal it serves, or ignoring dependencies. The consequence in practice is that if B were approved alone, it would stall in month four waiting for A, and the board would lose confidence in the next recommendation.

questions.prompt: A university IT office has a goal to cut student enrollment processing time from 10 working days to 3 working days within 12 months. The budget is $350,000. Three candidates were considered. P, an online document upload portal, is a strong fit to the goal and costs $200,000 over 5 months. Q, a records search upgrade, is a moderate fit because staff can verify transcripts faster, and costs $150,000 over 7 months. R, a campus Wi-Fi upgrade, has no link to the goal and costs $120,000. Steps 1 and 2 are done: each candidate has been scored against the goal, and the scenarios that fit the budget are P plus Q at $350,000, P plus R at $320,000, and Q plus R at $270,000. Step 3, the recommendation, is the only step missing. Which completion is correct?
choices: Recommend all three candidates, since they fit together and the board can decide later what to cut.
Recommend Q and R, since together they cost less than P and leave budget free for a later bid.
Recommend P and Q, state that both map to the enrollment goal, defer R because it has no link to the goal, and name the trade-off that campus Wi-Fi stays as it is.
Recommend P and R, the two cheapest options, since cost is the only criterion the board asked for, and leave the enrollment goal out of the statement.
questions.why: A correct recommendation names the goal each recommended component serves, stays within budget, defers the component with no link to the goal, and states the trade-off accepted.

questions.prompt: In portfolio governance, what does the term rationale mean?
choices: The vote the investment board takes to approve or reject a scenario.
A list of every project currently running in the organisation, with their budgets and owners.
The chain of reasoning that runs from a strategic goal, through the criteria used to rank options, to the specific components recommended.
The timeline showing when each component of a scenario will start and finish.
questions.why: The teaching text defines rationale as the chain of reasoning from goal, through ranking criteria, to recommended components, which is the first choice.

questions.prompt: A retailer's goal is to raise its share of orders placed online from 20 percent to 30 percent within 12 months. The available budget is $150,000. Three options are on the table: a checkout redesign that is a strong fit and costs $90,000; an in-store signage refresh that has no link to the goal and costs $60,000; and mobile push notifications that are a strong fit and cost $55,000. Which recommendation best supports governance decision-making?
choices: Recommend the checkout redesign and the mobile push notifications, which total $145,000, name the online share goal for both, defer the signage refresh, and state that in-store displays stay outdated as the trade-off.
Recommend all three options, since the total is only $55,000 over budget and the board can trim items later.
Recommend the checkout redesign and the signage refresh, which uses the full $150,000 and is the highest total spend, without naming the online share goal.
Recommend the mobile push notifications alone because it is the cheapest strong fit, and say nothing about the other options.
questions.why: Only the second choice stays within budget, ties each recommended component to the goal, defers the unlinked item, and states the trade-off.

questions.prompt: A board receives a recommendation to approve only a mobile claims intake project, which is a strong fit to the goal of cutting average claim handling time. That project needs a claims data service that is not in the proposed scenario. What is the main problem with this recommendation?
choices: The goal is too narrow, so the board should add more goals before deciding anything.
Governance should never approve a single component, so the recommendation must be rejected on principle.
The scenario ignores a dependency, so the project is likely to stall once the missing data service is needed, which would cost the board confidence in future recommendations.
The mobile project is too cheap to justify a board decision at all.
questions.why: A recommendation that depends on an absent component will stall, which the teaching text identifies as the consequence of ignoring dependencies.

lessons.explainPrompt: Imagine you are presenting a portfolio recommendation to your organization's investment board. In your own words, explain to a teammate how you would recommend one scenario and its components with a clear rationale, and name one limit or trade-off the board should accept with your recommendation.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing the strategic goal the board has set and the criteria it uses to rank options, such as strategic fit, dependencies and return. Then I would build two or three complete scenarios, each with its components, budget and sequence, and score them against those criteria. I would recommend the scenario that delivers the most fit to the goal within budget and respects dependencies, and I would say explicitly which components I deferred and why. The rationale should be one chain: this goal, these criteria, these components. The trade-off I would name is that the deferred work, here the legacy reporting, stays unimproved for another year, so the board should accept that known cost in return for faster progress on the goal.
rubricPoints: Links each recommended component to a specific strategic goal or ranking criterion
Compares at least two complete scenarios rather than one option
Accounts for dependencies and sequencing between components
Names a concrete trade-off or limit of the recommended scenario

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers portfolio recommendation, and explaining the rationale back to a teammate is the core skill.

lessons.plain: A portfolio is the set of projects and programs an organization funds to reach its goals. When leadership changes those goals, some items in the set may suddenly matter more, some less, and some may no longer fit at all. This objective is about tracing that ripple: starting from the changed goal, working out which components are affected, and deciding what to keep, pause, speed up, or stop. Think of a city council that switches its top priority from road building to flood defence. It must check which road projects still make sense, which new ones are needed, and how the budget and schedule change as a result.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your organization's top goal changes from growing market share to cutting operating costs. Name two projects in a portfolio that would most likely need to be reconsidered, and say why in one sentence each.
lessons.teach:
A strategic goal is a specific outcome the organization has committed to reach, such as entering a new market or reducing costs by a fixed percentage. A portfolio component is any project, program, or operational work grouped under the portfolio, and each one exists because it contributes to some goal. A prioritization criterion is a rule used to rank candidates, such as expected return, strategic fit, or a regulatory deadline.

Why this works: if every component is explicitly linked to the goal it serves, a change in that goal can be traced forward. Start by listing which goals changed and how: dropped, reweighted, newly added, or made stricter. Then, for each component, ask three questions. Does its benefit still count toward the revised goal? Has its priority score moved? Does it depend on, or enable, another component that is affected?

Worked example: a utility's goal moves from expanding service to new towns to improving reliability in existing towns. Step 1: the new-towns extension loses its strategic link, so its score drops. Step 2: a fibre backbone it depends on still improves reliability, so it is kept but may move earlier in the sequence. Step 3: a meter-replacement program gains priority because it now serves the top goal. Step 4: record each change and its rationale for governance review.

Common mistake: assuming the portfolio is simply re-ranked and nothing else moves. A goal change can break dependencies, strand money already spent, and pull staff away from work the new goal still needs.

Consequence: a project that keeps running on the old goal consumes budget and people the new goal requires, and the portfolio reports can look healthy while the organization delivers the wrong outcomes.

questions.prompt: A regional logistics firm changes its top goal from growing its share of rural deliveries to cutting the cost of each parcel by 15 percent. Its portfolio has three components. Step 1: the rural depot project loses its link to the new goal, so its priority score drops. Step 2: the route-planning software still counts toward cost savings, but it relies on the depot project's location data, so the team confirms that dependency is still valid. Step 3: the driver-training program gains priority because it reduces fuel and overtime costs. Step 4: The firm has two route planners. One is assigned to the rural depot project, which is being wound down, and the cost goal still needs one planner on the route-planning software. Which action completes the trace?
choices: Keep both planners on the rural depot project, since its spend is already committed.
Reassign one planner to the route software and log the change with its reason.
Cut the route-planning software entirely because the depot project it once supported has been wound down.
Leave staffing unchanged, since a reranked list does not move people between work.
questions.why: Step 4 applies the rule that a component the revised goal still needs keeps its place, so staff move to it and the change is recorded for governance review.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines a prioritization criterion?
choices: A record of money already spent on a component that may be stopped.
A rule for ranking candidates, such as expected return.
Any project, program, or operational work grouped under the portfolio.
A specific outcome the organization has committed to reach, such as entering a new market.
questions.why: A prioritization criterion is a rule used to rank candidates, and the other options describe a goal, a component, and a spending record.

questions.prompt: A water agency changes its top goal from cutting leakage by 10 percent to replacing aging pipes in the north district. A pumping station upgrade still helps the north district, but its benefit was originally counted only toward the leakage goal. Which action best applies the method to this component?
choices: Re-check whether its benefit still counts and whether its priority has moved.
Treat the upgrade as unaffected, because the portfolio can simply be re-ranked with nothing else changing.
Drop the pumping upgrade at once, since its old benefit no longer counts toward anything the agency funds.
Keep the upgrade at its old priority score, since its budget is already committed to the work.
questions.why: The method asks whether a component's benefit still counts toward the revised goal and whether its priority has moved, before deciding its place in the sequence.

questions.prompt: A school district changes its goal from raising enrolment to improving reading scores by a fixed margin. Its monthly reports show every project on schedule and within budget, so the portfolio looks healthy. What is the most accurate conclusion?
choices: The portfolio is aligned, since every project reports on time and within budget.
Green status proves little; trace each component to the new reading goal.
Enrolment projects should be kept because they were funded first.
The goal change is complete, so no further review is needed for the portfolio.
questions.why: On-time, on-budget reports do not show that components still serve the revised goal, which is the common mistake the teaching text warns about.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would work out the impact of a change in strategic goals on a portfolio. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing exactly what changed in the goals: which were dropped, reweighted, added, or tightened. Then I would go component by component and ask whether it still contributes to a revised goal, whether its priority has moved, and whether it depends on or enables something else that is affected. I would group the results into continue, re-sequence, pause, or stop, and check the dependency chain before recommending any of them. The main limit is that the goal change may be provisional, so I would present the impact to governance as scenarios with the reasoning shown, not as a final verdict. I would also flag that stopping work can leave sunk costs and customer commitments that need separate treatment.
rubricPoints: Identifies exactly which strategic goals changed and how
Traces each affected component back to the goal it serves
Considers dependencies and sequencing, not just re-ranking
Names a limit such as sunk costs or provisional goals and presents results for governance decision

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a changed-goal situation and defending the impact on each component adds the most, and no current mission covers portfolio decisions.

lessons.plain: A portfolio is the set of projects and programs an organization funds to reach its goals. A portfolio roadmap is a high-level picture of when those pieces start and finish, which must come first, and how each one links to a business goal. Building one means sitting down with the people who own the money, the outcomes, and the work, agreeing on the order, and checking that every item earns its place. Think of a city planning road works for the next three years: no street gets dug up before the water main beneath it is replaced, and every project should serve a stated civic goal.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your organization has three candidate projects: a new customer self-service portal, a central data warehouse, and a reporting dashboard that reads its numbers from the warehouse. Which should be scheduled first, and why might the answer differ from whichever one the sales director wants most?
lessons.teach:
Key terms. A portfolio roadmap is a high-level timeline showing the order in which portfolio components (projects, programs, or work streams) start, overlap and finish over months or years. A dependency is a condition where one item cannot start or finish properly until another item is done, such as a dashboard that needs the warehouse to already hold data. Sequencing is the ordering of items on the timeline, based on dependencies, available capacity and priority. Strategic alignment means each item can be traced to a named organizational goal, such as reduce customer churn by 10 percent this year. A key stakeholder is a person or group with authority over funding, outcomes or delivery, whose agreement the roadmap needs.

Why it works: a roadmap turns a list of good ideas into a plan people can commit to. Ordering by dependency prevents rework and idle teams. Tying each row to a goal gives leaders a reason to say yes or no. Involving stakeholders early surfaces conflicts before money is spent.

Worked example. Goal: grow repeat customers. Step 1: list the candidates and the goal each serves. The portal serves self-service ordering, the warehouse serves a single view of each customer, and the dashboard serves tracking the repeat rate. Step 2: map dependencies. The dashboard depends on the warehouse; the portal depends on neither. Step 3: sequence the warehouse first, the dashboard after it, and the portal in parallel. Step 4: check alignment. The warehouse supports the goal directly, while the portal supports it indirectly, so the portal ranks lower if capacity is tight. Step 5: review the order with the sales director and the finance owner, and record their agreement.

Common mistake: sorting items by whoever argues loudest, or discovering dependencies only when delivery is already underway. The consequence is that the dashboard team waits idle for data, and budget is spent on a report nobody can populate.

A roadmap is trustworthy only when every row names its goal and its blockers, and when the stakeholders who fund the work have seen the order and accepted it.

questions.prompt: A regional credit union wants to cut average loan approval time from six days to two days this year. Its portfolio team has four candidates, each mapped to that goal. Step 1: list the candidates and the goal each serves. The shared document store holds all applicant files in one place. The automated income-check rules engine decides approvals from those files. The mobile photo upload lets applicants send pay stubs from their phones. The staff refresher trains branch staff on the new forms. Step 2: map dependencies. The rules engine needs files in the document store, and the mobile upload also writes to that store. The staff refresher depends on neither. Step 3: [missing; the learner must supply this step]. Step 4: check alignment. The rules engine cuts approval time directly, while the mobile upload and the refresher support the goal indirectly, so they rank lower if capacity is tight. Step 5: review the order with the lending head and the risk officer and record their agreement. Which Step 3 completes the worked example correctly?
choices: Start the document store first, then the rules engine and the mobile upload after it, with the staff refresher running in parallel because it has no dependency.
Build the rules engine first, since it is the most aligned item, and connect it to the document store once that store is ready.
Sequence the items by which sponsor asked for them first, so the mobile upload goes first because the applicant asked loudest.
Start all four items at the same time so no team waits, and fix the links between them when they reach integration.
questions.why: Sequencing must follow dependencies: the store has to exist before the rules engine and mobile upload can use it, and the refresher has no blocker so it can run alongside.

questions.prompt: A city water utility has two candidate projects. Project A installs pressure sensors that flag leaks in the pipe network. Project B replaces the customer billing portal. The utility's named goal for the year is to cut non-revenue water loss from 22 percent to 15 percent. Which justification best ties a roadmap decision to that goal?
choices: Both projects should be funded equally so that neither sponsor feels overlooked by the roadmap.
Project B should go first because it will finish sooner and make the roadmap look more complete by mid-year.
Project B should go first because customers have complained about the billing portal for three years.
Project A should go first because its sensors target the water loss the goal names, and Project B has no measured link to that loss figure.
questions.why: A decision is strategically justified when it traces to the named goal; only the sensors act directly on the measured water loss, so that is the defensible reason to rank Project A higher.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's roadmap shows a route-optimization tool that needs a live GPS feed from the trucks. The GPS feed project is scheduled to finish eight months after the tool build starts, because the two were sorted by which executive pushed harder. What is the most likely consequence for a running delivery system?
choices: The tool is automatically connected to a substitute feed with no added cost or risk.
The roadmap becomes more aligned with strategy because the executive's priority was honored.
The tool team sits idle or builds against no real data, and budget is spent on a tool that cannot yet produce usable routes.
The tool team finishes early and the GPS feed is then built faster to catch up.
questions.why: Ignoring a dependency means the dependent item waits or is built on nothing usable, which wastes budget and delays the benefit the goal needs.

questions.prompt: A hospital network is building its portfolio roadmap for a patient-scheduling upgrade. The team wants the roadmap to be trustworthy before funds are released. Which combination of features best meets that standard?
choices: Each row lists a start date and an owner, with the dependencies recorded in a separate file for the delivery team only.
The roadmap covers five years in monthly detail so that leaders can see every possible future change at once.
Each row names the goal it serves and its blockers, and the funding stakeholders have seen the order and accepted it.
The roadmap is approved by the project manager alone, since the manager is accountable for delivery.
questions.why: A roadmap is trustworthy when every row traces to a goal and shows its blockers, and the stakeholders who fund the work have accepted the order.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would build a high-level portfolio roadmap with key stakeholders, showing where sequencing and dependencies fit in and how each item links to a strategic goal. Name one limit or tradeoff of the roadmap you produce.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing the candidate portfolio components and writing next to each the specific organizational goal it serves, so that every row is traceable to strategy. Then I would map dependencies: which items need data, approvals or outputs from others before they can start or finish. I would sequence the items around those dependencies and available capacity, placing items with no blockers in parallel. Next I would walk the draft through with the key stakeholders, such as the sponsor who funds the work and the owners who deliver it, and record where they agree or push back. One limit is that the roadmap is a high-level forecast, not a commitment to dates. Dependencies and priorities shift as goals change, so the sequence must be reviewed at each governance cycle. Another tradeoff is that a stakeholder-agreed order can favor politically strong items over the best strategic fit, so I would flag any row where the goal link is weak.
rubricPoints: Each roadmap item is tied to a specific named strategic goal, not a generic alignment claim.
Dependencies are identified and used to drive the sequence of items.
Key stakeholders review and agree the order, and their input is recorded.
Names a limit such as the roadmap being a forecast that must be revisited as goals or priorities change.

suggested.rationale: Building a roadmap under competing stakeholder priorities is best practised by reasoning through a realistic exam-style scenario, and no listed mission or planned engine covers portfolio planning.

lessons.plain: A governance model is the agreed setup for who makes which decisions about a group of projects, how those decisions get made, and what rules they follow. Think of a city council: some bodies meet regularly to set direction, others approve specific spending, and everyone knows which body has the final say on what. In portfolio management, the model defines the committees and boards, the written policies they apply, who has the authority to approve or stop work, and who is responsible for preparing and carrying out each decision. Without it, every decision becomes a debate about who is allowed to make it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has ten projects competing for one shared budget, and two senior managers each believe they should approve the final funding list. What must be settled first, before anyone debates which projects are most valuable?
lessons.teach:
Start with the core terms. A portfolio is a group of projects, programs and related work managed together so that money and people are spent on the right things. A governance model is the designed setup that controls how decisions about that portfolio are made. It has four parts. Structure is the set of bodies that meet to decide. A steering committee gives direction and resolves conflicts for a defined body of work. A governance board, sometimes called a portfolio board, usually holds formal approval authority over funding and major changes. Policies are written rules that say what must happen, such as 'any project above a set budget needs board approval'. Decision rights state who is allowed to approve, reject or change a specific kind of decision. Responsibilities state who prepares the information, who carries out the decision and who must be consulted.

Why it works: a decision is final when the body allowed to make it has seen the right information under a rule everyone accepted in advance. That ends repeated arguments about authority.

Worked example: a team asks to add a 1.5 million dollar project. Step 1: the policy says requests over 1 million dollars go to the governance board. Step 2: the project manager prepares the business case, which is their responsibility. Step 3: the portfolio office checks the case against the policy and schedules it for the next board meeting. Step 4: the board holds the decision right and approves or rejects it. The steering committee is not the decision-maker here, because its rights cover direction for its own program only.

Common mistake: forming a committee and calling it governance without writing down what it may decide. Members then discuss at length, nothing is clearly approved, or each member assumes someone else will decide.

Consequence: in a running portfolio, unclear decision rights mean work starts without funding, or one manager quietly blocks every change. Written decision rights are what keep the portfolio moving.

questions.prompt: A city transport agency runs a depot software programme with its own steering committee. Its written policy says any single change under 400,000 euros is decided by that programme's steering committee, and any change at or above 400,000 euros goes to the portfolio governance board. A depot analyst requests a 250,000 euro change and prepares the costing, which is the analyst's responsibility. Step 1: the policy places a 250,000 euro change under the depot steering committee. Step 2: the analyst prepares the costing. Step 3: ___. Which completion correctly finishes the chain?
choices: The analyst approves it, because they prepared the costing and hold the responsibility for it.
The depot steering committee approves or rejects it, because its decision right covers changes under the threshold for its own programme.
The portfolio office approves it after checking the costing, because the office is the decision-maker for small changes.
The portfolio governance board approves it at its next meeting, since all funding decisions go there.
questions.why: Under the threshold the decision right sits with the depot steering committee for its own programme, while preparing the costing and checking it are responsibilities, not approvals.

questions.prompt: A written rule states that any vendor contract above 50,000 dollars needs a second review before signing. In governance terms, this rule is best described as:
choices: A steering committee, because it gives direction for vendor work.
A decision right, because it names who may approve vendor contracts.
A policy, because it is a written rule saying what must happen.
A responsibility, because it says who prepares the contract paperwork.
questions.why: A policy is a written rule stating what must happen, and this rule does exactly that without assigning an approver or creating a body.

questions.prompt: A regional bank's portfolio has a steering committee that meets every two weeks and discusses a proposed mobile-banking feature at length. Nothing is recorded as approved, and two members each say the other should decide. What is the most likely underlying cause?
choices: Nobody has written down which body may approve this kind of decision, so authority is unclear.
The committee has too few members to reach a quorum on a feature of this size.
The feature's cost is too low to need any approval at all.
The bank has no written policy telling the team how to submit requests.
questions.why: A committee that discusses without written decision rights cannot tell which body is allowed to approve, so members defer to each other and nothing is decided.

questions.prompt: A data-cleanup project of 300,000 dollars has been approved by the governance board, and the approval names a delivery manager. Who holds the responsibility to carry out the work, and who holds the decision right over any later change to its budget?
choices: The board holds both, since approval and execution cannot be separated.
The delivery manager holds both, since the board's approval passed all authority down to them.
The steering committee carries out the work, and the delivery manager approves budget changes.
The delivery manager carries out the work, and the board keeps the decision right over major budget changes.
questions.why: Responsibilities say who carries out work, while decision rights say who may approve changes, and here the delivery manager executes while the board keeps the budget-change right.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a new teammate the difference between a steering committee and a governance board, and name one limit of a governance model that is too rigid.
lessons.modelAnswer: A steering committee sets direction and resolves conflicts for a defined body of work; it guides and advises. A governance board holds formal approval authority over portfolio-level decisions such as funding and major changes, and the policies say which decisions must reach it. The key idea is decision rights: the board decides, the committee steers, and the policy states the threshold that routes a request to each. A limit of a rigid model is that every small change waits for a formal meeting, which slows delivery and pushes people to work around the process. Governance should be proportionate: high-value decisions go to the board, while routine ones are delegated to managers within set limits. The model also needs periodic review, because the policies drift away from reality as the portfolio changes.
rubricPoints: Steering committees provide direction and resolve conflicts for a defined body of work
Governance boards hold formal approval authority over portfolio-level decisions like funding
Decision rights and thresholds in written policy determine which body decides
A rigid model slows delivery and encourages workarounds, so decisions should be proportionate

suggested.rationale: Naming the right governance mechanism for a decision point is exam-style reasoning, and no current mission or planned engine covers governance structures directly.

lessons.plain: A portfolio is the set of projects and programs an organization runs together. Portfolio management standards are the written rules for how that set is handled: how work is described, how it is scored, how decisions are recorded, and who signs off on what. Protocols are the step-by-step routines that carry those rules out. This objective is about building that rulebook from two sources: what your organization already has, such as past templates and lessons, and widely recognized outside practices. The goal is standards that fit your organization rather than a generic copy.
lessons.guessPrompt: Three teams in your organization score and approve projects in three different ways, so the steering committee cannot compare them. What would you establish first, and where would you look for rules to base it on?
lessons.teach:
Start with the definitions. Organizational process assets (OPAs) are what your organization already owns and can reuse: policies, templates, past decision records, lessons learned, and historical data on how earlier projects performed. Enterprise environmental factors (EEFs) are conditions you did not create but must work within, such as regulatory rules, risk appetite, culture, and existing tools. Industry standards are published frameworks and practice guides from outside bodies. You borrow the parts that fit rather than adopting them whole. Tailoring means adjusting any of these to the size and risk of your portfolio.

Why it works: standards give every proposal the same shape, so the governance body can compare and decide on like-for-like information. Protocols are the repeatable routines that carry the standards out, such as a monthly scoring cycle and the place where decisions get recorded.

Worked example. A company runs 40 projects with no common scoring. Step 1: review OPAs and find an old scoring template plus notes from three failed projects that skipped risk review. Step 2: check EEFs; a regulator requires an audit trail for spend above a set amount. Step 3: take a benefit-scoring approach from an industry standard and trim it to five criteria. Step 4: write the standard: every proposal uses the five criteria, and any project above the spend threshold gets a risk review before the steering committee sees it. Step 5: write the protocol: a monthly scoring cycle, with each decision logged by the portfolio office.

Common mistake: copying an outside framework wholesale, which ignores your actual conditions, or inventing new rules and discarding existing templates that already work.

Consequence: if standards are not written down and applied the same way, the steering committee compares unlike proposals each month, and the portfolio's priorities quietly drift.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital network runs 12 improvement projects with no shared approval format. The portfolio lead works through the standard in this order. Step 1: she reviews organizational process assets (OPAs), meaning the organization's own reusable material such as templates, policies, and past decision records, and finds an old funding request form plus a log showing two projects were approved with no cost-benefit figure. Step 2: she checks enterprise environmental factors (EEFs), meaning conditions the organization did not create but must work within, and finds that the board caps any single project at a fixed share of the annual capital budget. Step 3: she takes a four-criterion scoring approach from a published industry practice guide and trims it to fit the network's size. Step 4: she writes the standard: every proposal uses the four criteria, and any project above the board's cap gets a formal financial review before the steering committee sees it. Step 5 is missing and is the one you must supply: the protocol that carries the standard out and records each decision. Which completion correctly supplies Step 5?
choices: Run a quarterly scoring cycle where the portfolio office logs each approval or rejection decision in one shared record.
Let the steering committee score each proposal informally at whichever meeting it happens to be discussed.
Adopt the industry guide's full framework unchanged so the network does not have to write any new rules of its own.
Delete the old funding request form so every project starts from a clean template with no inherited assumptions.
questions.why: A protocol is a repeatable routine that carries the standard out, and here that means a scheduled scoring cycle with each decision logged by the portfolio office, which is the pattern the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: A project manager lists her team's lessons-learned register, a regulator's audit-trail requirement, and a published practice guide. Which one is an organizational process asset (OPA) as the teaching text defines the term?
choices: The published practice guide that the team may borrow parts from.
The regulator's requirement that spend above a set amount has an audit trail.
The organization's appetite for risk, which sets how much uncertainty leaders accept.
The lessons-learned register holding records of how earlier projects went.
questions.why: OPAs are assets the organization already owns and can reuse, such as lessons learned and past records, whereas the regulator's rule is an environmental factor and the practice guide is an outside industry standard.

questions.prompt: A portfolio office at a logistics firm adopts an outside framework word for word, without changing its criteria to match the firm's budget size or approval rules. What is the main risk the teaching text identifies for this choice?
choices: The framework becomes illegal once it is copied into the firm's own documents.
The framework ignores the firm's actual conditions, so its criteria may not fit how the firm works.
The firm loses its existing templates, which are the only record of past decisions.
The steering committee is forced to meet more often than the firm's governance calendar allows.
questions.why: The teaching text names copying an outside framework wholesale as a common mistake because it ignores the organization's real conditions, and tailoring is the remedy.

questions.prompt: A portfolio office has 25 active projects, and each month the sponsors submit proposals using different criteria and different formats. The steering committee still has to decide which proposals to fund. What is the consequence the teaching text warns about if the standards are not written down and applied the same way?
choices: The committee rejects every proposal, because each one fails a single shared checklist.
The portfolio office stops logging decisions, so the regulator has no audit trail to review.
The projects finish faster, because sponsors stop spending time on formal documentation.
The committee compares unlike proposals each month, and the portfolio's priorities drift without anyone noticing.
questions.why: Without a common shape, the committee compares unlike information each cycle, and the teaching text says the portfolio's priorities quietly drift as a result.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would turn an organization's existing assets and outside industry standards into portfolio standards and protocols, and name one limit or tradeoff you would watch for.
