lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by inventorying what we already have: past templates, policies, decision logs, and lessons from projects that went well or badly. Those are our organizational process assets, and they show us what has worked here. Next I would check the enterprise environmental factors, the outside conditions we must follow, such as regulatory audit requirements or our stated risk appetite. Then I would look at published industry standards and borrow only the pieces that match our size and risk, which is tailoring. I would write the standard as the rule, for example one scoring model for every proposal, and the protocol as the routine, such as a monthly scoring cycle with logged decisions. The tradeoff I would watch is over-tailoring: if we adjust the standard so much that it no longer matches the outside practice we claim to follow, auditors and new hires will struggle to trust it.
rubricPoints: Identifies organizational process assets such as templates, policies, and lessons learned as a starting source
Identifies enterprise environmental factors such as regulation and risk appetite as constraints on the standards
Explains that industry standards are adopted selectively and adjusted through tailoring
Distinguishes a standard (the rule) from a protocol (the repeatable routine that applies it)

suggested.rationale: Deciding which organizational assets and outside standards to build from is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style situation rather than through a single mission.

lessons.plain: A portfolio is the set of projects and programs an organization funds to reach its goals. The processes around it are the repeatable ways that set is managed: how promised benefits are tracked, how information is collected and shared, how risks are handled, how stakeholders stay involved, and how people adjust when things change. Defining a process means writing down how one of these works for the first time. Modifying it means changing that written way because the old one no longer fits. This objective is about deciding which process to set up or adjust, and making sure the change goes through the governance structure rather than being made quietly by one person.
lessons.guessPrompt: A portfolio keeps learning about project problems only after the budget is spent. Which of the five process areas would you change first, and why would changing it help more than adding extra status meetings?
lessons.teach:
Five process areas are in scope. Benefits realization is checking, after delivery, that the value a project promised actually appears. Information management is deciding what data is collected, who owns it, where it is kept, and how often it is reviewed. The risk process is how risks are identified, scored, assigned an owner, and escalated when they pass a limit. Stakeholder engagement is how affected people are identified, what they need to know, and how their input is gathered. Change management is how new or altered ways of working are introduced to people and kept in place.

These processes matter because they turn memory and personal judgment into shared rules. The governance body can only see whether the portfolio is delivering what it promised if the measurement rules are written down and followed.

Worked example: three digital projects have shipped, but quarterly reports show no rise in customer retention. Step 1: the benefits process has no measurement after go-live, so nobody is tracking the benefit. Step 2: draft a change that gives each project a benefit owner, a retention measure, and a review six months after launch. Step 3: submit the change to the steering committee, which approves it because it alters who is accountable. Step 4: communicate the new step to sponsors and set a rollout date.

Common mistake: treating process definition as paperwork. A procedure that nobody follows, or one changed informally without approval, makes the documented process and the real one drift apart.

Consequence: if the risk process is changed without updating escalation thresholds, risks that cross a limit may never reach the committee, and decisions get made on stale information. A process change is only complete when the approval and the thresholds move together.

questions.prompt: A regional transit agency runs four rail-upgrade projects. Its risk process scores each risk for likelihood and impact on a 5-by-5 grid, where score equals likelihood times impact. The portfolio rule is that any risk scoring 15 or more goes to the portfolio steering committee. Worked trace: Step 1: the signalling project lead scores a new risk at likelihood 4 and impact 5, a total of 20. Step 2: the risk is assigned to the signalling workstream lead as its owner. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the committee decides whether to fund a mitigation and records that decision in the risk register. Which completes Step 3?
choices: The project lead updates the risk register and waits for the next quarterly review before any escalation is considered.
The risk is closed once an owner is named, because ownership transfers accountability away from the portfolio.
The score is halved because the risk sits in one project rather than across the whole portfolio, so it stays below the limit.
Because 20 is above the threshold of 15, the risk is escalated to the steering committee for review.
questions.why: The escalation threshold of 15 is applied to the scored risk, and a score of 20 crosses it, so the risk must go to the steering committee.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits change management as a portfolio process?
choices: Measuring whether a project's promised value shows up in the figures after go-live.
Introducing new or altered ways of working to people and keeping them in place once adopted.
Identifying the people a portfolio affects, what they need to know, and how their input is gathered.
Deciding which data is collected, who owns it, where it is stored, and how often it is reviewed.
questions.why: Change management covers how new or altered ways of working are introduced to people and sustained, which is the fourth option in the teaching text's own terms.

questions.prompt: A retail bank's portfolio office quietly moved its benefit reviews from six months after launch to twelve months, without taking the change to its governance committee. What is the most direct risk this creates?
choices: The documented benefits process and the real practice drift apart, so the committee cannot rely on what it is shown.
The bank must pay a fee to the external auditor because the review interval was lengthened.
Project sponsors automatically lose their accountability for the benefits their projects promised.
The committee gets too many benefit reports and cannot decide which to read first.
questions.why: An informal change that bypasses approval makes the written process and the real one diverge, so the governance body loses a reliable view of delivery.

questions.prompt: A hospital-supply company is setting up its portfolio information management. Which decision is most clearly an information management decision rather than a stakeholder or risk decision?
choices: Deciding which clinic managers must be consulted before a new ordering system changes their daily work.
Deciding which order-volume data is collected each month, who owns that data, where it is kept, and how often it is reviewed.
Deciding that each supplier-integration project must name a risk owner who reports to the steering committee.
Deciding that any risk scoring above a set limit must be escalated to the committee within five working days.
questions.why: Information management covers what data is collected, who owns it, where it is kept, and how often it is reviewed, which is the choice about order-volume data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a portfolio process needs to be defined from scratch or modified, and name one limit or tradeoff of changing a process in the middle of a reporting cycle.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking whether a process exists at all. If a benefit, risk, or information step has never been written down, we define it. If it exists but no longer fits, for example because projects now span more business units or the escalation limits are missed, we modify it. Either way the change goes to the governance body that owns the process, usually the steering committee, for approval. The main tradeoff of changing a process mid-cycle is comparability. If the risk scoring method changes halfway through a quarter, the scores before and after cannot be compared directly, so the committee may misread a trend. My practice would be to record the change date, restate the affected figures under the new rule where possible, and only switch at a reporting boundary unless the current process is causing real harm.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes defining a process that does not yet exist from modifying one that no longer fits
Names the governance body that approves the change, such as the steering committee
Identifies a concrete limit or tradeoff, such as losing comparability of data across a mid-cycle change
Suggests a practical safeguard, such as switching at a reporting boundary or restating figures

suggested.rationale: Choosing which process to define or change and naming the approving body is best practiced by reasoning through exam-style portfolio situations rather than by memorizing definitions.

lessons.plain: A portfolio management plan is the written rulebook for how an organization runs its whole collection of projects as one group. It answers practical questions before trouble starts: who decides what, who must be told when something goes wrong, how much uncertainty the organization accepts, which measured values trigger a higher-level review, and how competing requests are ranked when money or people are short. Think of it as the house rules for a shared kitchen: everyone can cook, but everyone knows who owns the stove, when to call the manager, and what to do when supplies run low. A good plan is short enough that people read it and specific enough that two people facing the same decision reach the same answer.
lessons.guessPrompt: A portfolio has five projects sharing one budget, and one project team wants to spend more than its allocation. Before reading further, what would you expect a well-designed plan to say should happen, and who should decide?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A portfolio is the set of projects, programs and ongoing work that an organization groups together so it can be steered as a whole. A portfolio management plan is the document that sets the rules for running that set. It covers five elements named in this objective. Roles name who does what and who holds decision rights. Escalation procedures describe how a problem moves upward, to whom, and within what time. Risk tolerance is the amount of uncertainty the organization accepts across the portfolio, stated in plain terms. Thresholds are measurable trigger values, such as a budget overrun percentage or a schedule slip in days, that cause a defined action. A prioritization model is the agreed method for ranking candidate work, usually by weighing expected value against risk and cost.

Why it works: the plan turns judgment calls into repeatable ones. When a threshold is crossed, nobody has to debate whether this case is serious enough, because the rule already answered that.

Worked example. A portfolio has three projects and a shared budget of 1,000 units. The plan sets a threshold: any project forecast to exceed its budget by more than 10 percent is escalated to the steering committee. Project B forecasts 12 percent over. Step 1: the threshold is 10 percent and the forecast is 12 percent, so the trigger fires. Step 2: the escalation route says the project manager informs the portfolio office within two working days. Step 3: the steering committee chooses among funding the overrun from contingency, cutting scope, or stopping the project, and records the decision.

Common mistake: writing thresholds as adjectives such as significant or major. Those words cannot fire an action, so every overrun becomes a fresh debate.

Consequence: without a clear threshold and route, an overrun can sit unseen inside one team until it has consumed the shared contingency that other projects depended on.

questions.prompt: A regional clinic network sets a portfolio threshold: any project forecast to exceed its budget by more than 5 percent is sent to the network's portfolio board. The imaging upgrade has a 600,000 budget and is forecast to finish 6.5 percent over. Step 1: 6.5 is greater than 5, so the trigger fires. Step 2: the project manager informs the portfolio office within three working days. Step 3 is missing. Which choice correctly completes the process?
choices: The project manager absorbs the overrun in the next monthly report without telling the board, since 6.5 percent is a small amount.
The board decides how to handle the overrun, such as funding it from contingency, cutting scope, or stopping the project, and records that decision.
The portfolio office raises the threshold to 10 percent so that the case no longer fires.
The board waits until the project reaches 15 percent over before deciding, because acting early is premature.
questions.why: Once a threshold fires and the route has informed the portfolio office, the governing body makes and records the decision, which is the step the plan exists to trigger.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches a threshold as the term is used in a portfolio management plan?
choices: The agreed method for ranking candidate work by weighing expected value against risk and cost.
A measurable trigger value, such as a percentage overrun or a number of days late, that causes a defined action when crossed.
A named person or group that holds the right to approve a particular kind of decision.
A written statement of how much uncertainty the organization is willing to accept across its portfolio.
questions.why: A threshold is defined in the text as a measurable trigger value that causes a defined action, which is the only option matching that definition.

questions.prompt: A portfolio plan says: escalate any significant cost problem to the director. What is the main weakness of this wording?
choices: The word significant cannot be tested against a number, so it cannot fire an action, and every case becomes a fresh debate.
A director can judge significance better than any fixed rule, so the wording is actually sound.
The plan omits the currency unit, which is the only real defect in the sentence.
Directors should never receive cost escalations, because the project manager alone owns the budget.
questions.why: The teaching text identifies adjectives like significant as unable to trigger an action, which is exactly the failure described in the first option.

questions.prompt: A portfolio plan states that only the steering committee may approve any funding increase above a set amount for a project. Which element of the portfolio management plan does this sentence define?
choices: Risk tolerance
Roles
Prioritization model
Thresholds
questions.why: Naming who holds decision rights over a specific approval is the job of the roles element, not the threshold figure, the ranking method, or the uncertainty statement.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a portfolio management plan must contain and why a numeric threshold is more useful than a vague one. Name one limit or tradeoff of having a rigid threshold.
lessons.modelAnswer: A portfolio management plan is the shared rulebook for the whole set of projects. It names roles and decision rights, the escalation path for problems, the risk tolerance the organization accepts, numeric thresholds that trigger action, and the model used to rank competing work. A numeric threshold is more useful than a vague one because it can be applied without debate. The rule more than 10 percent over budget goes to the steering committee fires the same way for everyone, while a significant overrun gets argued case by case. The tradeoff is rigidity. A fixed threshold can escalate a small, harmless change, or miss a dangerous one that stays just under the line. So the plan should review its thresholds at each governance cycle and allow the committee to override one with a recorded reason.
rubricPoints: Lists the core parts of the plan: roles, escalation procedures, risk tolerances, thresholds and a prioritization model
Explains that a numeric threshold triggers action consistently, unlike a vague word
Names a real limit of rigid thresholds, such as false alarms or missed near-threshold risks
Notes that thresholds should be reviewed and overridable with a recorded reason

suggested.rationale: The core skill here is explaining what a portfolio plan contains and the tradeoffs of its thresholds, which no listed mission or planned engine currently practices.

lessons.plain: A portfolio is the set of projects, programs and other work an organization chooses to fund together so it can reach its goals. Every so often someone has to decide something about that set: which pieces to start, how much money to put behind them, what order to deliver them in, or what the overall plan looks like. This objective is about making those calls and getting them approved through the rules the organization already agreed on, such as which group signs off, how big a decision must be before it moves up a level, and who is allowed to say yes. Instead of asking for a generic sign-off, you name the exact forum and rule that applies.
lessons.guessPrompt: A portfolio team wants to move 2 million of unspent budget from a project that is behind schedule to a new project nobody has funded yet. Who do you think should approve that move, and why would a project manager not simply make the change alone?
lessons.teach:
Key terms first. A portfolio is the group of projects, programs and operational work that an organization funds and manages together. A component is one item inside that group, such as a single project or program. A governance model is the agreed set of bodies, rules and responsibilities that decide what happens to the portfolio. Decision rights are the written answer to who is allowed to decide what. A steering committee is a standing group of senior leaders that approves portfolio-level decisions. An escalation threshold is a measurable limit, such as a cost overrun above a set percentage, that tells you a decision has to move up to a higher body. A roadmap is a time-ordered plan of planned deliveries.

Why it works: the governance model separates routine calls that a portfolio manager can make from calls that need a wider group. Without that separation, either everything waits for committee time, or one person quietly reshapes the portfolio on their own, and nobody can later explain why money moved.

Worked example. A component is 15 percent over its approved budget. Step 1: compare the overrun against the threshold in the governance model, say 10 percent. Step 2: the threshold is crossed, so the decision leaves the portfolio manager's authority. Step 3: prepare a decision paper with the revised cost, the impact on the business case and two options. Step 4: send it to the steering committee named in the decision rights table, and record the approval or rejection with a date.

Common mistake: treating approval as a conversation in a hallway. A verbal yes from one sponsor is not the approval the model requires, and the change can be challenged and reversed later.

Consequence: if a roadmap or budget change is made without the required approval, teams start work the portfolio never funded, and the budget reports stop matching reality. Approval through the defined model is what makes a portfolio decision real.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm governs its portfolio with a rule that any roadmap delivery slipping more than 3 months must go to its portfolio review board. Its warehouse-automation component's go-live moves from March to August, a 5-month slip. Step 1: compare the slip (5 months) with the threshold (3 months). Step 2: the threshold is crossed, so the change leaves the portfolio manager's authority. Step 3 is left blank. Step 4: the board named in the decision rights table reviews the change, and the outcome is recorded with a date. Which action correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Wait for the next scheduled board meeting before preparing any paperwork
Update the roadmap in the planning tool and notify the warehouse teams of the new date
Write a decision paper with the revised go-live date, the dependent components and two options
Get a verbal go-ahead from the sponsor and tell the board at its next meeting
questions.why: Once a threshold is crossed, the required step is to prepare a decision paper that gives the board the revised date, the impact and options, so the board can decide on evidence.

questions.prompt: In a portfolio governance model, what is an escalation threshold?
choices: The minimum number of steering committee members needed to hold a quorum
A measurable limit, such as a cost overrun above a set percentage, that tells you a decision must move to a higher body
The date by which a roadmap must be published to the wider organization
A written list of which individuals are allowed to approve each type of spending
questions.why: The teaching text defines an escalation threshold as a measurable limit that signals a decision has to move up to a higher body.

questions.prompt: A portfolio manager at a retail firm finds that a component is 6 percent over its approved budget. The governance model sets the escalation threshold at 10 percent. What is the correct handling?
choices: Stop the component until a sponsor signs a written statement accepting the overrun
Ask the sponsor for a verbal yes and treat that as the approval the model requires
Send the change to the steering committee because any overrun needs committee approval
Treat it as a routine call within the portfolio manager's authority and record the decision
questions.why: Since 6 percent is below the 10 percent threshold, the decision stays with the portfolio manager, and the choice to record it is the one that keeps the budget reports accurate.

questions.prompt: A sponsor in a public-sector agency gives a verbal yes in a corridor to a budget increase for one component. The team starts the extra work the same afternoon, and no decision paper or committee record exists. What is the main problem?
choices: The sponsor lacked the seniority to speak for the portfolio at all
The team should have waited for the next annual planning cycle before starting any extra work
The increase is too small to need any formal record under most governance models
The change lacks the approval the governance model requires, so it can be challenged and reversed and the budget reports may stop matching reality
questions.why: A verbal yes from one sponsor does not satisfy the defined approval route, which leaves the funding change open to challenge and divergence from reported budgets.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that once a steering committee has agreed to a budget change in principle, the project manager can go ahead and start spending. Explain to them how a portfolio decision should really be made and obtained, naming one limit or tradeoff of relying on the committee.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would tell them an in-principle agreement is not a formal approval. The governance model defines the forum, the decision right and the recorded outcome, and the change is valid only when that record exists. First I would check whether the amount crosses an escalation threshold, because that decides whether the committee must decide at all or the portfolio manager can. If it must go up, I would bring a decision paper with the cost impact, the change to expected benefits and the options, then wait for the minuted approval. The tradeoff is real: a committee gate adds delay, so for urgent items the model should define an expedite path, such as a time-boxed emergency decision by a named chair, rather than letting people skip the gate. Otherwise the spend is unfunded and the reports will be wrong.
rubricPoints: Names the governance body or decision right that owns the decision.
Checks the decision against an escalation threshold before acting.
Requires a recorded approval, not a verbal or in-principle agreement.
Notes the tradeoff of delay and any defined expedite path.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a realistic approval situation adds the most here, and no current mission or planned engine covers portfolio governance directly.

lessons.plain: Authorizing portfolio structure means formally approving which work an organization will fund and run as part of its portfolio. Activating means releasing those approved pieces so teams can start spending money and staff time on them. Think of a building company: before crews start a new house, someone checks the approved plan, the budget, and the permit, then gives the go-ahead. In portfolio management, the supporting artifacts are the documents that show why the work exists and who agreed to it, such as the business case, the funding approval, and the roadmap entry. The skill is checking that each component has the right paperwork before activation, and holding back any component whose paperwork is missing or out of date.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has started work on a new initiative that appears in a status spreadsheet, but nobody can find a signed business case or a funding approval for it. Should the portfolio manager treat it as authorized, and why?
lessons.teach:
A portfolio is the set of programs and projects an organization runs together to reach its strategic goals. Each item in that set is a component. Authorization is the formal decision, made by people with the right authority, that a component may belong to the portfolio and may receive funds and people. Activation is the step that actually releases the component to start consuming those resources. The two are kept separate on purpose: a decision on record comes first, and activation follows only when that decision is backed by evidence.

The evidence is the set of supporting artifacts. The business case explains the expected benefit and cost. The funding approval names the budget and its source. The roadmap entry places the component in time next to other work. The governance approval record shows who decided and when. These artifacts work because they let anyone later trace why a component exists and whether it still deserves its resources, and they catch work that began on a verbal promise.

Worked example. A proposal for a fleet-tracking upgrade arrives. Step one: the portfolio manager reads the business case and confirms its benefit links to a stated strategic objective. Step two: she checks that the funding approval matches the amount requested. Step three: she checks the roadmap so the upgrade does not overload the same staff at the same time. Step four: she records the approval with the decision-maker's name and date, and only then releases activation. If step two fails because the approved amount is lower than the request, activation waits until the funding is corrected.

Common mistake: treating a status report or a kickoff meeting as authorization. A component that appears in a tracker has not necessarily been approved.

Consequence: unauthorized components consume shared people and money and distort the portfolio totals, so reported performance no longer matches what the organization actually funds.

questions.prompt: A city library system proposes a self-checkout expansion to reduce queues at its three busiest branches. The portfolio coordinator works through the proposal. Step one: the business case shows the expansion supports the stated objective of improving service access, so the benefit link is confirmed. Step two: the funding approval is for 85,000 and the request is also 85,000, so the amounts match. Step three: the roadmap shows the expansion would fall in the same quarter as a catalog migration that uses the same two staff members, so the coordinator moves the expansion to the following year. Step four is missing from this account. After step three, what must happen before activation is released?
choices: Activation begins at once, because the business case already proves the benefit.
The approval is recorded with the decision-maker's name and date, then activation is released.
A status update is sent to the steering group so they know the expansion is underway.
The hardware vendor is asked to start installation so the revised schedule can be met.
questions.why: Authorization is only complete when the decision is on record with who made it and when, and activation follows that record, so recording the approval is the required step before release.

questions.prompt: In portfolio terms, what is the difference between authorization and activation?
choices: Activation is the monthly review of a running component, while authorization is the initial kickoff meeting.
Authorization is the formal decision that a component may receive funds and people, and activation is the step that releases it to consume them.
Authorization and activation are two names for the same decision, recorded in different systems.
Authorization releases a component to start using resources, and activation is the earlier paperwork that approves it.
questions.why: Authorization is the decision on record that a component may belong to the portfolio and receive resources, and activation is the later release that lets it actually start consuming them.

questions.prompt: A component shows up on the program tracker after a kickoff meeting. Staff have started booking time and a team has drawn budget, but no funding approval or governance approval record exists. What is the most likely consequence for the portfolio?
choices: Nothing changes until the annual audit, when the missing paperwork is discovered.
The component consumes shared people and money without authorization, so reported totals stop matching what is actually funded.
The portfolio's reported totals become more accurate, because the tracker shows the component.
The component is safe to continue, since a kickoff meeting counts as an informal approval.
questions.why: A component that appears in a tracker without a decision on record is consuming shared resources unauthorized, which distorts portfolio totals and makes reported performance unreliable.

questions.prompt: A proposed training platform has a business case that links it to a strategic objective and a funding approval that matches the request. However, the governance record does not name who made the decision or when. Should activation be released now?
choices: Yes, but only if the sponsor confirms by email that they supported the idea.
No, the whole proposal must be restarted from the business case.
Yes, because the business case and funding approval are enough evidence on their own.
No, activation waits until the decision is recorded with the decision-maker's name and date.
questions.why: The decision must be on record with who made it and when before activation, so the missing governance record blocks activation even though the other artifacts are present, and the fix is to complete that record rather than restart the proposal.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate new to portfolio work why a component should not be activated just because it appears in the tracker, and name one limit or tradeoff of waiting for complete artifacts before the team starts.
lessons.modelAnswer: A tracker entry only shows that someone wrote the work down. It does not show that the right decision-makers approved it, that money was set aside, or that it fits the roadmap. So before activation I check the business case against a strategic objective, the funding approval against the requested amount, and the decision record with its name and date. The tradeoff is real: waiting for complete artifacts can delay a time-sensitive piece of work and frustrate the team, and sometimes the sponsor is under pressure to start now. I would rather name that delay openly and escalate it to the sponsor for a decision than start unapproved work and create funding and staffing conflicts later.
rubricPoints: A tracker entry or status report is not evidence of authorization.
Authorization is a decision by people with authority; activation releases resources after that decision.
Specific artifacts such as business case, funding approval, roadmap entry, and decision record must be checked.
Names a real tradeoff, such as delay versus unapproved spending, and a way to handle it, such as escalation.
Connects unauthorized activation to distorted portfolio totals or resource conflicts.

suggested.rationale: Deciding whether a component is authorized from a messy set of artifacts is an exam-style judgment best practiced through a situation to reason through.

lessons.plain: Before a company can judge whether its group of projects is paying off, someone has to gather the numbers that matter from many places and put them together in one view. The portfolio governance model is the agreed rulebook that decides which numbers those are, how each one is measured, how often it is reported, and who is responsible for it. Collecting means pulling each agreed measure from its source, such as project status reports, finance records, or delivery tracking. Consolidating means combining those separate figures into one set that can be compared across the whole portfolio, so a manager can see the big picture without reading every project file. The job is to use the agreed measures, not whichever numbers happen to be easy to find.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you need one schedule number for a whole portfolio made of three projects of very different sizes, what would you compute, and why might a simple average of each project's schedule ratio mislead you?
lessons.teach:
A portfolio is the group of projects, programs and operations that an organization manages together to reach its strategic goals. The governance model is the agreed set of rules for how that portfolio is directed and checked. It names the performance metrics, the target values, the data sources, the reporting frequency and the owner of each measure. A metric is a measurement with a defined method, such as the percentage of planned benefits realized. A key performance indicator, or KPI, is a metric the governance model has singled out as a headline measure of success. Consolidation is the step of combining per-project figures into portfolio-level figures using the same definitions, so the results can be added or compared.

Why it works: the governance model fixes definitions in advance, so two projects reporting schedule performance mean the same thing. Without a shared definition, combining their numbers produces a figure that looks precise but says little.

Worked example. The governance model defines Schedule Performance as earned work divided by planned work to date, with a target of 0.95 or higher, collected monthly. Step 1: Project A has planned 40 and earned 36, so its ratio is 0.90. Step 2: Project B has planned 20 and earned 20, so its ratio is 1.00. Step 3: Project C has planned 50 and earned 40, so its ratio is 0.80. Step 4: Consolidate by summing the underlying figures, not the ratios. Total planned is 110 and total earned is 96, so the portfolio figure is 96 divided by 110, about 0.87.

Common mistake: averaging the three ratios gives 0.90, which looks close to target. That average gives the small projects the same weight as the large one.

Consequence: in a running portfolio, the averaged figure hides that the largest project is lagging. The team would wrongly report the portfolio as nearly on target and delay the escalation or resource reallocation that the governance model calls for. The correct consolidated figure of 0.87 falls below the 0.95 target and triggers that response.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital network's governance model defines Appointment Timeliness as clinic visits started on time divided by visits scheduled, with a target of 0.90 or higher, collected monthly. Clinic North has 30 scheduled visits and 27 started on time, a rate of 0.90. Clinic East has 12 scheduled and 9 on time, a rate of 0.75. Clinic South has 58 scheduled and 46 on time, a rate of about 0.79. Step 3, not shown, is the consolidation step: produce the network-level figure using the governance model's rule for combining per-clinic figures. What is the network-level Appointment Timeliness figure?
choices: 0.75, the lowest clinic rate, since it is the weakest point in the network
0.81, the average of the three clinic rates
0.82, the total on-time visits divided by the total scheduled visits
0.85, the rate for Clinic North plus the rate for Clinic South
questions.why: Consolidation combines the underlying counts (82 on time out of 100 scheduled) rather than averaging the ratios, so the network figure is 0.82.

questions.prompt: In a portfolio governance model, what distinguishes a key performance indicator (KPI) from an ordinary metric?
choices: A KPI is measured by a different method than other metrics, using a formula the owner chooses each month
A KPI is a metric the governance model has singled out as a headline measure of success
A KPI is a figure produced by adding per-project results together, while a metric is produced by a single project
A KPI is any metric whose target value is higher than 1.0
questions.why: A KPI is an ordinary metric with a defined method that the governance model has chosen as a headline measure of success; the other options describe features that are not what makes a KPI distinct.

questions.prompt: A portfolio of three product projects reports Cost Performance, defined by the governance model as earned value divided by actual cost. Alpha has earned 150 and actual cost 200, a ratio of 0.75. Beta has earned 10 and actual cost 10, a ratio of 1.00. Gamma has earned 60 and actual cost 90, a ratio of about 0.67. The target is 0.90 or higher. A manager proposes reporting the portfolio figure as the average of the three ratios, about 0.81. What is the best response?
choices: Consolidate by summing earned values and actual costs to get 220 divided by 300, about 0.73, which is below target and should trigger the governance escalation
Report 1.00 because Beta is the only project exactly on its cost baseline
Drop Gamma from the consolidated figure because it has the lowest ratio and is not representative
Report 0.81 because it is the most transparent summary of the three projects
questions.why: The consolidated figure must use summed underlying figures under the shared definition, so the averaged 0.81 is the misleading number, and the correct consolidated figure of about 0.73 is the one that should be compared to target and escalated.

questions.prompt: A city transit portfolio's governance model defines Ridership Benefit Realization as realized benefit points divided by planned benefit points to date, with a target of 0.85 or higher, collected quarterly. The consolidated figure for the portfolio is 0.68, and the largest project, which holds most of the planned benefit points, is the main contributor to the shortfall. What should the portfolio manager do according to the governance logic in the teaching text?
choices: Escalate the shortfall and consider reallocating resources toward the lagging largest project, since the consolidated figure is below the 0.85 target
Average the project ratios again next quarter to smooth out the largest project's results
Report the portfolio as nearly on target because the smaller projects are performing well
Wait for the next full year of data before acting, because quarterly figures are too noisy to trigger a response
questions.why: A consolidated figure below the governance target, driven by the largest lagging project, is the situation the governance model says should trigger escalation or a resource-reallocation decision.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why the governance model must define each metric, its method and its source before anyone starts collecting data, and name one limit of consolidated portfolio numbers that they should still question.
lessons.modelAnswer: The governance model has to fix each metric before collection because the consolidated figure is only as meaningful as the agreement behind the inputs. If one project counts completed work in story points and another counts it in hours, adding them produces a number that means nothing, and the portfolio view will mislead decision-makers. Defining the method, the source, the frequency and the owner up front lets us collect the same thing from every project and combine it correctly. The limit to keep in mind is that a consolidated number can hide a single project that is far off target. A portfolio average can look healthy while one large component is failing, so I would still check the per-project breakdown before deciding nothing needs escalating.
rubricPoints: The governance model defines metrics, methods, sources, frequency and owners before collection
Consolidation must use the same definitions across projects so the results are comparable
Consolidated figures should be built from underlying totals, not averages of ratios
A limit: a portfolio-level number can hide a lagging component, so review the breakdown

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining why consolidation depends on shared definitions and where it can mislead, which is best practiced by articulating it back.

lessons.plain: Portfolio monitoring means keeping a regular, steady watch over a group of projects and work items bundled together to reach shared business goals. Think of a ship's captain who checks speed, fuel and course every few hours rather than only when the ship hits a rock. The watch happens through three tools: reports that summarise status on a schedule, dashboards that show key numbers at a glance, and audits that check whether those numbers are true and the rules were followed. The point is to notice drift early, while there is still time to act.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your portfolio has four projects, and every monthly status report says they are on track. What would you check before you believed the reports, and why?
lessons.teach:
A portfolio is a set of projects, programs and operational work grouped so they can be managed together toward strategic goals. Portfolio performance is how well that whole group is delivering the value it was approved for. Monitoring means checking that performance on an ongoing basis, not just at the end. Three techniques carry most of the load. A report is a scheduled written summary of status against plan. A dashboard is a live or regularly refreshed view of a small set of key indicators, such as cost variance, schedule variance and benefits realised. An audit is an independent check that the figures are accurate and that governance rules, such as approval gates and reporting thresholds, were actually followed. Monitoring works because each technique catches a different failure: reports explain, dashboards alert, and audits verify.

Worked example. Suppose governance sets a rule that any component whose cost runs more than 10 percent over its baseline gets a formal review. The dashboard shows Project C at 14 percent over. Step one: confirm the threshold was crossed and the figure is correct. Step two: audit the source by comparing the dashboard number with the finance ledger, which reveals a contract was reclassified into Project C from another project. Step three: separate the true overrun from the accounting shift. Step four: if the overrun is real, take it to the governance body with a recommendation, such as pausing new spend on C and moving unallocated funds to a higher-value component.

Common mistake: treating a green dashboard as proof of health. Counting completed tasks or activity rather than outcomes and benefits can hide a component that is busy but not delivering value.

Consequence: when monitoring data is stale or unaudited, a failing component keeps drawing funds that could have been reallocated, and the decision is taken months later than it should have been.

questions.prompt: A regional bus operator runs a portfolio of four components. Governance rule: any component whose schedule runs more than 15 percent behind its approved baseline gets a formal review. The dashboard shows Component Q at 18 percent behind. Step 1: confirm the threshold was crossed and the figure is correct. Step 2: audit the source by comparing the dashboard against the scheduling tool's change log, which shows Q's baseline was moved in March with no governance sign-off. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: if the real delay is significant, take it to the governance body with a recommendation, such as pausing new spend on Q and reallocating its unused budget to a component that is on track. What belongs in step 3?
choices: Close Component Q immediately because it breached the 15 percent threshold, without further checks.
Report the 18 percent figure to the board unchanged and skip further checks, since the audit already found a problem.
Accept the new baseline as the plan of record, since the dashboard now shows Q as green.
Measure the slip against the original approved baseline so the real delay is separated from the unapproved re-baseline.
questions.why: Step 3 separates the true delay from the accounting effect of the unapproved baseline change, which requires measuring against the original approved baseline.

questions.prompt: A city transit authority wants an independent check that its component cost figures match the finance ledger and that its approval gates were followed. Which monitoring technique is designed for this purpose?
choices: A benefits register maintained by the component sponsors
A dashboard refreshed every hour with cost and schedule indicators
A scheduled written report summarising status against plan
An audit, which is an independent verification of figures and governance compliance
questions.why: An audit is the independent check that verifies figures are accurate and governance rules were followed, while dashboards alert and reports explain.

questions.prompt: A software firm's dashboard shows component Delta with 40 of 40 planned tasks closed and a green status. The benefit tracker shows that no customers have adopted the feature Delta was approved to deliver. What is the best monitoring response?
choices: Close the audit file, since the dashboard figures are accurate.
Ask the team to log more tasks so the dashboard reflects more activity.
Keep Delta green because all planned work is complete.
Flag Delta to governance as not delivering value, and judge it on the adoption outcome rather than task completion.
questions.why: Task completion measures activity, not outcomes, so a green status can hide a component that is busy but not delivering the benefit it was approved for.

questions.prompt: A portfolio manager at a hospital group must explain to the steering committee why a clinical software component has slipped three months behind its approved plan. Which technique best suits producing that explanation?
choices: A dashboard, because it alerts the committee to the slip in real time
An audit, because it independently verifies the cause of the slip
A benefits register, because it lists the planned value of the component
A scheduled written report, because it explains status against plan in narrative form
questions.why: Reports explain status against plan, dashboards alert, and audits verify, so explaining the reason for a slip calls for a written report.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says our portfolio dashboard is green, so we do not need to audit the reports this quarter. Explain to them how reports, dashboards and audits work together, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on dashboards alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would push back on that, though not on the dashboard itself. Reports, dashboards and audits each do a different job. Reports give the context and narrative behind the numbers. Dashboards give fast signals, usually a handful of indicators checked against thresholds, so we notice drift early. Audits check that those numbers are accurate and that our governance rules were followed, for example that a component crossing its cost threshold actually got reviewed. The main limit of dashboards is that they only show what feeds them. If a data source is stale, a cost is misclassified, or a team reports activity instead of benefits, the dashboard can stay green while the portfolio drifts. So a green dashboard is a starting signal, and we still need a periodic audit to confirm it before we make any reallocation decision.
rubricPoints: Reports explain status and context on a schedule, dashboards give fast threshold-based signals, and audits verify accuracy and compliance.
A green dashboard is only as reliable as its data sources and metric definitions.
Monitoring should track outcomes and benefits, not just activity.
Findings from monitoring should trigger a defined escalation or reallocation decision when thresholds are crossed.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining how the three monitoring techniques complement each other and where each one falls short, which is best practised by articulating it.

lessons.plain: When a project in a portfolio runs into a problem it cannot fix alone, someone has to pass it upward to the person who has the authority to decide. Managing and escalating issues means keeping a clear log of problems, judging who can actually resolve each one, and sending it there with enough facts and a specific request so the decision happens in time. Think of a smoke alarm in a building: the job is not to put out every fire yourself, but to make sure the people who can act hear about it quickly and with the right details.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team in your portfolio has been blocked for five days waiting on a shared test environment. Only the director who controls that environment can reassign it, and the team lead has been emailing the project manager every day with no result. What should the portfolio manager do first, and why?
lessons.teach:
An issue is a problem that is already happening and is affecting a project's ability to meet its goals. This differs from a risk, which is something that might happen later. An issue log is the running register where each issue is recorded with its owner, its impact, the date it was raised, and its status. Escalation means passing an issue to a higher level of authority when the current owner cannot resolve it within their own power. A decision-maker is the person or body with authority over the resource, scope, or priority in question. Escalation works because decisions made close to the authority that owns the resource are faster and less likely to bounce back. Delay is costly, because the impact of an open issue usually grows each day it stays unresolved.

Worked example. Project B needs a shared test environment owned by Project C for three weeks. The issue is logged with its impact: a two-week slip to Project B and a delayed benefit date on the roadmap. The portfolio manager checks whether the project manager can resolve it alone. They cannot, because the environment is shared across the portfolio. The manager identifies the decision-maker, which is the governance board or the owner with allocation authority. They send a short brief with two options, a recommended option, and a decision date. They track it, and if no answer arrives by that date, they escalate one level.

Common mistake: escalating without a recommendation or a deadline, or sending it to someone who lacks authority, so it bounces back and time is lost. If left unresolved, Project B slips, its benefit date moves, and any project depending on it on the roadmap stalls as well.

An escalation is only useful when it reaches the right person with a clear decision to make and a date by which it must be made.

questions.prompt: Mara manages Project Kestrel at a freight company. Kestrel needs four developer days each week from the shared platform team, which belongs to Project Orion. The issue is in the log with its impact: a one-week slip to Kestrel and a later benefit date on the roadmap. Mara cannot resolve it alone because the platform team serves several projects. She has identified the platform owner as the decision-maker and sent a short brief with two options, a recommended option, and a decision date of 14 March. The date passes with no reply. What should Mara do next?
choices: Escalate one level to the next authority over the platform team's allocation, keep the same brief, and track it against a new date.
Reassign four developer days from Kestrel's own team without asking anyone, since the slip is already happening.
Resend the same brief to the platform owner with the decision date moved back two weeks.
Mark the issue as closed in the log until the platform owner responds.
questions.why: When the decision date passes without an answer, the issue moves up one level to someone with authority over the resource, with a clear decision and a new date attached.

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes an issue from a risk in a project portfolio?
choices: A risk is recorded in the issue log, while an issue is recorded only in the risk register.
An issue is always cheaper to resolve than a risk, so issues can be deferred.
Both are the same thing, differing only in which team member owns them.
An issue is a problem already happening that affects goals, while a risk is something that might happen later.
questions.why: The teaching text defines an issue as a present problem affecting goals and a risk as a possible future event, which is the distinction the option states.

questions.prompt: At a regional bank, Project Tern's data migration is stalled for ten days because a compliance team's time is needed for checks. The Tern project manager cannot resolve this alone. What is the most appropriate first step for the portfolio manager?
choices: Wait for the compliance team's manager to notice the delay on their own.
Identify the decision-maker with authority over the compliance team's time and send a short brief with options, a recommendation, and a decision date.
Ask Tern's developers to skip the compliance checks so the migration can continue.
Send the issue straight to the bank's chief executive with no recommendation attached.
questions.why: The decision belongs to whoever holds authority over the shared resource, so the portfolio manager should identify that person and give them a clear decision to make by a set date.

questions.prompt: A portfolio manager escalates an issue about a shared test environment, but the message comes back unresolved after two weeks. Which explanation best accounts for this outcome?
choices: The escalation went to a sponsor by default, and sponsors never make resource decisions.
The escalation lacked a clear recommendation or deadline, or was sent to someone without authority over the resource.
Issues should always be kept in the risk register until they cause a schedule slip.
Escalations only work when they are raised in a formal steering meeting rather than by message.
questions.why: The teaching text names missing recommendations, missing deadlines, and sending to someone without authority as the causes of escalations bouncing back and losing time.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you decide whether an issue in a portfolio should be handled by the project manager or escalated to a decision-maker, and name one limit or tradeoff of escalating too quickly or too slowly.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by asking whether the owner of the issue has the authority to resolve it without affecting other projects. If the fix stays inside one project's budget, scope, and people, the project manager handles it and logs it. If it touches a shared resource, priority, or the roadmap, I escalate to whoever owns that decision, usually the governance board or the resource owner. When I escalate, I send the impact in plain terms, two or three options, a recommendation, and the date a decision is needed. The tradeoff is timing. Escalating too quickly floods decision-makers with small problems and erodes their attention, so the real urgent ones get less focus. Escalating too slowly lets the impact grow before anyone with power sees it. I try to set a clear threshold up front so the team knows which issues go up and when.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes an issue already happening from a risk that might occur
Explains that escalation goes to whoever holds authority over the resource or decision
Notes that a good escalation includes impact, options, a recommendation, and a decision date
Names a tradeoff: escalating too early overloads decision-makers, too late lets impact grow

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style escalation situation adds the most here because the skill is choosing the right decision-maker and timing, which no listed mission covers.

lessons.plain: A portfolio is the set of projects, programs and other work an organization funds at the same time. Things change constantly: a project asks for more money, a deadline slips, a sponsor leaves, or the market shifts. Change management here means a deliberate way of proposing a change, checking its effect on the whole portfolio, deciding whether to approve it, and recording what was decided. The goal is to let good changes through while making sure no single change quietly pulls the portfolio away from the goals it was set up to serve. Think of it as a checkpoint that keeps the whole fleet heading the same way.
lessons.guessPrompt: A sponsor asks to move two engineers from a strategic modernization project to an urgent but low-value cost-cutting task, and says it is only for two weeks. Before any teaching, what is the first thing you would want to check before saying yes?
lessons.teach:
Key terms. A change request is a formal written proposal to alter something in the portfolio: its scope, budget, schedule, people, or which components are included. A change control board, often shortened to CCB, is the group with authority to approve or reject those requests. Strategic alignment means the work funded in the portfolio still traces back to the organization's stated goals.

Why it works. Portfolios are shared pools of money and people, so a change to one component moves capacity that other components depend on. A formal step forces the proposer to show the impact on benefits, dependencies and other components before the change happens, instead of discovering the damage later. Recording the decision also creates an audit trail that explains why the portfolio looks the way it does.

Worked example. Step one: the request arrives asking to move two engineers for two weeks. Step two: the portfolio manager asks what goal the move serves and which strategic objective it weakens. Step three: the analysis shows the modernization project's milestone falls inside that window and is tied to a regulatory deadline. Step four: the CCB rejects the move, or approves it only with a replacement resource and a revised date, and records the decision with its reasons.

Common mistake. The usual error is approving changes one at a time in isolation, so each looks small while the cumulative effect quietly removes the work that supported the strategy. Evaluate the whole portfolio after each material change, not just the requested item.

Consequence. Without this discipline, the portfolio can keep reporting green on individual projects while its aggregate benefit drifts away from the goals leadership approved, and no one can explain how that happened.

questions.prompt: A hospital network's portfolio office receives a written request to move one data analyst off a patient-scheduling upgrade for three weeks so she can build a grant-reporting dashboard. Step one: the request is logged in writing with its reasons. Step two: the portfolio manager asks which strategic goal the dashboard serves and which goal the move weakens; the answer is that the scheduling upgrade supports the goal of shorter clinic waiting times. Step three is missing. Step four: the change control board approves the move on condition that a backup analyst is named, and records its reasons. Which step belongs in the gap at step three?
choices: The portfolio's status report is sent to leadership showing all projects green.
The analyst's manager makes the move alone and informs the board after the work starts.
The grant dashboard is treated as a new project and funded without any review.
The analysis shows the scheduling upgrade's milestones and dependencies that the analyst's absence would delay.
questions.why: Step three is where the proposer must show the impact on benefits, dependencies and other components before the board decides, and that is the analysis of the scheduling upgrade's milestones and dependencies.

questions.prompt: A university research office has four grant-funded studies sharing one statistician. A principal investigator asks to borrow the statistician for a month from a study that supports the institution's stated goal of improving graduate outcomes, to help a study that does not map to any stated goal. What is the most appropriate handling under a formal change process?
choices: Submit it as a change request so the board can check which goal the move weakens and what it delays.
Reassign the statistician informally and update the status report at the end of the month.
Let the statistician decide, since the statistician knows the workload best.
Approve the move because the investigator has seniority and the request is short.
questions.why: A formal change request makes the proposer show the effect on strategic goals and other components before the board decides, which is the purpose of the change process.

questions.prompt: A retail chain's portfolio team approves five budget shifts over one quarter. Each shift moves under 5 percent of a program's budget, and each is approved on its own merits. After the fifth, the customer loyalty program has lost its entire data team and its benefit targets have quietly slipped. Which error most likely caused this outcome?
choices: The board met too often and spent too much time on small requests.
The loyalty program's sponsor should have requested a larger budget at the start of the quarter.
The budget shifts were recorded in writing, which created an audit trail that hid the problem.
Each change was judged alone, and the portfolio was not re-evaluated as a whole after each material change.
questions.why: The common error is approving changes one at a time in isolation so that their cumulative effect removes the work supporting the strategy; the fix is to evaluate the whole portfolio after each material change.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm skips recording its portfolio change decisions, reasoning that each approval was sensible when it was made. Eighteen months later, every project reports green, but the portfolio's total benefit is well below what leadership approved and no one can say which decisions caused the drop. What is the main consequence the firm is experiencing?
choices: The firm's board is legally required to reverse every decision made in the last eighteen months.
The portfolio cannot show how it came to look the way it does, so the drift away from approved goals goes unexplained.
The firm must immediately cancel all projects because green reports are always a sign of failure.
The firm has created too many change requests, which has slowed the delivery of every project.
questions.why: Without a recorded decision trail, the portfolio can keep reporting green on individual projects while its aggregate benefit drifts, and the reasons for that drift cannot be reconstructed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a mid-cycle request to add a new project to the portfolio should be approved, and name one limit or tradeoff of the process you use.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by treating the request as a formal change, not a favor. I would ask what strategic objective the new project supports and how it ranks against current components, then check what it consumes: people, budget and shared tools. Next I would look at dependencies, meaning which active projects lose capacity or milestones if this one starts. I would bring the impact summary to the change control board with options, such as delaying the new project, funding it from contingency, or swapping out a lower-value item, and record the decision and the reasons. The tradeoff is that this adds delay and paperwork, so a fast-moving opportunity may be missed. I would mitigate that with a defined fast lane for small, low-impact changes while keeping full review for anything that shifts the strategic balance.
rubricPoints: Treats the request as a formal change that goes through a defined review.
Checks alignment of the change with the portfolio's strategic objectives.
Assesses impact on capacity, budget and dependencies across the whole portfolio.
Records the decision and its rationale for audit.
Names a real limit, such as added delay, and a way to mitigate it.

suggested.rationale: Deciding whether a change protects strategic alignment is best practiced by reasoning through an exam-style situation with competing demands.

lessons.plain: Portfolio balancing means looking at everything your organization is working on at once, which is the portfolio, and deciding how to spread limited people, money and tools across those pieces so the total delivers the most value toward the organization's goals. Think of a household splitting a fixed monthly budget between rent, savings and a holiday: spending more on one thing leaves less for the others. Prioritizing means ranking the pieces so scarce resources go first to the ones that matter most. Balancing means checking that the overall mix is not too risky, too short-term, or too concentrated in one area.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your organization has ten projects but enough engineers for only six. Two projects are both strongly backed by leadership and need the same two specialists. What would you check before deciding which one gets them, and why?
lessons.teach:
A portfolio component is any project or program grouped under the portfolio. Capacity is the people, money and tools actually available in a period. Demand is what the components together ask for. Strategic objectives are the organization's stated goals that the portfolio is meant to serve. Prioritizing ranks components by how much they advance those objectives, whether they are mandatory, and what they depend on. Balancing then checks the chosen mix against risk, time horizon and investment type. It works because resources are finite, so the value of the whole portfolio depends on where capacity goes, not only on whether each piece runs well.

Worked example. Capacity is 12 engineer-months this quarter. Component B, compliance reporting, is mandatory and needs 3. Component A, customer portal, supports the revenue goal and needs 6. Component C, an internal tool upgrade, has weak links to any goal and needs 4. Component D, a pilot routing feature, is strategic but uncertain and needs 3. Step 1: fund B (3 used, 9 left). Step 2: fund A (6 used, 3 left). Step 3: D fits exactly in the remaining 3, so fund it. Step 4: C is deferred to next quarter. Total used is 12. Balance check: one high-risk pilot sits among core work, which is acceptable.

Common mistake: ranking by whichever sponsor is loudest, or spreading capacity thinly so every component runs at 80 percent and none finishes. Consequence in a running system: if a compliance component is starved to protect a feature, the organization can miss a regulatory deadline, and the feature gains nothing if it ships late.

A portfolio is balanced when its scarce resources are committed in order of strategic value, mandatory need and dependency, and the resulting mix is checked for risk and time horizon.

questions.prompt: A regional clinic network has 15 analyst-weeks of capacity this quarter. Component P, a medication-safety audit, is mandatory and needs 6 analyst-weeks. Component R, an identity service upgrade, needs 4 and must finish before Q can start. Component Q, a patient-reminder feature, supports the retention goal and needs 5. Component S, a sales forecasting tool, has weak links to any goal and needs 5. Worked so far: Step 1, fund P (6 used, 9 left). Step 2, fund R because Q depends on it (10 used, 5 left). Step 3 is missing. Which completion of Step 3 is correct?
choices: Split Q in half, funding 2.5 weeks of it, so that some capacity remains for S.
Defer both Q and S so that 5 weeks stay unused as slack for emergencies.
Fund S because its sponsor has asked for it twice this month.
Fund Q, which fits exactly in the remaining 5 weeks and serves the retention goal with its dependency already met; S is deferred.
questions.why: Q is strategic, its dependency R is already funded, and it fits the 5 remaining weeks exactly, while S has weak links to any goal and so waits.

questions.prompt: In this unit's terms, what is 'capacity'?
choices: The total of what all components together ask for in a period.
The list of projects and programs grouped under the portfolio.
The people, money and tools available in a period.
The stated goals of the organization that the portfolio is meant to serve.
questions.why: The teaching text defines capacity as the people, money and tools actually available in a period, which is the finite pool that must be allocated.

questions.prompt: A team has 10 engineer-weeks this quarter. Component M, a mandatory security audit, needs 4. Component N, a growth feature that supports a revenue goal, needs 5. Component O, an experimental AI tool, is strategic but uncertain and needs 3. Component P, a legacy report cleanup with weak links to any goal, needs 4. Using prioritization first (mandatory need, then strategic value, then dependency), which pair should be funded?
choices: M and N, since the mandatory audit and the growth feature use 9 of the 10 weeks and O's 3 weeks would not fit.
O and P, because together they avoid the largest single cost.
N and P, because together they cover the revenue goal and the cleanup.
M and O, so the uncertain pilot is not left out of the plan.
questions.why: Mandatory M is funded first, then the higher-value strategic N, and the 1 remaining week cannot hold O or P, so M and N is the correct pair.

questions.prompt: A healthcare nonprofit ranked its portfolio by which executive sponsor pressed hardest in meetings and funded the loudest one. This left a mandatory regulatory filing about 2 weeks short of the capacity it needed. What is the most accurate description of the error?
choices: The team ranked by sponsor loudness instead of strategic value and mandatory need, which risks missing the regulatory deadline.
Capacity was not really finite, so the shortfall was only a scheduling issue.
The team balanced risk well, since funding the loudest sponsor is a valid way to build a mix.
The team should have spread the 2 weeks across all components so that none is starved.
questions.why: Ranking by whoever is loudest is a named common mistake, and starving a mandatory compliance item can cause a missed regulatory deadline, while spreading capacity thin is a separate error.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide which portfolio components get scarce engineers this quarter when demand exceeds capacity. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would list every component with its demand, its link to a stated strategic objective, and whether it is mandatory or blocks others. I would fund mandatory work first, then rank the rest by strategic value and dependencies, and commit capacity down the list until it runs out. Then I would check the mix for risk and time horizon, so we are not funding only safe short-term work or only one large bet. The main tradeoff is that the ranking depends on how well we estimated strategic value, which is often judgment rather than measurement. Deferred components lose momentum and their teams may leave, so I would record the decision, the reasons, and a date to revisit it.
rubricPoints: Fund mandatory or dependency-blocking work before discretionary work.
Rank the rest by contribution to named strategic objectives, not by who asks loudest.
Check the resulting mix for risk, time horizon and investment type.
Name a tradeoff, such as judgment-based scoring or the cost of deferring components.

suggested.rationale: A reasoned scenario with competing components and a fixed capacity exercises the prioritization and balance judgment that memorized rules would not.

lessons.plain: Resource allocation means deciding who or what works on which part of the portfolio. The resources are people, software tools, technology such as servers or licences, and money. Supply and demand analysis compares two lists. Supply is what you actually have available in a given period, such as hours from a specialist team. Demand is what the projects and programmes are asking for in that same period. When demand is higher than supply, something will slip. When supply sits idle, money is being wasted. A portfolio manager uses this comparison to move resources away from low-value or waiting work and toward the components that matter most for the strategy.
lessons.guessPrompt: Four engineers each have 100 usable hours next month, and three projects together ask for 460 hours of their time. Before reading on, what would you do first, and why might the projects' own plans look fine even though the total does not fit?
lessons.teach:
Supply is the usable capacity of a resource in a period: the hours, licences, servers or budget you can really spend after leave, training and work already committed has been removed. Demand is what the active components ask for in that same period. The gap is demand minus supply. A positive gap is a shortfall that will cause slippage. A negative gap is idle capacity that costs money. Reallocation means moving an existing resource from one component to another. It is a governance decision and must be recorded. This analysis works at portfolio level because each project's own plan can look feasible while the shared pool is oversubscribed. Only the portfolio view shows the collision.

Worked example. A pool of four integration specialists has 100 usable hours each per month, so supply is 400 hours. Three components request 180 hours (A, a regulatory deadline), 160 hours (B, a revenue feature) and 120 hours (C, an internal tool). Step 1: sum the supply, which is 400. Step 2: sum the demand, which is 460. Step 3: the gap is plus 60 hours, a shortfall. Step 4: rank the components by strategic value, so A and B stay funded. Step 5: defer C by one month. That frees 120 hours, covering the gap with a 60-hour buffer. The sponsor of C is told and the roadmap is updated.

A common mistake is to accept each team's request as fixed, or to count a specialist as supply without checking that the person has the skill for the work. Overallocation shows up later as missed dates on the most important component and burnout across the pool.

In a running portfolio, skipping this analysis means the regulatory deadline for A slips quietly while everyone believes the plan works.

questions.prompt: A product studio has five UX designers, each with 90 usable hours per month after leave and already committed support work is removed. Supply is therefore 450 hours. Three components request time this month: Mobile checkout 200 hours, Loyalty redesign 180 hours and Accessibility audit 110 hours, a total demand of 490 hours. Step 1: sum the supply, which is 450. Step 2: sum the demand, which is 490. Step 3: calculate the gap as demand minus supply and state what its sign means. Step 4: rank the components by strategic value and decide which are funded this month. Step 5: record any reallocation as a governance decision. Only Step 3 is left for you to complete here.
choices: The gap is minus 40 hours, which is idle capacity that costs money.
The gap is plus 40 hours, which is a surplus to be handed to the next month.
The gap is plus 490 hours, which equals the total demand.
The gap is plus 40 hours, which is a shortfall that will cause slippage.
questions.why: Demand minus supply is 490 minus 450, which is plus 40, and a positive gap is a shortfall that will cause slippage.

questions.prompt: In portfolio performance analysis, what does the supply of a resource measure?
choices: The total budget approved for the portfolio across all years, including future periods.
The number of people on the payroll multiplied by a standard 40-hour week.
The usable capacity left after leave, training and already committed work are removed, for the same period as the demand.
The demand of the active components added together for the period.
questions.why: Supply is the capacity you can genuinely spend in a period once leave, training and committed work are taken out, so it is not raw headcount or total approved budget.

questions.prompt: A shared pool of 300 cloud licences is available this quarter. The active components request 255 licences in total. The gap is minus 45. What is the correct response according to the analysis?
choices: Treat the gap as a shortfall and defer the lowest-value component until licences free up.
Increase the demand estimate so the gap becomes zero before the next review.
Ignore the negative gap, since unused licences cause no cost to the portfolio.
Recognise the 45 spare licences as idle capacity that costs money, and consider a recorded governance decision to reallocate them to a component with unmet need.
questions.why: A negative gap means idle capacity that costs money, and moving a resource to another component is a governance decision that must be recorded.

questions.prompt: Each project in a portfolio has a plan that looks feasible on its own. Why must the supply and demand analysis still be done at portfolio level?
choices: Because the portfolio budget always has to match the sum of project budgets exactly.
Because each project's plan can look feasible while the shared pool is oversubscribed, and only the portfolio view shows that collision.
Because individual project plans never include any work that consumes shared resources.
Because project managers are not allowed to calculate their own capacity figures.
questions.why: Only the combined view of the shared pool reveals when several individually feasible plans together ask for more than the pool can supply.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how supply and demand analysis tells you when to reallocate people or money across a portfolio, and name one limit of the method.
lessons.modelAnswer: Supply and demand analysis puts every component's requests for a shared resource next to the usable capacity of that resource for the same period. Usable capacity means the time left after leave, training and existing commitments. If demand exceeds supply, there is a gap. The portfolio manager then ranks the components by strategic value and decides what to defer, reduce or fund, records the decision, and tells the affected sponsors. If supply exceeds demand, the surplus can be redeployed. One limit is that the numbers are only as good as the estimates.
