Demand forecasts are often optimistic, and a skill mismatch can hide inside a headcount total, so the analysis needs a check on who can actually do the work.
rubricPoints: Defines supply as usable capacity and demand as requested work for the same period.
Calculates the gap and says whether it is a shortfall or a surplus.
Recommends a specific reallocation tied to strategic value, with the decision recorded.
Names a limit such as estimate quality or skill fit.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine has the learner run a portfolio-level supply and demand comparison, so an exam-style situation to reason through adds the most.

lessons.plain: Imagine a group of building jobs that all serve one goal, such as getting a new bridge open before winter. Each job has its own schedule, but the group as a whole needs a plan and a way to tell whether the goal is still on track. Updating the roadmap means changing the timeline of that group when facts change. Measuring aggregated performance means adding up how each job is doing and checking that total against the goal the group exists for. This lesson covers how a manager keeps that timeline honest and uses the total to decide what to change.
lessons.guessPrompt: A portfolio has three projects aimed at one business goal. One project is badly behind, but the other two are on schedule. Should the portfolio roadmap change, and what would you check before deciding?
lessons.teach:
A portfolio is a group of projects and programs managed together because they share a strategic goal, such as cutting customer wait times by a set amount. A roadmap is a timeline that shows which components are planned to start, deliver, or finish, and when. Aggregated performance means combining the measures from each component, such as forecast benefit, schedule, and cost, into one portfolio-level view that you can compare against the goal. This works because a portfolio can look healthy project by project while still missing its goal. Adding the parts together exposes that gap, and the roadmap shows the response as new timing, so decisions are visible and reviewable.

Worked example. A portfolio targets a 20 point improvement in dispatch on-time rate by year end. It holds three projects. Step 1: each project's forecast contribution is A 8 points, B 7 points, C 5 points, for a total of 20 points, which meets the goal. Step 2: a monthly review shows B's data-quality fix has slipped, so B's forecast falls to 3 points. Step 3: the aggregated forecast is now 16 points, or 80 percent of the goal. Step 4: the roadmap is updated. B's second phase is deferred, C's start is pulled forward if its team has capacity, and the change and its approval are recorded. Step 5: the aggregate is recalculated next cycle.

Common mistake. Teams move roadmap dates to match what was planned, or report each project as green and never recalculate the portfolio total against the goal. Consequence: the portfolio reports success while the target is missed, and the gap appears only at year end, when the options to reallocate resources are gone.

A roadmap is only useful when its dates reflect the current aggregated forecast against the goal.

questions.prompt: A city transit agency has a portfolio goal to raise on-time bus departures by 9 points by year end. It holds three projects: transit signal priority with a forecast contribution of 4 points, a new depot scheduling tool with 3 points, and a driver rostering redesign with 2 points. The forecasts total 9 points, which meets the goal. Step 1 is done. In Step 2, a monthly review shows the rostering redesign has stalled and its forecast falls to 0 points. Step 3 is missing. Which action completes the chain the teaching text describes?
choices: Recalculate the aggregate forecast at 7 points, about 78 percent of the 9-point goal, then update the roadmap and record the change and its approval.
Wait until year end to measure, since a 2-point gap may still close on its own.
Keep the roadmap dates unchanged so the original plan stays visible to the sponsor.
Report the portfolio as green because the signal and depot projects are each still on schedule.
questions.why: The correct chain recalculates the portfolio total against the goal, then changes the roadmap to reflect that new total and records the decision, which matches the teaching text's sequence of recalculate, respond, and record.

questions.prompt: A portfolio of four projects has each project reporting green status. The summed forecast contribution is 14 points against a 20-point goal. Which reading best reflects the teaching text?
choices: The portfolio is on track because no single project is red.
The portfolio is probably fine until the final quarter, when projects usually speed up.
The portfolio will need a cost review, but its goal progress is not in question.
The portfolio is behind its goal, because the aggregate shows a 6-point gap that individual project status hides.
questions.why: The teaching text explains that a portfolio can look healthy project by project while still missing its goal, and that adding the parts together exposes the gap.

questions.prompt: A hospital portfolio targets a 10-point reduction in patient wait times. Its three projects currently forecast 3, 2, and 1 points, for a total of 6 points, which is 60 percent of the goal. One project has spare team capacity and another has a stalled phase. What roadmap response best matches the teaching text?
choices: Add a fourth project to the portfolio, because any new work will close the gap.
Move every project's dates back to match the original plan so the timeline looks consistent.
Keep the roadmap as baselined and report the gap at year end.
Pull forward the start of the project with spare capacity, defer the stalled phase, and record both changes with their approvals.
questions.why: The teaching text's response to an aggregate gap is to change the roadmap timing, such as deferring a stalled phase and pulling forward work where capacity exists, and to record the change and its approval.

questions.prompt: A portfolio team moves its roadmap dates each month so they match the original planned dates, and each project reports green. What is the most likely consequence, according to the teaching text?
choices: The roadmap becomes more accurate because dates are always reset to the plan.
Resource reallocation becomes easier because every project starts from the same baseline.
The portfolio reports success while the goal is missed, and the gap appears only at year end when reallocation options are gone.
The sponsor receives an early warning, because the dates keep changing.
questions.why: The teaching text names this as a common mistake: moving dates to the plan and never recalculating against the goal hides the shortfall until it is too late to act.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would update a portfolio roadmap when the aggregated forecast falls below the business goal. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by recalculating the aggregated forecast, adding each component's current contribution toward the goal rather than relying on the original plan. If the total is short, I would look at which component's forecast dropped and why, then decide how to close the gap: defer or narrow the affected work, move forward a component that is ready and has capacity, or reallocate people or budget. I would update the roadmap with the new dates and record the change and who approved it. The main limit is that moving work forward depends on real capacity, so a plan that looks fine on paper can fail if the receiving team is already committed. Another tradeoff is that deferring one component delays its own benefits, so the change should be checked against the goal, not just the schedule.
rubricPoints: Recalculates the aggregated forecast against the goal instead of trusting individual project status
Chooses a specific roadmap response such as deferring, narrowing, or pulling forward a component
Records the change and its approval so the decision is traceable
Names a real limit, such as capacity or delayed benefits from deferral

suggested.rationale: A scenario where the learner must recalculate a portfolio total and choose a roadmap response adds more than reading, and no listed mission covers portfolio roadmaps.

lessons.plain: A portfolio is the set of projects and programs an organization is running at once. Keeping portfolio records means saving the paperwork that explains how that set was chosen and managed: the charters and business cases, the people who approved each decision and when, and the ranked order that decided which work got money or staff first. Organizations and regulators often require this evidence to be complete, accurate, and retrievable for years. The core idea is that a decision you cannot prove is treated as if it was never properly made.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a portfolio board funded a project in March and then changed the priority order in June, what would an auditor need to see to understand both decisions, and what would be lost if the March document were simply edited to show the June order?
lessons.teach:
A portfolio record is a dated, owned piece of evidence about how a portfolio was run. Three kinds matter most. Artifacts are the working documents, such as charters, business cases, and status reports. Approvals are the recorded decisions, showing who had the authority to say yes, when, and on what basis. Prioritizations are the ranked orders of components, together with the criteria and scores that produced them. Maintaining records means keeping them complete, accurate, findable, and unaltered after the fact, for as long as the organization or a regulator requires.

Why this works: an auditor or governance body cannot rely on memory or good intentions. They rely on a trail in which every decision links to a stated basis and a named approver. The mechanism is simple. Each record has an owner, a version, a date, and a link to the decision it supports. A change creates a new version instead of overwriting the old one, so both the earlier and later states remain visible.

Worked example. In March a portfolio board scores three projects, ranks them, and funds the top two. Step 1: the prioritization record stores the criteria, the scores, the ranking, and the minutes. Step 2: the approval record names the approvers, their authority, and the date. Step 3: in June the board moves funding from project B to project C. Step 4: the team adds a June version of the ranking with the new reason and the new approval, linked back to March. Step 5: at audit, both versions and the reason for the change are visible.

Common mistake: treating records as a one-time filing task, or overwriting documents so the history disappears. Another frequent error is accepting a verbal or chat-based approval with nothing written down.

Consequence: when a regulated or funding decision lacks an approval record, an audit finding can force the portfolio to reopen the decision, pause work, or explain the gap to a regulator. The cost falls on delivery teams, who must stop and reconstruct history.

questions.prompt: A regional water utility's capital committee ranks four pipe-replacement projects in January using a scoring sheet with criteria for risk, customer impact, and cost, then funds the top two. The January ranking, scores, criteria, and minutes are stored as one record, and the committee chair's signed approval is stored as a separate record naming the approvers, their authority, and the date. In April the committee moves funding from project West-3 to project River-7 after a main break. The team does two things: Step 1, it saves an April ranking as a new dated version with the new scores and the reason for the change. Step 2, it attaches an April approval record naming the approvers, their authority, and the April vote date. Step 3 is missing from this record. Step 4: at a regulator's inspection, the January and April versions and the reason for the change can all be retrieved. Which missing Step 3 completes the process?
choices: Overwrite the January ranking with the April scores so the file shows only the current position
Delete the January version because the April ranking supersedes it and keeping both causes confusion
Link the April version back to the January version so the change and its reason are traceable
Email the April summary to the committee chair and treat the chair's reply as the approval record
questions.why: Linking the new version back to the earlier one keeps both states visible and connects the change to its stated basis, which is what lets the inspector see the history.

questions.prompt: Which item is best described as a prioritization record under records maintenance?
choices: A monthly status report showing budget spent against plan for each project
An email thread in which a director agrees to a funding change
A ranked order of portfolio components together with the criteria and scores that produced that order
A project charter that names the sponsor and the high-level goals
questions.why: A prioritization record is defined as the ranked order of components plus the criteria and scores behind it, while the other options are an artifact, a status report, and an informal approval.

questions.prompt: A portfolio analyst updates a status report in place each month, replacing the previous month's figures, and the team argues the record is fine because the figures shown are always current. What is the main compliance problem?
choices: Current figures are never allowed in a record, so the analyst should have stored only forecasts
The status report should be kept in an email system rather than a document repository
The earlier states are lost, so an auditor cannot see how the portfolio looked at each past decision point
The status report lacks a version number, so it cannot be stored in the same folder as approvals
questions.why: Overwriting removes the history that a changed record must preserve, so auditors cannot reconstruct earlier states, which is the core failure the records rule is meant to prevent.

questions.prompt: At a steering meeting, a sponsor verbally agrees to move contingency money from one project to another. Two weeks later the team writes up the decision from memory, listing the sponsor as approver with no written basis or meeting date confirmed. What is the right handling?
choices: Record the sponsor's name and the meeting date, flag the missing written basis as a gap, and obtain a written approval that names the approver, authority, and basis
Accept the write-up as the approval record because the sponsor did agree in the meeting
Wait until the next quarterly audit and let the auditor decide whether the memory-based note is acceptable
Store the decision as a prioritization record only, since funding moves are always prioritization decisions
questions.why: An approval must show who had authority, when, and on what basis, so a memory-based note with no confirmed date or basis should be flagged and replaced by a written approval rather than accepted as is.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a portfolio team should keep dated, versioned approval and prioritization records instead of updating one master document, and name one limit or tradeoff of keeping that much history.
lessons.modelAnswer: A master document only shows the current state, so anyone reviewing it cannot tell when a decision changed or who approved the change. Versioned records keep each prioritization and approval with its date, approver, and reason, and each new version links back to the one it replaced. That lets an auditor or sponsor trace why a project lost funding in June even though it was ranked high in March. The tradeoff is effort and storage. Every change now needs a documented version, and the team must maintain retention rules, access controls, and an index so the history stays searchable rather than becoming a pile of files. Teams can also be tempted to record every minor edit, which buries the decisions that matter. The practical answer is to version the decisions and approvals, not every draft.
rubricPoints: Versioned records preserve the history of a decision instead of overwriting it.
Each record should show the owner, the date, the approver, and the reason for the decision.
Records must be retrievable and retained for as long as organizational or regulatory rules require.
Tradeoff: more history means more documentation effort, storage, and access control to manage.

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario where the learner must decide what records an audit would need is a better test of this objective than any listed mission.

lessons.plain: Before a company can decide how to handle risk across all of its projects together, it has to agree on how much uncertainty it is willing to live with. Think of a household deciding how much it can afford to lose on one investment. Some families accept a chance of a big loss for a chance of a big gain; others want steady, predictable outcomes. A portfolio is a group of projects managed together to meet shared goals, so the same question applies to the whole group: what limits apply, and would the different people affected by the work, such as the sponsor, the finance team, and the end users, accept those same limits? This lesson covers how to set acceptable levels of risk for a portfolio.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two sponsors each run a portfolio of five projects with the same total budget and the same list of risks. Sponsor A runs a fast-growing startup that needs to win market share quickly. Sponsor B runs a regulated utility that must keep service running and answer to a regulator. Without any further teaching, what would you guess is a reasonable level of risk for each, and why might the two answers differ even though the projects are identical?
lessons.teach: Risk appetite is the amount and type of risk an organization is willing to pursue in order to reach its goals. Risk tolerance is the acceptable variation around a specific objective, such as a budget overrun of up to a stated percentage or a schedule slip of a few weeks. Risk capacity is the most risk the organization can absorb before it suffers serious harm, such as breaching a loan agreement or losing a key customer. Stakeholder tolerance is how much variation a particular group is prepared to accept, and it may be narrower or wider than the organization's position. A portfolio threshold is an aggregate limit, set for the whole group of projects, that triggers escalation when it is crossed. Why this matters: a single project can look acceptable on its own while the portfolio is not, because project risks are often connected. Several projects may depend on the same vendor, team, or data source, so their risks add together. Worked example: a portfolio has three projects, each with a 20 percent chance of a $300,000 overrun. Step one: the expected overrun for each project is 20 percent of $300,000, which is $60,000. Step two: add the three, giving $180,000. Step three: compare this with the board's portfolio threshold of $150,000. Each project passes a per-project limit of $400,000, but the portfolio breaches its threshold, so the right response is escalation or a reserve decision rather than acceptance. Common mistake: setting one risk level for everyone, or copying the sponsor's appetite onto a finance team that must absorb the losses. A portfolio that accepts each project's risk separately can exceed what the organization can absorb, and the first visible warning often arrives only when several overruns land in the same quarter. Acceptable portfolio risk is therefore set at the aggregate level, checked against stakeholder tolerance, and kept below risk capacity.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs four warehouse-automation projects. Each has a 25 percent chance of a $200,000 overrun, and the board's portfolio threshold for the group is $180,000. Work through it. Step one: the expected overrun for each project is 25 percent of $200,000, which is $50,000. Step two: add the four projects to get $200,000 for the portfolio. Step three is missing. Which choice completes it and gives the correct response?
choices: Compare $200,000 with the $180,000 portfolio threshold; the threshold is breached, so escalate or make a reserve decision.
Divide $200,000 by four to get $50,000, then accept because the average is below the threshold.
Multiply $200,000 by four to get $800,000, then cancel the two projects with the largest expected overruns.
Check each project against a $100,000 per-project limit, and accept the portfolio because every project is under it.
questions.why: The portfolio threshold is an aggregate limit, so the aggregate expected overrun of $200,000 is compared with it, and crossing it calls for escalation or a reserve decision rather than acceptance.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit's board says the organization can absorb up to $1.2 million in losses before it breaches its credit covenant and risks serious harm. Which term best describes that $1.2 million limit?
choices: Risk appetite, the amount and type of risk the organization is willing to pursue to reach its goals.
Stakeholder tolerance, the variation one particular group is prepared to accept.
Risk capacity, the most risk the organization can absorb before it suffers serious harm.
Risk tolerance, the acceptable variation around one specific objective.
questions.why: Risk capacity is defined as the most risk an organization can absorb before serious harm, which matches the covenant-breach limit described, while the other terms refer to willingness, a single objective, or a single group.

questions.prompt: A software company has five projects that all depend on the same cloud vendor. Each project has a 30 percent chance of an $80,000 overrun, and the portfolio threshold is $100,000. Which response fits the portfolio risk, given that projects sharing a dependency add their risks together?
choices: Reduce each project's budget by the full $80,000 so that no overrun is possible.
Ignore the threshold, because the vendor dependency is outside the portfolio's control.
Escalate or make a reserve decision, because the aggregate expected overrun of $120,000 exceeds the $100,000 threshold.
Accept the risk, because each project's $24,000 expected overrun is well below a $150,000 per-project limit.
questions.why: Adding the five expected overruns gives $120,000, which crosses the aggregate threshold, so the correct response is escalation or a reserve decision rather than acceptance based on individual projects.

questions.prompt: A city council sets one acceptable schedule-slip level of 10 percent for every department's portfolio. The finance department, which must absorb any budget losses, is only willing to accept 4 percent. What is the main flaw in the council's approach?
choices: Schedule slips should always be measured in dollars rather than percentages.
The council should raise its level to match the finance department's higher tolerance.
A single risk level ignores that stakeholder tolerance can be narrower than the organization's position, so the level should be checked against each group that absorbs the loss.
Finance should not be consulted because only the council's position determines acceptable risk.
questions.why: Stakeholder tolerance may be narrower or wider than the organization's position, and copying one level onto a group that absorbs the losses ignores that difference, so acceptable risk must be checked against each stakeholder's tolerance.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide what level of risk is acceptable for a portfolio, and name one limit or tradeoff you would have to manage in that decision.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the organization's risk appetite, meaning how much uncertainty leadership is willing to take on for growth, and check it against risk capacity, the most the organization can absorb before serious harm. Then I would turn that into a portfolio threshold, an aggregate limit covering all projects combined, because individual projects can each look acceptable while their combined exposure is not. Next I would test that threshold against stakeholder tolerance. Finance may accept far less variation in cash flow than the sponsor does, and both views need to be visible. The tradeoff is that a tighter threshold protects the organization but may block valuable projects and slow delivery. I would take that disagreement to the governance body for a decision instead of quietly choosing one side.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes risk appetite, risk tolerance, and risk capacity
Sets the acceptable level at the aggregate portfolio level, not only per project
Checks the organizational level against the tolerance of key stakeholders
Names a real tradeoff, such as protection versus lost value or delivery speed, and says how it is resolved

suggested.rationale: Deciding an acceptable portfolio risk level is a judgment that is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario with conflicting stakeholder views, and no listed mission covers it directly.

lessons.plain: A portfolio risk management plan is a written plan that explains how an organization will spot, rate, respond to, and monitor risks across a whole group of projects and programs, not just one project at a time. A portfolio is that group of related work, chosen to serve the organization's strategy. The plan has to follow the rules set by governance, meaning the senior leaders and committees who decide how the group is run and how much risk they will accept. Think of a city's flood plan. Each neighborhood has its own small plan, but the city plan decides what counts as a citywide emergency, who makes the call, and how fast it gets escalated.
lessons.guessPrompt: If every project in a portfolio manages its own risks well, why might the portfolio as a whole still be exposed?
lessons.teach:
A portfolio is a group of projects, programs, and ongoing operations grouped to meet strategic goals. Aggregate risk means the combined effect of risks across all those components, which can be larger than any single component's risk. Governance risk guidelines are the rules set by the body that oversees the portfolio: how much risk is acceptable, the rating scale to use, the thresholds that trigger escalation, who may approve each kind of response, and how often reporting happens. A portfolio risk management plan turns those guidelines into a working method: the risk categories, the rating approach, the escalation thresholds, the response authority for each level, the reporting cycle, and the review schedule.

Why it works: a risk that looks minor inside one project can become serious when several projects depend on the same thing. Responses are chosen at the level where the authority and the view both exist.

Worked example: three projects each depend on one vendor. Project B rates a vendor delay as medium in its own register. The portfolio plan says any risk that touches two or more components is re-rated at portfolio level. The portfolio view combines Project B's delay with Project A's identical dependency and Project C's shared testing window. The combined rating crosses the governance threshold, so the risk escalates to the steering committee within the set time. The committee chooses a mitigation: move Project C's testing window and fund a second vendor source.

Common mistake: copying each project's risk process into the portfolio plan with no portfolio-level thresholds. Shared risks then never cross a line that triggers escalation, and nobody with authority sees them.

Consequence: when the vendor slips, all three projects miss together, and the organization learns about it late, when options are fewer and costlier.

A portfolio risk plan is only useful when its thresholds, authorities, and reporting rhythm are written to match what governance has said it will accept.

questions.prompt: A regional water utility runs three capital projects that all depend on one pump supplier. Its portfolio risk plan says a risk touching two or more projects is re-rated at portfolio level by adding the component scores together. Governance sets an escalation threshold of 10: any portfolio score above that must go to the governance board. Project X rates the supplier delay at likelihood 2 times impact 3, which is 6. Project Y rates the same delay at likelihood 3 times impact 2, which is 6. Step 1: the risk touches two projects, so it is re-rated at portfolio level. Step 2: the portfolio score is 6 plus 6, which is 12. Step 3 is missing. What should happen next?
choices: Keep the risk at project level, because each project's own score of 6 is below the threshold
Escalate the risk to the governance board, because the portfolio score of 12 is above the threshold of 10
Accept the risk without action, because a summed score is not a real rating and should be ignored
Draw down a contingency reserve held by Project X, because the risk is now funded
questions.why: The portfolio-level score of 12 exceeds the governance escalation threshold of 10, so the risk must go to the body that holds authority at that level.

questions.prompt: In portfolio risk management, what does aggregate risk mean?
choices: The combined effect of risks across all the portfolio's components, which can exceed any single component's risk
The total budget reserved to pay for responses to risks in the portfolio
The average of every project's risk ratings, used to smooth out outliers
The rating a single project gives its own highest-scoring risk
questions.why: Aggregate risk is the combined effect across all components of the portfolio, and the teaching text notes it can be larger than any single component's risk.

questions.prompt: A portfolio has three projects that each rate a shared supplier risk as low. The portfolio plan copies each project's risk process and has no portfolio-level thresholds. What is the most likely result?
choices: Each project rates its own risk correctly, so the portfolio is protected by its parts
Shared risks never cross an escalation line, so no one with authority sees them
The steering committee sees the risk early and funds a second source
The risk is re-rated automatically and escalated within the set time
questions.why: Without portfolio-level thresholds, a shared risk never reaches a trigger that escalates it, so the people with authority remain unaware of it.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches what makes a portfolio risk plan useful?
choices: It is detailed enough to list every risk each project has ever logged
It uses a vendor's standard template so that auditors recognise it
Its thresholds, response authorities, and reporting rhythm match what governance has said it will accept
It gives every project the freedom to set its own escalation limits
questions.why: The teaching text says a plan is only useful when its thresholds, authorities, and reporting rhythm are written to match governance's stated acceptance levels.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a portfolio risk management plan differs from individual project risk plans, and name one limit or tradeoff of writing it to follow governance risk guidelines.
lessons.modelAnswer: A project risk plan covers one project's risks, owned by its manager, with responses that project can approve. A portfolio risk plan covers the whole group, looks at risks that span several components, and sets the escalation thresholds and response authority that governance has defined. Its main job is to catch shared risks, such as a common vendor or a shared testing window, that no single project would rate high enough to escalate. The tradeoff is that governance guidelines are often set at a high level and may be out of date. Aligning the plan closely to them can make it slow to respond to new risks that the guidelines did not anticipate, so the plan needs a review cycle that lets the thresholds be revisited.
rubricPoints: Portfolio plans cover risks that span multiple components, which project plans miss
Portfolio plans set escalation thresholds and response authority from governance guidelines
Aggregate or combined ratings can reveal shared risks no single project rates high
Alignment to governance can slow response to risks the guidelines did not anticipate
A review cycle lets thresholds and guidelines be updated

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning about how a portfolio plan links governance thresholds to shared risks and explaining that to others, which no current mission or planned engine covers directly.

lessons.plain: Portfolio dependency analysis means looking at how the projects in a portfolio rely on each other, and asking what happens to the whole collection when one piece slips. A portfolio is a group of projects and programs managed together to reach shared business goals. Some pieces share people, money, systems, or an output that another piece needs. A risk in one place can therefore travel to places that look unrelated on paper. Mapping those links early lets a portfolio manager see which risks matter most and keep watching them over time.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose Project A is running late, and Project B needs A's output but is on track against its own plan. Before reading on, what would you check first to decide whether the portfolio's goal is at risk?
lessons.teach:
A dependency is a link where one component needs something from another before it can finish or succeed. The something might be a finished deliverable, a shared team, a shared budget, or a decision. An interdependency is a dependency that runs both ways or loops through several components. A dependency map is a diagram or table listing each component and the links between them, with the type of each link. A propagation path is the route a delay or failure takes as it moves from one component to the next. Dependency analysis means building that map, marking the links that could carry risk, and tracking them with triggers, which are measurable signals such as a missed handoff date.

Worked example. A portfolio has three projects. Project 1 builds a vehicle tracking platform. Project 2 builds a driver app that needs Project 1's location data. Project 3 builds a billing portal that needs Project 2's data and also draws on the same integration team as Project 1. Step one: list the links. Project 1 to Project 2 is a technical handoff, and Project 1 to Project 3 is a shared team. Step two: Project 1 slips four weeks because of a vendor delay. Step three: the shared team is pulled into catch-up work, so Project 3 loses capacity. Step four: Project 2 cannot start integration until its data arrives, so it slips too, and Project 3 is blocked again. Project 3 may still report green on its own plan until the late weeks.

A common mistake is rating each project's risk alone and adding up the scores. That misses the shared team and the handoff, which move together. In a running portfolio this means the dashboard shows Project 3 as healthy while its benefits are already at risk, so escalation and reserve decisions arrive late.

Dependency analysis makes these hidden paths visible before they become the portfolio's main problem.

questions.prompt: A regional insurer runs three projects. Project Alpha builds a new claims intake form and must hand its validated claim schema to Project Beta, which builds the adjuster workbench. Project Gamma builds a customer letters engine and shares the same document-testing team with Beta. Worked through: Step 1, the links are Alpha to Beta, a technical handoff, and Beta to Gamma, a shared team. Step 2, Alpha slips five weeks because its schema sign-off is delayed by a legal review. Step 3, Beta cannot begin integration until the schema arrives, so Beta slips too. Step 4, [MISSING]. Which step completes the analysis?
choices: Beta's delay pulls the shared document-testing team away from Gamma, so Gamma loses testing capacity and slips even though its own tasks are on track.
Alpha should be rated again on its own, and the test team should be left alone until the legal review ends.
Gamma is unaffected because it does not receive any data directly from Alpha.
Gamma's own plan is still green, so no change is needed to its schedule until its own milestones slip.
questions.why: Because Beta's delay moves the shared testing team, the propagation path reaches Gamma through the shared-team link even though Gamma has no direct data link to Alpha.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines an interdependency as used in portfolio dependency analysis?
choices: A single task inside one project that must finish before another task in the same project can start.
A link that runs in both directions between two components, or a link that loops through several components.
A budget line that is shared by every project in the portfolio and reviewed once a quarter.
A risk score that combines the likelihood and impact of a problem in one component.
questions.why: An interdependency is defined in the teaching text as a dependency that runs both ways or loops through several components, which is the only option that matches that definition.

questions.prompt: A payments modernisation project and a fraud-scoring project both rely on the same platform engineering team. The team's capacity is shared, not a deliverable handed over. Which trigger best tracks this link so a problem is seen early?
choices: The annual satisfaction score of the platform engineers.
A missed date for the shared team's committed handoff or capacity commitment to one of the projects.
The total number of stories closed in each project in the last sprint.
The date the fraud-scoring project's final report is approved by the steering group.
questions.why: A trigger is a measurable signal tied to the link itself, and a missed handoff or capacity date on the shared team is the measurable signal the teaching text names for tracking that link.

questions.prompt: A health-benefits company rated its three portfolio projects separately on risk, scored each at a low level, and concluded the portfolio had little risk. Three months later, one benefit was at risk. What was the core mistake?
choices: The scores were rounded down, so the portfolio total should have been higher.
The company rated each project alone and added the scores, so it missed the shared team and handoff links where a delay in one project could move into the others.
The company used too few triggers, so the scores did not update often enough.
The company should have rated benefits instead of risks in each project.
questions.why: Rating each component alone and summing the scores hides the links that carry a delay from one component to another, which is the common mistake the teaching text describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who leads one project in this portfolio how dependency analysis changes what they should report about their own project's risk. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Dependency analysis changes the report because my project's risk is no longer just my schedule and budget. I need to show which other projects depend on my outputs and which resources we share, since a slip here can push delays onto them. So I would list each handoff with its date and owner, and flag any shared team or budget. I would also set a trigger, such as a handoff date moving by more than two weeks, that tells the portfolio team to act before the delay spreads. The main limit is that the map is only as good as the links people remember to record. Informal dependencies, like a team quietly helping another project, often go missing, so the map needs regular review. The approach also takes time to maintain, so it should cover the links that carry real risk, not every connection.
rubricPoints: Dependency analysis reports the links to other components, not only the project's own schedule and budget
Shared resources and handoffs are flagged because they can carry delay to other components
Triggers or thresholds signal when to escalate before a delay spreads
A real limit is named, such as incomplete or informal links, or the effort of keeping the map current

suggested.rationale: A portfolio-level scenario with several linked projects is best reasoned through in an exam-style situation, since no listed mission covers portfolio dependency mapping.

lessons.plain: A portfolio is the whole collection of projects and programs an organization funds to reach its goals. A risk register is a shared list of things that might go wrong, with who owns each one and what is being done about it. A portfolio-level risk register keeps one such list for the whole collection, not just for each project. It links each risk to the strategic goal it could block, and it records risks that individual projects have passed upward because they are too big for one team to handle. Think of a household budget that tracks the overall picture, not only each bill on its own.
lessons.guessPrompt: Three projects in one portfolio each have a small risk that the same key supplier will be late. Each project team rates its risk as minor. Why might the portfolio still be in trouble, and what single list would reveal the problem?
lessons.teach:
A portfolio is the set of projects and programs an organization runs together to reach its strategic goals, such as entering a new market or reducing customer churn. A component is one project or program inside that portfolio. A risk is an uncertain event that, if it happens, changes an outcome. A risk register is the list that records each risk, its likelihood, its impact, its owner, and the response being taken. A portfolio-level risk register is the version kept for the whole portfolio. It differs from project registers in two ways. First, every entry links to the strategic goal it threatens. Second, it includes component risks that a project has escalated, meaning passed upward because the project cannot handle them alone or because their combined effect crosses a threshold the portfolio has set.

Why it works: a single project may see a risk as small, while the portfolio sees the same cause touching several components and one goal. Aggregating risks and linking them to goals makes that pattern visible.

Worked example: three projects each depend on one shared cloud vendor. Project A rates vendor delay as low. Project B rates it medium. Project C rates it low. Entered on the portfolio register, the three entries share one cause, and together they threaten the goal of launching the new service in the second quarter. The portfolio owner assigns a single risk owner, sets a response, and reviews it at each governance meeting until the risk is closed or accepted.

Common mistake: copying project registers into the portfolio register without merging shared causes. Duplicates hide the common cause and leave the goal link missing.

Consequence: if escalated risks are not entered and reviewed, the portfolio can miss a strategic goal while every individual project still reports green.

The portfolio register is only useful when each entry is current and each risk owner has agreed to own it.

questions.prompt: A regional bank runs three projects: a mobile app rebuild, a branch self-service kiosk pilot, and a fraud alerts upgrade. Each project register lists the same risk: the identity verification vendor's contract ends in June and renewal terms are unsettled. Each project rates it low. The portfolio manager builds the portfolio entry in these steps. Step 1: notice that all three project entries share one cause, the vendor contract end. Step 2: merge them into one portfolio entry and keep references to the three projects. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: assign one named owner who agrees to hold the risk. Which action completes step 3?
choices: Keep the three project entries separate so each project can track its own copy of the risk
Set the likelihood to the lowest of the three project ratings so the register looks stable
Close the entry once the vendor says informally that it is interested in renewing
Link the merged entry to the strategic goal it threatens, which is growing digital account openings by 20 percent this year
questions.why: Linking the merged entry to the strategic goal it threatens is the step that makes a portfolio register different from a copy of the project registers.

questions.prompt: Which best describes an escalated component risk on a portfolio-level register?
choices: A risk a project passes upward because it cannot handle it alone, or because its combined effect with other component risks crosses a threshold the portfolio has set
A risk that every project has rated as high likelihood at the same time
Any risk a project has ever recorded in any register, including ones that were closed years ago and never reviewed by anyone
A risk that the portfolio sponsor owned from the first day the portfolio was approved
questions.why: An escalated component risk is one moved upward by a project because it cannot handle it alone or because the combined effect crosses a portfolio threshold.

questions.prompt: A hospital network runs four projects. Each project register rates its staffing risk as low. No entry on the portfolio register links staffing to the goal of opening two new clinics in 2025. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: The portfolio reports green on every component while the clinic-opening goal is at risk and nobody with portfolio authority sees it
The clinics open early because each project is under budget
The portfolio register escalates the staffing risk automatically after one quarter
The system merges the four staffing risks into one owner, which removes the gap
questions.why: Without escalation and a goal link, each project looks healthy on its own while the shared staffing cause threatens the goal unseen.

questions.prompt: Four projects in a school district all depend on one bus-routing software licence that expires before the new term. The district's goal is 95 percent on-time bus arrivals at the start of term. Which action should the portfolio register take?
choices: Leave each project's entry as rated, since each rating is low and the licence is a project matter
Merge the four entries into one, link it to the on-time arrival goal, assign one owner, and review it at each governance cycle
Hold the risk outside the register until the licence has actually expired, then log it as an issue
Keep only the highest-rated project entry and delete the rest to reduce clutter
questions.why: Merging the shared cause, linking it to the goal, assigning one owner, and reviewing it at governance is what the portfolio register is for.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who leads one project in our portfolio why a risk they rated as low might still belong on the portfolio risk register. Name one limit or tradeoff of keeping a single register for the whole portfolio.
lessons.modelAnswer: A risk can look small inside one project and still matter for the portfolio. If the same cause, such as a shared vendor, a common skill shortage, or one regulatory change, affects several projects, the portfolio sees a combined exposure that no single project sees. Escalating it means the risk gets a portfolio-level owner, a linked strategic goal, and a response that is coordinated across teams. The tradeoff is that one register takes effort to keep current. Entries can go stale, and a long list can hide the few items that matter most. So the register needs a clear escalation threshold, regular owner reviews, and merging of duplicate entries, or it becomes a document nobody trusts.
rubricPoints: Explains that a portfolio register aggregates risks that look small within one project but share a cause or threaten a common goal
Mentions escalation: passing a risk upward when a project cannot handle it alone or when a threshold is crossed
Names a real limit or tradeoff, such as upkeep effort, stale entries, or long lists hiding priorities
Notes that each entry needs a named owner and a link to a strategic goal

suggested.rationale: Explaining escalation and aggregation to a teammate, including a tradeoff, is the core skill here and no listed mission or planned engine covers portfolio risk registers.

lessons.plain: A portfolio is a group of projects and programmes that an organisation runs together to reach its goals. Risks are uncertain events that could hurt or help those goals. Building understanding and ownership means making sure the people who fund, use or are affected by those risks know what each risk is, how big it could be, and who is responsible for watching it. A risk nobody understands or owns is a risk nobody manages. Communication is the tool: the right message, to the right people, at the right time, with a clear request for a decision or action. Think of a shared weather forecast that tells each team what to pack and who checks the sky.
lessons.guessPrompt: A portfolio manager has spotted a supplier problem that could delay three projects at once. The sponsors have not heard about it yet. Before any teaching, what is the most important thing to get right in how the manager tells them, and why?
lessons.teach:
A stakeholder is anyone who can affect or is affected by the portfolio, such as sponsors who fund it, project managers who run its pieces, and business leaders who will use the results. A portfolio risk is an uncertain event that could affect the portfolio's strategic goals, often one that crosses several projects. Ownership means one named person is accountable for watching a risk and carrying out its response. Understanding means the stakeholder can state the risk, its likely impact, and what they are being asked to do.

Why it works: people act on risks they feel are theirs. A risk that sits in a spreadsheet tends to be read as someone else's problem until it becomes an issue. Good communication turns a list of facts into a decision request. The portfolio manager states the risk in business terms, gives the size of the exposure, names the proposed owner, and asks for a specific choice, such as accept, reduce, or fund a contingency.

Worked example. Three projects in a portfolio all depend on one vendor for a licensing component. Step one: the manager confirms the risk is shared, since a vendor delay would push all three back about six weeks. Step two: she writes the message in plain terms: the vendor may slip, and the impact is a six-week delay to three revenue-linked projects. Step three: she proposes an owner, the vendor-management lead, and a response, an evaluation of a second supplier. Step four: she asks the sponsor to approve a small study budget by Friday. Step five: she asks each sponsor to restate the risk, its impact and the decision needed, back to her.

Common mistake: sending the full risk register and assuming it has been understood. A register is a record, not a conversation.

Consequence: in a running portfolio, an unowned risk escalates late, when fewer responses are still available, and the sponsor learns of it from a delayed status report.

questions.prompt: A retail chain runs four store-refit projects that all depend on one imported fixture supplier. Step one: the portfolio manager confirms the risk is shared, since a customs hold would delay all four refits by about five weeks. Step two: she writes the message in plain terms: the supplier's shipments may be held at the border, and the impact is a five-week delay to four projects that reopen stores in the holiday season. Step three is missing. Step four: she asks the regional director to approve a small budget for a backup freight option by Thursday. Step five: she asks each project sponsor to restate the risk, its impact and the decision needed, back to her. Which choice correctly completes step three?
choices: Names the procurement lead as owner and proposes a response of pre-clearing shipping paperwork with a customs broker.
Names the finance analyst as owner and asks the sponsors to vote on the full risk register at the next governance meeting.
Waits until the shipment is actually held and then escalates the problem to the regional director.
Sends the complete risk register to all four sponsors and assumes they will review it before the next status report.
questions.why: Step three is where the manager names a single accountable owner and proposes a specific response, which the teaching text describes as part of turning facts into a decision request.

questions.prompt: In portfolio risk communication, what does ownership mean?
choices: One named person who is accountable for watching a risk and carrying out its response.
A written record in the risk register showing which project created each risk.
Holding the budget that the portfolio has set aside for all of its risks.
Being the sponsor who funds the portfolio and approves its major changes.
questions.why: The teaching text defines ownership as one named person being accountable for watching a risk and carrying out its response, which is the option that matches that definition.

questions.prompt: A portfolio manager emails a 60-page risk register to five sponsors and reports that the risks have been communicated. What is the main gap?
choices: The sponsors were not given a spreadsheet, which is the only format they can read.
The sponsors should have received the register only after an issue has already occurred.
A register is a record, not a conversation, so no risk was stated in business terms, no owner was named, and no decision was requested.
The register is too long, so the manager should have sent only the top three risks by score.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that sending the full register and assuming it was understood is a common mistake, because a register is a record rather than a conversation that gets a decision.

questions.prompt: A program manager tells a board member: The new billing system carries some risk, so please keep an eye on it. Which statement best identifies what is missing for the board member to have real understanding?
choices: The message names no owner, gives no size of the impact, and asks for no specific decision.
The message should have waited until the risk became an issue, to avoid alarming the board.
The message should have included a formal risk log number so it can be traced in the register.
The message should have been written as a score from one to five rather than in plain words.
questions.why: Understanding means the stakeholder can state the risk, its likely impact, and what they are being asked to do, and the message gives none of those three things, nor a named owner.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to portfolio work why a portfolio manager should get each stakeholder to restate a shared risk and its owner, and name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Restating is the cheapest test that the message landed. When a sponsor says back, in their own words, what the risk is, what it would cost, who is watching it, and what they must decide, the manager knows the message was understood rather than just delivered. It also makes ownership explicit: a stakeholder who has agreed to a role is more likely to act on it. The tradeoff is time and sensitivity. Repeated check-ins take effort across a busy portfolio, and some senior people find being asked to restate things patronising, so the manager should keep it brief and focused on the decision. Restatement also does not settle the risk itself. It shows understanding, so the manager still needs a documented decision on the response and a named owner.
rubricPoints: Restating confirms understanding, not just delivery of the message.
Ownership needs one named, accountable person for the risk and its response.
Names a real limit, such as time cost or friction with senior stakeholders.
Understanding does not replace a documented decision on the risk response.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the idea back to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine teaches stakeholder communication directly.

lessons.plain: When a group of projects is run together as a portfolio, some money or time should be kept back at the top level for surprises that no single project can cover alone. That shared holding is the portfolio management reserve. Working out how big it should be means looking at all the risks across the whole set of projects together, not one project at a time, and then asking the people who govern the portfolio to approve it. Think of it like a household emergency fund set aside for the whole family rather than separate pots for each child's bills.
lessons.guessPrompt: Three projects in one portfolio each keep their own small contingency fund for their own risks. Why might the portfolio still need a separate fund held at the top level, and who should decide how big it is?
lessons.teach:
A portfolio management reserve is a sum of money, or a block of time, that the portfolio itself holds back. It is not assigned to any one component. A component is one project or program inside the portfolio. Each component usually keeps its own contingency reserve for risks it can see. The portfolio reserve exists for what those local reserves cannot cover: risks that span several components, or risks nobody has identified yet.

Aggregate risk exposure means the total impact of all portfolio risks combined. Exposure is roughly the size of a risk's impact multiplied by how likely it is. You must not simply add component figures, because some risks are linked. Two components that depend on the same vendor can fail together. Linked risks are called correlated risks, and they can make combined exposure larger than the separate totals suggest.

Worked example. Component A holds a contingency of 0.5 million. Component B holds 0.8 million. Component C holds 0.4 million. The local total is 1.7 million. Step one: check for shared risks. A and B both rely on one vendor. If that vendor fails, A and B together need 0.6 million beyond their own contingencies. Step two: size the portfolio reserve to cover that shortfall. Step three: write a recommendation that states the amount, the scenario it covers, the trigger that releases it, and the approver, then obtain approval from the governance body.

Common mistake: treating the reserve as a general fund any manager can spend, or sizing it as the simple sum of local contingencies. Consequence: if the reserve is too small, one vendor failure can overrun several components at once and the portfolio misses its targets. If it is too large, capital sits idle that other investments could use. A reserve is only sound when its size, its release triggers and its approver are written down and agreed.

questions.prompt: A regional logistics firm runs three components. X is warehouse automation with a contingency of 0.3 million. Y is routing software with a contingency of 0.6 million. Z is driver training with a contingency of 0.2 million. X and Y both buy sensors from one supplier. Step one: identify the shared risk. If that supplier fails, X and Y together need 1.2 million. Step two: size the portfolio reserve to cover the part of that need that the local contingencies of X and Y cannot cover. Step three: write the recommendation with the amount, the scenario, the release trigger and the approver, then obtain governance approval. Step two is left blank here. What amount should the portfolio reserve be sized to in step two?
choices: 0.3 million
1.2 million
0.9 million
0.6 million
questions.why: X and Y hold 0.9 million of local contingency against a 1.2 million shared need, so the portfolio reserve must cover the 0.3 million shortfall, and Z is not part of the shared scenario.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines a portfolio management reserve?
choices: A reserve held by the portfolio itself for risks that span several components or that nobody has identified yet
The total of all component contingencies added together
A general fund that any manager can draw on whenever a cost rises
A contingency each component holds for the risks it can see on its own
questions.why: The teaching text defines the portfolio reserve as money or time the portfolio holds back, not assigned to any one component, for cross-component and unidentified risks.

questions.prompt: Component P holds a contingency of 0.2 million, Component Q holds 0.4 million and Component R holds 0.5 million. P and R both run on one cloud host. If that host fails, P and R together need 0.9 million. Which portfolio reserve size is correct for this scenario?
choices: 0.9 million, the full scenario cost
0.2 million, the amount beyond P and R's combined local contingencies of 0.7 million
0.0 million, because the local contingencies cover the event
1.1 million, the sum of all three contingencies
questions.why: Sizing the reserve means covering only the shortfall after the affected components' own contingencies (0.9 minus 0.7 equals 0.2 million), and Q is not involved in the shared risk.

questions.prompt: A component manager with a cost overrun of 0.15 million asks to draw on the portfolio reserve. The overrun comes from a risk unique to that component, and its own contingency could cover it, but no release trigger or approver has been agreed. What is the right response?
choices: Hold the request until the agreed trigger and governance approval are in place, and check whether the component's own contingency should absorb it first
Release the funds, because the reserve is a general fund for any shortfall
Split the reserve equally among all components before deciding anything
Cut the reserve by the overrun amount, since no approval is needed for a reduction
questions.why: The teaching text says a reserve is only sound when its size, release triggers and approver are written down and agreed, and it is meant for cross-component or unidentified risks, not single-component overruns.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to portfolio work how a portfolio management reserve differs from component contingencies, how you would size it from aggregate exposure, and one limit or tradeoff of holding it.
lessons.modelAnswer: A component contingency belongs to one project and covers that project's known risks. The portfolio management reserve sits above those and is held by the portfolio itself. I would size it by listing the component risks, estimating each one's exposure, and then checking where risks are linked, such as two components relying on the same vendor. Linked risks can fail together and push combined exposure above the simple sum, so I would size the reserve to cover a realistic stressed case rather than the average. The tradeoff is that money or time held in reserve is not working in any component, so an oversized reserve delays other value, while an undersized one leaves the portfolio exposed. Before anyone draws on it, I would need the governance body to approve the amount, the triggers that release it, and who signs off each release.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes the portfolio reserve from component contingency reserves.
Sizes the reserve from aggregate exposure, accounting for correlated risks rather than a simple sum.
Names the tradeoff of holding too much or too little reserve.
States that the reserve needs governance approval with defined release triggers.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers portfolio-level reserve sizing, so an exam-style scenario to reason through adds the most.

lessons.plain: Stakeholders are the people and groups who care about a portfolio of projects, such as sponsors, team members, customers, regulators or suppliers. Analyzing them means finding out what each one expects from the portfolio and how much power they have to help or block it. You do this by talking with people in meetings, holding one-on-one interviews, and sending out surveys, then writing down what you learned. It is like asking around a neighbourhood before you build a fence: you learn who cares, what they want, and who can make the work easier or harder.
lessons.guessPrompt: A portfolio has five projects, and one of them will change how a regional operations team works every day. Before you talk to anyone, which group do you think you should understand first, and why?
lessons.teach: A stakeholder is anyone who affects or is affected by the portfolio. Internal stakeholders work inside your organization, such as sponsors, executives and staff. External stakeholders sit outside it, such as customers, regulators and suppliers. An expectation is what a stakeholder wants to see happen, including deadlines, quality, cost and how they want to be told about progress. Influence is how much a stakeholder can shape decisions, approve funding or stop work. Analysis means gathering evidence about both. Meetings show group dynamics, interviews reveal private concerns and reasons, and surveys measure how many people share a view. Each method covers a gap in the others, which is why you combine them. Worked example: a portfolio includes a cutover that will pause dispatch for two hours. Step 1: list the groups affected. Step 2: interview the operations director, who reveals that zero unplanned downtime is non-negotiable. Step 3: survey forty field staff, which shows training is their top worry. Step 4: record the director's influence as high, since they approve the cutover window. Step 5: plan a monthly one-on-one with the director and a training briefing for staff. A common mistake is treating the sponsor's opinion as the whole picture, or trusting survey averages without asking who did not respond. In a running system, a high-influence group left unheard can withhold approval at the last minute, so the cutover slips and the planned work piles up. The stakeholder analysis is only useful when it changes what you do next.

questions.prompt: A regional water utility is moving customer billing to a new system, and the switchover will suspend online payments for one night. Step 1: list the groups affected, which gives customers, the finance team and the state consumer regulator. Step 2: interview the finance director, who says that no payment can be lost or double-charged. Step 3: survey 200 customer service agents, which shows that scripts for the new screens are their top concern. Step 4 is missing from this plan. Step 5: schedule a fortnightly check-in with the finance director and a scripts walkthrough for agents. Which step 4 completes the analysis?
choices: Average the survey results across all 200 agents and report the mean to the steering committee as the group view.
Ask the project sponsor to name the stakeholders who matter and skip further gathering from the others.
Record each group's influence, such as high for the finance director who can approve the switchover night, so the attention given to each group matches its power to shape or stop the work.
Send a summary of the billing change to every customer by email so the group is informed.
questions.why: Step 4 is to record each group's influence, which tells you how much weight its expectations deserve before you choose the follow-up actions.

questions.prompt: Which pairing correctly classifies the stakeholders?
choices: Both are external, since a portfolio always sits apart from its organization
A department's own IT staff as external and a state regulator as internal
A department's own IT staff as internal and a state regulator as external
Both are internal, since both are paid through the same budget
questions.why: Internal stakeholders work inside your organization, so the department's IT staff are internal, while a state regulator sits outside it and is external.

questions.prompt: A team surveys 120 users of a booking app, gets 15 replies that are all very positive, and reports that the app is well liked. What is the main gap in this analysis?
choices: The team needed more positive responses before reporting anything at all.
Fifteen replies is too many, so the team should have surveyed fewer people.
The survey should have been a meeting instead, because meetings always give more honest answers.
The team has not asked who did not respond, so the result may not represent the wider group.
questions.why: Surveys measure how many people share a view, but averages are only trustworthy if you ask who did not respond, and here most users did not reply.

questions.prompt: A portfolio manager needs to learn why a deputy director quietly opposes a new reporting tool, and how many staff share that view. Which pairing of methods fits best?
choices: A survey to uncover the deputy's private reasons, and a meeting to measure how many people hold the view.
Two surveys, since surveys are the only method that can reveal private concerns.
Only a meeting, since group dynamics reveal every person's private reasons.
An interview to uncover the deputy's private reasons, and a survey to measure how many people hold the view.
questions.why: Interviews reveal private concerns and reasons, while surveys measure how many people share a view, so each method covers the gap the other leaves.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use meetings, interviews and surveys to find out each stakeholder's expectations and influence, and name one limit of relying on survey results alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing every internal and external group the portfolio touches, then use each method for what it does well. Meetings show how groups react to each other and where tension sits. Interviews let me ask the people with real decision power what they need, why, and what would make them say no. Surveys let me check whether a concern is shared across many people. Once I have the evidence, I rate each stakeholder on expectations and influence, and I write down the engagement I will do with each one. The main limit of survey results is that they measure only the people who answered, and people with strong influence are often too busy to respond. A survey can show that staff are worried about training while missing that a regulator with final approval has a different view. So I would never treat survey averages as the complete picture, and I would confirm the high-influence views in an interview.
rubricPoints: Defines stakeholders as internal or external and explains expectations and influence as separate things to analyze
Explains that meetings, interviews and surveys each reveal different information and are combined
Gives an example of how analysis changes the engagement plan for a specific stakeholder
Names a limit of survey data, such as non-response or missing high-influence views, and says how to close it

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a stakeholder situation with mixed interview and survey evidence adds more than reading definitions, and no listed mission covers this objective directly.

lessons.plain: An aggregate communication strategy is the single overall plan for how a whole group of projects, called a portfolio, talks to the people who care about it. Instead of each project inventing its own messages, the plan decides in one place who needs to hear what, through which channel, how often, and by when. Think of a city's master bus timetable: each route runs on its own, but one shared timetable stops buses bunching up and leaves no stop unserved. The plan answers five questions: who, what, how, through which tool, and when.
lessons.guessPrompt: A portfolio has four projects, and the board, the project managers and the finance team each want different updates. Before reading on, what single thing would you put in place so the three groups do not receive conflicting numbers or miss the updates they need?
lessons.teach: A portfolio is a set of projects and programs grouped to meet shared business goals. A stakeholder is anyone who can affect the portfolio or is affected by it. A communication strategy is the high-level approach: why we communicate, the principles we follow, and the overall balance between formal and informal channels. A communication plan is the detailed working version of that strategy. For each piece of information it names the recipients, the method, the vehicle, the timeline and the frequency. A method is the pattern of the exchange, such as one-way sending, pulling information from a shared source, or two-way discussion. A vehicle is the concrete medium, such as a one-page dashboard, a steering pack, or a weekly tracker. Frequency is how often a message repeats. Timeline is the specific due date for a one-off item. Aggregate means rolling each project's own plan into one portfolio view, so duplicates and clashes show up. It works because one view exposes overlaps, so leaders do not get three different status figures for the same project and nobody important is left out. Worked example: the board needs a portfolio health view monthly, so it gets a one-page dashboard plus a steering pack three business days before each meeting. Project managers need task detail weekly, so they get a tracker updated every Monday morning. Finance needs benefit figures quarterly, so it gets a benefits report. Step four: the regional operations team also needs project B status, so the plan points them to the same tracker as the project managers instead of making a separate report. One source feeds all three, so the numbers agree. Common mistake: listing channels such as email, meetings and an intranet without tying each one to a recipient and a purpose. Messages then go to people who do not need them, while the board receives its data late. Consequence: if two channels publish different status for the same project, leadership trusts neither, and decisions stall until someone reconciles the figures.

questions.prompt: A water utility runs three capital projects: a pipe replacement, a meter upgrade and a pump station rebuild. Its portfolio office builds one communication plan from the three project plans. Step one: the board receives a one-page risk view each quarter, issued five business days before the meeting. Step two: the contractor coordinator receives a weekly milestone list, pulled every Friday from the shared project register. Step three: the regulator liaison receives a monthly compliance pack, built from the same register. Step four: [missing]. Step five: the office confirms that the board, the coordinator and the regulator liaison all draw on the one register, so the numbers match.
choices: Compare each figure in the board pack with the shared register and fix any difference before the pack is released.
Ask each project manager to write a separate risk paragraph for the board so the board hears from every project.
Change the board's risk view from quarterly to weekly so the figures are always fresh.
Email the board pack to the regulator's inbox too, so both groups see the same figures at the same time.
questions.why: Checking each figure against the single shared register before release is the accuracy check that stops two versions of the same status from reaching leadership.

questions.prompt: A hospital's IT portfolio has a communication strategy and a communication plan. Which statement correctly separates the two?
choices: The strategy is the detailed schedule of who gets which report, and the plan is the reason the organisation communicates at all.
The strategy and the plan are two names for the same document, used at different stages of a project.

The strategy sets the reason for communicating, the principles and the balance of formal and informal channels, while the plan details recipients, method, vehicle, timeline and frequency for each item.
The strategy covers only informal channels such as chat, and the plan covers only formal channels such as board packs.
questions.why: The strategy is the high-level approach, and the plan is the detailed working version that names recipients, method, vehicle, timeline and frequency for each piece of information.

questions.prompt: A retail chain's portfolio has two projects. Each week, the store-rollout project sends leaders a green status from its own spreadsheet, while the same project's status from the finance tool shows red. Leaders now delay the funding decision. What is the most direct fix?
choices: Ask the store-rollout team to rename its spreadsheet so it is easier to tell apart from the finance tool.
Send both status figures to leaders every day so they can see the trend and decide which one to trust.
Point both channels at one shared status source so the same project shows one figure everywhere, then reconcile the current gap once.
Hold a longer weekly meeting so the two teams can debate which colour is right before leaders see anything.
questions.why: A single source feeding every channel removes the conflicting figures, which is the reason aggregating into one portfolio view exposes and prevents duplicate or clashing status.

questions.prompt: A regional council's portfolio needs a one-off data-retention notice sent to a regulator by 14 March. Which element of a communication plan records that specific date?
choices: Method, because the notice is a one-way send.
Timeline, because the timeline is the specific due date for a one-off item.
Frequency, because the notice repeats on a set cycle.
Vehicle, because the notice is delivered as a letter.
questions.why: Timeline is the element that holds the specific due date for a one-off item, while frequency describes how often a message repeats.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a new teammate how a single aggregate communication plan for a whole portfolio differs from each project's own communication plan, and name one limit or tradeoff of building one aggregate plan.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each project's plan covers only its own team and its own sponsor. An aggregate plan sits above them and maps every recipient group in the portfolio to the information it needs, the method and vehicle it should use, and a timeline and frequency that do not clash. Its main benefit is that overlaps are visible, so one data source can feed several audiences and the numbers agree. The tradeoff is cost and staleness. Building the aggregate view takes time up front and needs agreement across several project managers. If the plan is not reviewed, it drifts out of step with the projects, and a fixed cadence can overload some stakeholders while under-serving others. So the plan needs an owner and a scheduled review.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes the portfolio-level aggregate plan from individual project plans
Maps recipients, information needs, methods, vehicles, timelines and frequency together
Explains that a single source of data prevents conflicting figures
Names a real limit such as up-front effort, drift over time, or cadence that misfits some audiences
Notes the plan needs an owner and periodic review

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining how the plan components fit together and what tradeoffs an aggregate plan carries, which is best practised by talking it through.

lessons.plain: A portfolio is the set of projects and programs an organization funds and manages together. A portfolio roadmap is a time-ordered picture of what that set plans to deliver and roughly when. Engaging stakeholders about the roadmap means telling the people it affects, both out loud and in writing, what is planned, why it matters to them, and what is still uncertain, so they are aware of it before decisions land on them.
