Think of a city publishing its road-works schedule in advance: drivers who see it plan around it, while drivers who learn about it only when the road closes are annoyed. The goal is awareness, not agreement on every detail.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project sponsor hears from a colleague, the week before a budget meeting, that three projects on the roadmap were quietly moved back by a quarter. Why is the sponsor most likely upset, and what single communication would have prevented it?
lessons.teach:
A stakeholder is anyone who can affect or is affected by the portfolio, such as sponsors, finance, operations leads, and the teams doing the work. A roadmap is a sequenced view of planned work: themes, target time windows, and dependencies, meaning cases where one piece of work cannot start until another finishes. Awareness means a stakeholder knows what is planned, when, why, and what it changes for them. Oral communication is spoken: briefings, review meetings, one-to-one conversations. Written communication is documents such as one-page summaries, newsletters, and change notices. Awareness works because people adjust budgets, staffing, and their own plans only for changes they have seen early.

Worked example. The roadmap shows a billing rewrite targeted for Q3 that depends on a data platform targeted for Q2. Step one: list recipients, here finance, the billing operations lead, and the sponsors. Step two: send a one-page written summary that labels dates as target windows, not commitments, and names the dependency. Step three: walk through the same content orally at the monthly review, explaining what happens if the platform slips. Step four: ask each lead to restate in their own words what changes for their team. Step five: send written answers to the questions raised.

Common mistake: presenting target dates as firm commitments, or assuming a dense spreadsheet has been understood because it was sent. Consequence in a running portfolio: when the data platform slips, stakeholders who were told the dates were firm have planned around false dates, trust drops, and escalations arrive late.

Awareness is built by two-way exchange, repeated over time, with dates framed honestly.

questions.prompt: A regional credit union plans a mobile app redesign with a target window of Q2. That work depends on a new customer identity service targeted for Q1, so the app cannot go live until the identity service is in place. The portfolio team has already listed the recipients (branch operations, card services, and the sponsoring executive) and sent each of them a one-page written summary that labels Q1 and Q2 as target windows and names the dependency. Step still missing: the team has not yet held an oral review that walks through the same content and explains what happens to the app launch if the identity service slips. Which action completes the missing step?
choices: Re-send the one-page summary with a longer appendix of every task in the identity project.
Hold a review where the content is walked through orally, including what happens to the app launch if the identity service slips.
Confirm the Q2 app date as firm so that recipients stop asking about it.
Wait until the identity service is live before telling card services what the app will change for them.
questions.why: The worked pattern calls for an oral walkthrough that explains the consequence of a slip, which is the step the scenario has not yet done.

questions.prompt: In a portfolio roadmap, what does awareness mean for a stakeholder?
choices: The stakeholder knows what is planned, when it is planned, why, and what it changes for them.
The stakeholder can estimate the cost of each theme on the roadmap.
The stakeholder has approved the target dates on the roadmap.
The stakeholder has received a copy of every planning document in the portfolio.
questions.why: The teaching text defines awareness as knowing what is planned, when, why, and what it changes for the stakeholder.

questions.prompt: A portfolio manager sends a dense spreadsheet of roadmap dates to the finance director and then reports that finance is fully aware of the plan. Two months later finance has adjusted nothing and asks why it was not warned. What is the most likely gap?
choices: The manager assumed understanding from sending the material, with no two-way exchange to confirm it.
Finance should have been removed from the recipient list because it is not a stakeholder.
The spreadsheet should have been converted into a newsletter.
The dates should have been stated as firm commitments so finance would act on them.
questions.why: Sending a dense document does not prove understanding, and awareness requires a two-way exchange that the manager skipped.

questions.prompt: A packaging plant plans a line upgrade targeted for Q4 that cannot start until a supplier certification finishes, targeted for Q3. Which group should be treated as stakeholders for this roadmap item, using the broad meaning of the term?
choices: Only the sponsor who approved the budget.
Only the supplier that holds the certification.
The sponsor, the plant supervisors, procurement, and anyone whose budget or staffing the upgrade could change.
Only the plant supervisors who will run the new line.
questions.why: A stakeholder is anyone who can affect or is affected by the portfolio, which covers sponsors, finance, operations leads and the teams doing the work.

lessons.explainPrompt: You are about to brief a steering group on the portfolio roadmap for the next four quarters. Explain to a teammate how you would use both spoken and written communication to build the group's awareness of it, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with a one-page written summary sent before the meeting, so people arrive knowing the themes, target windows, and key dependencies. I would label every date as a target, not a commitment, so nobody plans around a promise we cannot keep. In the meeting I would walk through the same material orally, focusing on the two or three dependencies that would change someone's budget or staffing if they slipped. Then I would ask each leader to restate what changes for their team, because nodding is not evidence of understanding. Afterward I would send written answers to the open questions. The tradeoff is time: a pre-read plus a live walkthrough plus follow-up takes effort, and a group that never reads the summary may still need the discussion to carry the message.
rubricPoints: Uses both written pre-read and oral walkthrough, with a reason for each
Frames roadmap dates as targets or windows, not firm commitments
Checks understanding by asking stakeholders to restate impacts
Names a real limit or tradeoff such as time cost or uneven reading

suggested.rationale: Briefing a group clearly in speech and writing, then checking understanding, is the core skill here and no listed mission or engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: A communication plan is a written schedule of who needs to hear what, through which channel, and how often about a portfolio of projects. Maintaining the plan means checking it regularly to confirm it can still be carried out by the people, tools, and channels that actually exist. A capability is something the team can really do, such as producing a monthly summary, running a meeting with executives, or pulling accurate numbers from a system. When the plan asks for something the team cannot yet deliver, that difference is a gap. This objective is about finding those gaps, judging which ones matter, and closing them so the plan keeps working.
lessons.guessPrompt: A steering committee expects a consolidated risk summary every Monday, but the analyst who builds it is now on leave and nobody else has done it before. What is the first thing you would check before changing the plan, and why?
lessons.teach:
A communication plan lists stakeholder groups, the messages they need, the channels or vehicles used to reach them (such as email, dashboards, or meetings), the frequency, and the owner of each item. Maintaining the plan means reviewing it over time so it still matches what the portfolio needs and what the organization can actually deliver. Evaluating capabilities means asking, for each planned item, whether the people, skills, tools, data access, and time exist to produce it at the required quality and rhythm. A gap is the distance between what the plan requires and what is currently available.

Why this works: a plan on paper is only a promise. Most communication failures happen not because nobody planned a message but because the planned message depends on something missing, such as a data source that updates late, an owner who is overloaded, or a template nobody knows how to fill. Checking each commitment against real capability exposes these problems before a stakeholder notices them.

Worked example: the plan promises a risk summary to the steering committee every Monday by noon, built from three project tools. The review finds that the data from one tool is extracted by hand, takes two days, and only one analyst knows the process. Step 1: state the requirement (weekly, by noon Monday, accurate). Step 2: state the available capability (one analyst, manual extract, two days). Step 3: name the gap (timing and a single-person dependency). Step 4: choose a closure, such as cross-training a second analyst and moving the extract to Thursday, then record the change in the plan. Step 5: verify by running one full cycle and comparing the output against the governance accuracy checklist.

Common mistake: responding to a gap by telling people to communicate more or by adding another meeting. That adds load without fixing the capability underneath. A second mistake is updating the plan without testing that the fix works.

Consequence: in a running portfolio, an unclosed gap shows up as late or wrong figures reaching the committee, which erodes trust and can delay funding decisions. Close the gap at its source, then confirm it with a test run.

questions.prompt: A shared-services team promises its executive council a cost-variance summary (a table showing how actual spending differs from budget) every Friday at 9am. Step 1, the requirement: a weekly summary by Friday 9am, with figures current to Thursday close. Step 2, the available capability: a finance extract (a copy of data pulled from the accounting system) refreshes nightly at 2am, but the summary template is maintained by one contractor who works Mondays only, and the template's cost column has a known error that makes totals wrong. Step 3 is missing. Which statement correctly completes it by naming the gap?
choices: The finance extract refreshes too often, so the figures are unreliable and the refresh should be slowed down.
There is no gap, because the extract refreshes every night and so the Friday figures are current.
The team needs a daily stand-up with the executives so they see the spending numbers earlier in the week.
The gap is that a known template error cannot be corrected before Friday because the only person who can fix it is unavailable until Monday.
questions.why: The gap is the distance between the requirement (accurate figures by Friday) and the capability (a known fault that only one unavailable person can fix), so naming it is step 3.

questions.prompt: In this course's sense, what is a gap in a communication plan?
choices: The distance between what the plan requires and what is currently available to produce it.
A message that stakeholders have stopped reading.
A meeting added to the calendar after the plan was approved.
A stakeholder group that was left off the plan's list.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a gap as the distance between what the plan requires and what is currently available, which is the first option.

questions.prompt: A portfolio's monthly benefits report to the sponsor is due on the 5th and is built from a benefits tracker that only one analyst updates. That analyst is moving to another program next month. Which response best applies the capability review to this situation?
choices: Leave the plan as it is, since the report will still be produced on the 5th by whoever is available.
Move the due date to the 20th so the current analyst has more time to finish.
Document the tracker update process and assign a second named owner before the analyst leaves.
Send the sponsor a weekly reminder that the report is coming, so it is not forgotten.
questions.why: The single-person dependency is the gap, and the fix is to close it at its source by giving the tracker update a second owner before the capability disappears.

questions.prompt: A team changes its risk summary for the steering committee from weekly to daily, but does not check whether its data extract can support daily delivery. The extract currently takes two days to prepare by hand. What is the most accurate description of the problem?
choices: The plan is fine, because a daily promise shows the committee more commitment to stakeholders.
The committee needs more meetings to discuss the risk summary before the plan can work.
The team should add a note to the plan saying figures may be late, then publish daily anyway.
The plan now promises something the capability cannot deliver, so the gap is unclosed and late or wrong figures will reach the committee.
questions.why: A commitment that exceeds real capability leaves an unclosed gap, which the teaching text says shows up as late or wrong figures reaching the committee.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell whether our communication plan can still be delivered, and name one limit of that check.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would go through the plan line by line and, for each commitment, ask who produces it, with which tool and data, how long it takes, and whether that person and that time are actually available this quarter. Any answer like 'only one person' or 'the data arrives late' is a gap. For each gap I would decide whether to close it by changing the capability (training, data access, a second owner), by changing the channel or frequency so it fits reality, or by escalating if it needs budget. Then I would run one cycle and check the output against the accuracy checklist before calling the gap closed. The limit is that this check only shows what the team can do today. It cannot predict absences, tool outages, or changes in what stakeholders need, so the review has to repeat on a schedule and after any major change.
rubricPoints: Checks each planned item against real people, tools, data, and time
Names the gap as the difference between what is required and what is available
Chooses a fix that targets the cause, such as training, access, or a changed channel or frequency
Verifies the fix with a test cycle and updates the plan accordingly

suggested.rationale: No listed mission covers stakeholder communication planning, so an exam-style scenario to reason through gap closure adds the most here.

lessons.plain: Portfolio management is the practice of looking after a whole set of projects and programs as one group, so the organization funds the right ones and stops the wrong ones. Its processes are the repeatable steps it uses, such as how ideas are proposed, scored, approved, reviewed and stopped. Its protocols are the agreed rules for how those steps are carried out, such as who decides, what paperwork is needed and how a disagreement is escalated. Facilitating stakeholder understanding means helping the people affected by these steps see how the system works and why, so they use it correctly instead of guessing. It is like explaining the rulebook before the match starts, not only blowing the whistle during it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A department head is annoyed that their project was paused and says nobody explained how the decision was made. Before reading anything, what would you do first to help them understand the process, and what do you think they most need to know?
lessons.teach:
A portfolio is the full set of projects, programs and operational work an organization is running or considering. Portfolio management is the ongoing practice of choosing, prioritizing, funding, reviewing and stopping items in that set so they support the organization's strategy. A process is a repeatable sequence of steps, such as intake, scoring, approval and periodic review. A protocol is the agreed rule for how a step is carried out: who decides, which criteria apply, which form is used, how often the decision forum meets, and how a disagreement is escalated. Governance is the set of decision rights and oversight that makes these rules binding.

Facilitating understanding means making those processes and protocols visible and usable for stakeholders, including sponsors, team leads, finance and delivery staff. It works because people accept a decision more readily when they can see the criteria, the decision-maker and the route to appeal, and because consistent use of the same steps makes results comparable across items.

Worked example: a sponsor asks why their project was paused. Step 1: the facilitator confirms the item's record and the date it was last scored. Step 2: they show the agreed scoring criteria and how the project's score compared with the funding cut-off. Step 3: they name the forum that made the decision and its next review date. Step 4: they explain the appeal route and what new evidence would change the outcome.

Common mistake: sending the full governance handbook and assuming it has been understood. A document does not create understanding; a short walk-through of the actual decision record does.

Consequence: when stakeholders do not understand the protocol, they route requests around it, escalate informally and reopen decided items, which slows the whole portfolio and weakens the governance it depends on. Facilitation is therefore a control activity, not a courtesy.

questions.prompt: A university IT office is explaining a decision to a history department head, Dr. Okafor, who asked why the lab-refresh request was deferred to the next funding cycle. Step 1: the facilitator pulls the request record and confirms it was scored on 14 March. Step 2: the facilitator shows the agreed scoring criteria: strategic fit 40 percent, risk 20 percent, cost-benefit 40 percent. The request scored 58 against a funding cut-off of 65. Step 3 is missing. Which action completes the walk-through before the appeal route is explained?
choices: Send the full IT governance handbook so Dr. Okafor can read the rules directly.
Re-score the request with strategic fit weighted higher so it clears the cut-off.
Escalate the request straight to the steering chair without a decision record.
Name the forum that made the decision and give its next review date.
questions.why: The walk-through shows the decision-maker and the next review point, which is the step that makes the decision traceable before the appeal route is discussed.

questions.prompt: In portfolio management, what is the difference between a process and a protocol?
choices: A process and a protocol are two names for the same set of forms used in funding reviews.
A protocol is the funding cut-off figure, and a process is the scoring spreadsheet that produces the score.
A process is the agreed rule for who may approve a request, and a protocol is the sequence of steps that follows that approval.

A process is a repeatable sequence of steps such as intake or review, while a protocol is the agreed rule for carrying out one step, covering who decides, which criteria apply and how disputes escalate.
questions.why: A process is the ordered sequence of steps and a protocol is the agreed rule that governs how each step is run, including decision rights and escalation.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's operations director keeps emailing the CFO to reopen a warehouse-automation item that the portfolio forum already decided and funded. Which facilitation response best addresses the underlying problem?
choices: Remove the director from the distribution list so the emails stop.
Send the full policy manual and ask the director to read the section on reopening items.
Approve the reopening because the CFO has authority over the budget.
Show the director the decision record and the appeal route, including what new evidence would change the outcome.
questions.why: Stakeholders who understand the decision record and appeal route stop routing requests around the forum, whereas ignoring, overriding or merely sending documents does not build that understanding.

questions.prompt: A status report tells a sponsor that a project is funded because its score of 72 is above the cut-off of 70. Before the facilitator repeats that figure at a meeting, what accuracy check should come first?
choices: Quote the score as written, since the sponsor is unlikely to check the underlying record.
Wait until the next forum meeting before saying anything about the funding decision.
Recalculate the score using your own preferred weightings so the figure matches your expectations.
Confirm the item's record and the date it was last scored before quoting the score.
questions.why: Checking the record and the scoring date confirms that the figure being presented is current and traceable to the actual decision.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to the project office how you would help a stakeholder understand why a portfolio decision was made, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by pulling the actual decision record so the conversation is based on facts rather than memory. Then I would walk the stakeholder through the criteria the portfolio uses, the score their item received, and the forum that made the call, including its date. I would also show them the escalation route and what evidence could change the decision. The tradeoff is time: a proper walk-through takes a meeting or a recorded call, and it cannot be done for every item at once. So I would prioritize the requests with the largest effect on funding or delivery and give a standard one-page summary for the rest. This does not guarantee agreement, but it makes the decision transparent and the appeal route clear, which is what keeps people working inside the process.
rubricPoints: Grounds the explanation in the actual decision record and the agreed criteria, not memory or opinion
Names the decision-maker or forum, and the route for appeal or escalation
Identifies a real limit, such as time cost or inability to walk through every item, and how to manage it
Makes clear that understanding comes from a walk-through, not from sending documents alone

suggested.rationale: Explaining the process back in your own words to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed OpsForge mission or planned engine covers portfolio stakeholder communication.

lessons.plain: A portfolio is a group of projects and programs managed together toward shared goals. Whenever the portfolio team sends an update, such as a status report, a roadmap slide, or a decision note, someone should check that message before it goes out. This objective is about checking three things: whether it is correct, whether it agrees with the other messages around it, and whether it includes everything the rules require. Those rules come from governance guidelines, the agreed standards for how decisions and reports are prepared and approved. Think of it like proofreading a letter against the company template and the official records before you post it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A steering committee receives a portfolio status pack that rates Project Alpha green, but the schedule attached to the same pack shows it finishing three months late. Before reading any further, what should the portfolio manager do before this pack is circulated?
lessons.teach:
Accuracy means each figure or claim matches the record it comes from, called the source of truth, such as the schedule tool, the finance ledger, or the benefits register. Consistency means the same fact says the same thing everywhere it appears in the pack, the roadmap, and the verbal briefing. Completeness means the message contains every element that the governance guidelines require, such as the risk summary or the decisions needed from the committee. A baseline is the approved plan that progress is compared against, so it is the reference point for any claim about being on time or over budget.

Why check at all? Governance bodies make funding and priority decisions from these messages, so a wrong or partial message leads to wrong decisions.

Worked example. Step 1: list every claim in the pack. Alpha is green, budget is 92 percent spent, benefits forecast is 4 million. Step 2: trace each claim to its source of truth. The schedule shows a three-month slip against the baseline, so green is not accurate. Step 3: check consistency. The slide says green, the schedule says late, so one must be corrected and the reason recorded. Step 4: check completeness against the guidelines. The pack has no risk summary and no decisions section, so both must be added or the omission approved by the sponsor. Step 5: log who checked what, when, and what changed, then release.

Common mistake: checking only the summary slide and assuming the detail behind it is right.

In a running portfolio, an uncorrected green rating can lead the committee to approve further funding for a project that is already late, and the error then carries into the benefits forecast and other packs.

questions.prompt: A regional water utility's meter replacement pack makes three claims: the program is 61 percent complete, spend to date is 3.1 million against an approved budget of 4.5 million, and the benefits register shows 1.2 million in realised savings. Worked so far. Step 1: list every claim in the pack. Step 2: trace each claim to its source of truth. The 61 percent matches the asset tracker, the spend matches the finance ledger, and the savings match the benefits register, so all three are accurate. Step 3: check consistency. The roadmap and the verbal briefing both say 61 percent, so the facts agree across the pack. Step 4 is the one missing from this trace. Which option correctly completes it?
choices: Check the pack against the governance guidelines for every required element, such as the risk summary and the decisions needed; if any is missing, add it or record the sponsor's approval of the omission before release.
Send the pack to the sponsor for sign-off on the figures only, since committee members usually read the summary slide and not the detail.
Treat the pack as complete, because every figure is accurate and consistent, so completeness does not need a separate check.
Recalculate the completion figure from the spend ratio, since 3.1 divided by 4.5 is about 69 percent, and replace the 61 percent with that number.
questions.why: Completeness is its own check against the governance guidelines, and a missing required element must be added or its omission approved before the pack is released.

questions.prompt: A hospital IT portfolio pack says its electronic records project is seven weeks ahead of schedule. The approved baseline finish date is two weeks later than the current forecast, and the seven-week figure was measured against an earlier re-forecast. Which statement about the pack is correct?
choices: Both figures are acceptable as long as the pack labels which one it uses.
The schedule claim should be removed entirely, because schedule claims cannot be verified against any reference.
The seven-week claim is correct, because the earlier re-forecast is the most recent plan the team has.
The project should be described as two weeks late, because claims about being on time must be compared with the approved baseline.
questions.why: The baseline is the approved reference point for any claim about being on time, so the claim must be measured against it, which shows the project as two weeks late.

questions.prompt: A retail chain's portfolio pack states a benefits forecast of 2.4 million. The roadmap slide shows 2.1 million, the verbal briefing says 2.4 million, and the benefits register shows 2.1 million. What should the verifier do first?
choices: Average the two figures to 2.25 million and add a footnote explaining the gap.
Ask the briefing presenter to explain the difference at the meeting and leave the pack unchanged.
Keep 2.4 million, because the pack and the briefing agree and two sources outweigh one.
Trace the figure to the benefits register, correct the pack and the briefing to 2.1 million, and log the change and its reason.
questions.why: The benefits register is the source of truth, so the inconsistent items must be corrected to match it, and the change must be recorded with its reason.

questions.prompt: A transport authority's portfolio pack has passed the accuracy and consistency checks, but it has no risk summary and no decisions section, and the governance guidelines require both. What is the correct action before release?
choices: Hold the release and add the risk summary and decisions section, or record the sponsor's approval of any omission, before the pack goes out.
Release the pack now, because the guidelines only apply to packs that have already been challenged by the committee.
Shorten the pack so that the missing sections are no longer needed, then release it without recording any change.
Release the pack now, since the figures are correct, and promise the risk summary for the next cycle.
questions.why: Completeness is a separate requirement, and a required element that is missing must be added or formally approved as omitted before the pack is released.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a new teammate how you would verify a portfolio status report before it goes to the steering committee, and name one limit or tradeoff of that check.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing every claim in the report, such as status, budget, and benefits, and tracing each one to its source record, like the schedule tool or finance ledger, instead of trusting the summary slide. Then I would compare the claims with each other, because a green status next to a three-month slip in the schedule is a consistency failure that has to be fixed or explained. Last, I would check the report against the governance guidelines to confirm the required sections, such as risks and decisions needed, are present. The main limit is time: tracing every figure takes effort, so I focus on the items that drive decisions and on sections the guidelines name. The tradeoff is that a fast check can miss errors in low-visibility figures, so I record what I checked and the sample I used, which makes the gap visible to the reviewer.
rubricPoints: Traces each claim to its source of truth rather than trusting the summary
Checks that the same fact reads the same across all documents and briefings
Verifies required sections against the governance guidelines for completeness
Names a real limit or tradeoff, such as time or sampling, and how it is handled

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style situation where a report contradicts its own schedule adds the most practice in applying the accuracy, consistency, and completeness checks.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Supplies: Re-ranking a Portfolio After a Strategy Shift
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwater Transit Supplies Ltd is a fictional company that sells replacement parts and maintenance services to regional bus operators. Its executive board set two goals for the year: cut operating cost by 10 percent, and win back customers who had left for competitors. In month four the board changed the second goal. Customer retention, meaning keeping existing customers from leaving, now comes first, and the cost goal is reduced to 5 percent. Your role is portfolio manager. Six candidate initiatives are in the portfolio, and the governance board meets in three weeks to approve the funding plan. The candidates are: (A) a new online ordering portal, estimated at 900,000 with a projected return on investment (ROI, the financial gain divided by the cost, shown as a percentage) of 18 percent over three years; (B) a warehouse barcode system that cuts picking errors, estimated at 400,000 with an ROI of 25 percent, and which must finish before initiative A can link stock levels to orders; (C) a customer feedback and service-ticket tracker, estimated at 150,000, with no hard ROI but strong support from the sales team; (D) a fleet-parts supplier consolidation, estimated at 300,000 with a 30 percent ROI but a cost-saving benefit only; (E) a regulatory update to parts labeling required by a transport authority, mandatory by a fixed date; and (F) a loyalty discount program, estimated at 200,000, that the sales director strongly wants.

Complete the following sub-tasks.

1. Identify the prioritization criteria that apply to this decision (for example legislative requirements, dependencies, ROI, stakeholder expectations, and strategic fit), and rank candidates A through F against the new retention-first goal. Explain which criteria you used and why the cost-goal change alone does not decide the order.

2. Build two what-if portfolio scenarios that fund different subsets of candidates within a total budget of 1,200,000. For each, use a brief SWOT (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats) and note the main risk. Recommend one scenario with rationale suitable for the governance board.

3. Explain how the shift from cost reduction to customer retention changes the portfolio: which components gain or lose priority, and which dependency needs protecting in the roadmap. Then give a high-level sequence for the chosen scenario across the next four quarters, showing the order of work and where stakeholders must sign off.
subParts: Rank candidates against the new goal using prioritization criteria
Build two budget-limited scenarios and recommend one
Assess goal-change impact and sequence a four-quarter roadmap
modelAnswer: Strong answers name several criteria and apply them, not just ROI. Legislative requirement: item E is mandatory by a fixed date and must rank first regardless of ROI, because non-compliance creates legal exposure. Dependencies: B must finish before A can link stock to orders, so B has to be sequenced ahead of A even though A is the bigger customer-facing item. Strategic fit with the retention goal: C directly measures and reduces customer complaints, so it ranks high; F supports retention in a way but is a discount tool that may cut margin, so it ranks lower until its cost is tested. ROI: D has the best financial return but only serves the reduced cost goal, so it ranks mid-table. Stakeholder expectations: the sales director's support for F is noted but does not outweigh fit and cost. A good ranking might be E first (mandatory), C second (strong retention fit, low cost), B third (enabler for A, high ROI), A fourth (large retention benefit but depends on B), D fifth, and F sixth pending a cost test. The answer should explain that the cost-goal change alone does not decide the order because retention now carries more weight and the legal and dependency criteria sit above both goals.

Strong answers build two scenarios that stay within 1,200,000. Scenario one might fund E, C, B and A, totaling 1,750,000 if all are included, so it must drop one: fund E (mandatory, unavoidable), C (150,000), B (400,000), and A phased to 650,000 in year one, totaling 1,200,000 across the year. Scenario two might fund E, C, D and F, totaling 1,200,000 exactly if E is counted within the budget. Each scenario needs a SWOT: strengths (speed to customer benefit, legal compliance), weaknesses (partial scope for A), opportunities (B enables later automation), threats (competitor pricing, staff capacity). The main risk for scenario one is that A is only partly funded and retention gains arrive late. The main risk for scenario two is that F may erode margin while cost savings from D do not address the retention goal. Recommendation should favor scenario one, with rationale tied to the board's retention-first goal, the dependency of A on B, and the mandatory status of E. Governance language should be plain: the recommended option, why it beats the alternative, and what decision the board is asked to make.

Strong answers explain that the goal change moves retention-facing work, meaning C and A, up in priority, and moves cost-only work, meaning D, down. F becomes a candidate to hold until its margin impact is tested. The dependency to protect is B before A, since a delay in the warehouse system would hold back the portal's stock-linked ordering. A high-level four-quarter sequence might be: Quarter 1, complete E for the compliance deadline and start C; Quarter 2, finish C, begin B; Quarter 3, complete B and start the first phase of A; Quarter 4, finish the first phase of A and review F's cost case. Sign-off points should be placed at the start of each quarter for the board or steering group, with a check that the roadmap still reflects the retention goal. A common mistake is to schedule A first because it is largest and most visible, which breaks the B dependency and delays the customer benefit.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Foods: Overrun Request Through the Governance Model
scenarios.scenario: Brightwater Foods is a fictional grocery distributor with a portfolio of 14 active projects managed by its Portfolio Management Office (PMO), the team that keeps the portfolio's records, plans, and reporting consistent. Governance here means the set of structures, rules, and decision rights that determine who can approve what, and at which point. The portfolio has a Portfolio Steering Committee (a senior group of executives that makes the major portfolio decisions and owns the portfolio's direction), a Project Review Board (a working group that handles routine project issues), and a documented escalation threshold (a set limit above which a decision must move up to the next approval body). The Portfolio Management Plan sets the thresholds: changes to a project budget above 10 percent of the approved amount, or above 500,000 dollars, must go to the Steering Committee. Each project also has a named sponsor (the executive accountable for the project's benefits). The Warehouse Automation project has reported a request to increase its budget by 680,000 dollars, which is 17 percent over its approved amount. The sponsor believes the increase is needed to finish the work, and the Project Review Board has recommended approval. A second request for 150,000 dollars for a new analytics add-on has also arrived, and the portfolio has only enough capacity to fund either the add-on or a delayed Cold Chain Upgrade project. Complete the following as the portfolio's governance lead. 1. Identify which governance body must approve the Warehouse Automation budget increase, name the specific mechanism that calls for it, and explain why the Project Review Board's recommendation alone is not enough. 2. Describe the escalation path if the Steering Committee rejects the increase and the sponsor disagrees, and state who may take that disagreement further. 3. Explain how the portfolio's prioritization model should be used to decide between the analytics add-on and the Cold Chain Upgrade, and what record the governance model requires once the decision is made.
subParts: Identify the approving body and the mechanism for the Warehouse Automation budget increase.
Describe the escalation path after a rejection and who may take the disagreement further.
Explain the use of the prioritization model for the add-on versus Cold Chain Upgrade decision and the required decision record.
modelAnswer: The approving body is the Portfolio Steering Committee. The mechanism is the escalation threshold written into the Portfolio Management Plan: any budget change above 10 percent of the approved amount or above 500,000 dollars must move up from the Project Review Board to the Steering Committee. The request is 17 percent over, and 680,000 dollars is above the 500,000 dollar limit, so it meets both triggers. A threshold is a defined limit that changes who has authority to decide, and decision rights are the rules that say which body is allowed to approve a given kind of change. The Project Review Board's recommendation is advice that feeds the decision; it does not carry the authority to approve at this size. Common mistake: treating a favourable recommendation from a lower body as an approval. The consequence is that spending begins without the authority the governance model requires, and the overrun can later be reversed or audited as an unauthorized commitment.

If the Steering Committee rejects the increase and the sponsor disagrees, the first step is to record the rejection and the reasons in the decision log. The sponsor may then request a formal reconsideration at the next Steering Committee meeting, supported by new information such as a revised cost estimate or a reduced scope option. The escalation path ends at the Steering Committee because it is the highest portfolio approval body in this model; the sponsor cannot go to the Project Review Board to overturn it. If the disagreement concerns the benefits case rather than the cost, the matter can be raised with the executive who chairs the Steering Committee, who decides whether it needs a fresh review. Common mistake: having the sponsor fund the increase from a different project's budget to avoid the vote, which bypasses the governance decision. The consequence is that the portfolio's budget totals no longer match the approved plan, and the reporting to executives becomes unreliable.

The prioritization model is the agreed method for ranking proposals by criteria such as strategic fit, expected benefits, risk, and cost, and it is documented in the Portfolio Management Plan. Both the analytics add-on (150,000 dollars) and the Cold Chain Upgrade are scored against the same weighted criteria, and the one with the higher score is recommended to the Steering Committee, which has the authority to fund or defer it. Because the portfolio has capacity for only one, the score comparison should be shown with its assumptions, such as the expected benefit of each item and the risk tolerance set by the Steering Committee. The required record is a decision entry in the portfolio decision log that states the options, the scores, the approving body, the date, the rationale, and any conditions. Common mistake: deciding informally by whichever sponsor pushes hardest and recording only the outcome. The consequence is that the decision cannot be traced or defended later, and the deferred project's sponsor has no clear basis for appeal.

scenarios.title: Harrowgate Freight: Engineer Shortfall and a Vendor Overrun
scenarios.scenario:
Harrowgate Freight is a fictional mid-sized logistics company. Its portfolio governance board meets monthly. A portfolio is the set of projects and ongoing programs an organization groups together so they can be funded, ranked, and tracked against shared goals. You are the portfolio manager. This quarter's dashboard, which is a summary screen of key metrics, shows three things. Project Atlas, a warehouse-routing upgrade worth 40 percent of the portfolio's strategic value, has slipped six weeks because it is waiting on data engineers. Project Beacon, a customer-invoicing rebuild that is reported green and ranked fourth by strategic value, has a shared engineering pool that is overcommitted. The shared data engineering pool supplies 3.0 full-time equivalents (FTE, meaning one person working full time for one quarter, so 3.0 is three full-time people), while the portfolio's total demand is 4.5 FTE. Atlas needs 2.0 FTE, Beacon needs 1.5 FTE, and a smaller internal tools project needs 1.0 FTE. Separately, Beacon's software licence vendor has quoted a 12 percent cost overrun, which is above the 10 percent threshold the governance board set for reporting. The overrun has not yet been reported to anyone outside the Beacon team.

1. Using supply and demand analysis, which compares the capacity available with the capacity requested, state the shortfall and recommend how the 3.0 FTE should be split across Atlas, Beacon, and the tools project, explaining the strategic reasoning.
2. Decide how the vendor overrun should be escalated, which means passing an issue up to the people with authority to resolve it. Name the decision-maker and the deadline.
3. Name the portfolio record you would update so that the reallocation and its approval can be audited later, and list what it must contain.
subParts: Supply and demand shortfall and reallocation
modelAnswer: Start with the gap. Demand is 4.5 FTE and supply is 3.0 FTE, so the shortfall is 1.5 FTE. Supply and demand analysis means comparing these two numbers for each resource type so you can see where the pressure is and decide what to do about it. Because the pool cannot cover everything, you must rank the demands by strategic value rather than split the capacity evenly. Atlas carries 40 percent of strategic value and is the item that is already slipping, so it gets its full 2.0 FTE first. The remaining 1.0 FTE is split between Beacon and the tools project. Beacon is green and ranked fourth, so it can accept a lower allocation of 0.5 FTE for its critical work only, and the tools project gets 0.5 FTE. Check the arithmetic: 2.0 plus 0.5 plus 0.5 equals 3.0, which matches supply. The unmet demand is 1.0 FTE from Beacon and 0.5 FTE from the tools project, a total of 1.5 FTE. Those deferred items must be shown to the board as scope or schedule impacts, and any request for extra contractor capacity should go through change control, which is the formal process for approving a change before it is made. A common mistake is to shift people quietly so the dashboard still looks green for Beacon, which hides the real gap. The consequence in a running system is that Beacon's invoicing rebuild slips with no one having approved the delay, and the board loses the ability to judge whether Atlas's benefits are still on track.

Under the governance rules, a cost overrun above the 10 percent threshold is an issue that must be escalated, which means raised to the person who has the authority to decide on it, not simply noted in a report. The 12 percent vendor overrun is above threshold, so it should not wait for the monthly board meeting. The right escalation is a written notice to the executive sponsor of the Beacon project within 48 hours, copied to the governance board chair, since the sponsor controls Beacon's budget and the chair controls portfolio-level decisions. The notice should state the overrun amount, the cause, the options (such as renegotiating the licence, reducing seats, or accepting the cost with a documented business case), and a decision requested by the next scheduled board meeting or sooner if the vendor contract has a signing date. A common mistake is to hold the issue until the next monthly report because the amount seems small relative to the portfolio. The consequence is that the company could sign or extend the licence at the higher price before anyone with authority has approved it, which can lock in spend for a year or more and reduce the room to act later.

The record that proves the decision was made properly is the portfolio decision log, which is the controlled list of prioritization decisions, approvals, and the artifacts that support them. Some organizations call this the portfolio register or change log, but the purpose is the same: anyone reviewing it later should be able to reconstruct what was decided, why, and by whom. The entry for this reallocation should include the date and the version of the portfolio plan before and after the change, the supply and demand figures used (3.0 FTE supply, 4.5 FTE demand, 1.5 FTE shortfall), the strategic value scores that justified the ranking, the specific allocation for each component (Atlas 2.0, Beacon 0.5, tools 0.5), the deferred demand and who accepted it, the change request reference and its approval status, the named approver and the date of approval, and a link to the dashboard snapshot that triggered the decision. A common mistake is to record only the final allocation without the reasoning, so that a later auditor cannot tell whether the decision followed the governance rules. The consequence is that a compliance review or a later dispute about why Beacon's scope slipped cannot be answered from the records, which can create regulatory and internal audit findings even if the decision itself was sound.

scenarios.title: Harrow Lantern Logistics: Aggregate Risk Tolerance and a Reserve Request
scenarios.scenario:
Harrow Lantern Logistics is a fictional regional freight company running a three-part portfolio. Component A is a warehouse automation project with a 4,000,000 budget, owned by Dina Okafor. Component B is a customer portal rebuild with a 3,500,000 budget, owned by Ravi Patel. Component C is a fleet telematics upgrade with a 3,000,000 budget, owned by Lena Brandt. The total portfolio budget is 10,500,000. You are the portfolio manager. Your job is the portfolio-level view across all three components, not the day-to-day schedule of any one project.

The board has set a risk tolerance, meaning the measurable limit on how much risk the organisation will accept across the portfolio. Risk appetite is the general willingness to take risk; tolerance is the number that puts a boundary around it. The board's statement says the aggregate expected loss from known risks must not exceed 8 percent of total portfolio budget. Expected loss for a single risk is its probability multiplied by its cost impact. Aggregate expected loss is the sum of those values across the portfolio. Eight percent of 10,500,000 is 840,000.

Each component keeps its own risk register, a list of risks with owners, probabilities and impacts. The components have reported these expected losses: A 310,000, B 220,000, and C 150,000, a combined 680,000. Separately, the customer portal can only launch once the warehouse system publishes a stock-level data feed. Dina's team estimates a 40 percent chance the feed slips by six weeks, which would cost about 600,000 in delayed launch revenue and rework. Ravi has not counted this in his register because the risk sits in Component A's register. Also, the telematics upgrade and the warehouse project share one cloud vendor contract, which has a price-increase clause nobody has yet costed.

The board meets in ten days and wants a recommendation: is the portfolio within tolerance, and if not, what portfolio management reserve should be requested? A portfolio management reserve is a pool of money held at portfolio level, outside any single component's budget, for risks that cross components or cannot yet be assigned to one owner.

Answer the following:

1. Determine whether the portfolio is within the board's aggregate risk tolerance, and show your arithmetic.

2. Describe how the cross-component dependency should be recorded in the portfolio-level risk register, including who should own it and how it should be linked to the portfolio's strategic goals.

3. Recommend the size of the portfolio management reserve, explain the approval route, and state what mitigation would bring the portfolio back within tolerance.
modelAnswer: The known component exposures total 680,000 (310,000 plus 220,000 plus 150,000). The dependency risk is 40 percent multiplied by 600,000, which equals 240,000 of expected loss. Once it is counted, the aggregate becomes 920,000. The board tolerance is 840,000, so the portfolio is over tolerance by 80,000. A strong answer says plainly that the portfolio is not within tolerance, and points out that the breach is hidden because the dependency is sitting in Component A's register where it looks like a small part of A's exposure, and not in the portfolio view. The unpriced telematics vendor clause should also be noted as an unquantified item that could add more exposure.

The dependency should be entered in the portfolio-level risk register as its own entry, not left only in Component A's register. The entry should describe the cause (the warehouse feed is required by the portal launch), the effect (a six-week slip and about 600,000 cost impact), the probability (40 percent), and the expected loss (240,000). Ownership should be split clearly: the portfolio manager owns the portfolio-level entry and its reporting, Dina Okafor owns the mitigation actions on the feed, and Ravi Patel owns the launch-side response. Each entry should link to a strategic goal, here faster customer self-service and reliable stock visibility, so the board can see why the exposure matters. Escalated component risks that cross a boundary belong in the portfolio register with a named link back to their source register, so that the same risk is not counted twice and not dropped. The vendor price clause should be logged as an open item with an owner and a date for costing.

The reserve should be sized to the expected loss of the unowned cross-component dependency, 240,000, so that the exposure is funded centrally instead of being absorbed silently by one component. The request should go to the board, or the sponsor's governance group if the board has delegated reserve approval, with the tolerance breach stated openly. A good answer also offers a mitigation option that lowers the exposure and is more realistic than simply asking for money: for example, agreeing a two-week schedule buffer in the warehouse feed plan that reduces the probability from 40 percent to 25 percent. Then the dependency's expected loss becomes 150,000, and the aggregate becomes 830,000, which is within the 840,000 tolerance. The best recommendation pairs the mitigation with a smaller reserve held for the residual risk, and notes that the board should approve both the mitigation commitment and the reserve, with the vendor clause costed before the next review.

scenarios.title: Conflicting roadmap dates at Northgate Freight Solutions
scenarios.scenario:
Northgate Freight Solutions is a fictional mid-sized freight company with a portfolio of twelve projects grouped under one portfolio roadmap. A roadmap is a plan that shows which projects will happen in which time periods, so that people can see how the work fits together. The portfolio office, the team that manages the portfolio's processes and reporting, sends a monthly stakeholder newsletter to about forty people: regional operations managers, finance partners, and two external carrier vendors. Stakeholders are anyone who can affect the portfolio or be affected by it, and they are either internal (inside the company) or external (outside it, such as vendors). The governance board is the group that approves changes to project dates and budgets, using written governance guidelines that define who must approve what and in what order.

Last week, the governance board met and deferred the Warehouse Automation project from Q3 to Q4, pending a budget review. The minutes are filed in the shared governance folder. The newsletter drafted by a junior analyst, Priya Raman, still says Q3, and it was partly based on a slide from the previous month. Two regional managers have already told their carrier vendor that the new scanner rollout starts in Q3. A third regional manager mentioned that his team has no login to the portfolio dashboard, the online tool that shows current project dates, so he cannot check dates himself. You are the portfolio communications lead, and you own the communication plan. Your manager has asked you to resolve this before the next newsletter goes out in two days.

1. Identify the communication gap in this case. Say which stakeholder group is missing information, which source is the most reliable, and what change you would make to the communication plan's methods, recipients, or frequency so that a similar gap is less likely.
2. Describe the accuracy, consistency, and completeness check you would run on the draft newsletter against the governance guidelines before it is sent, and name what you would correct.
3. Explain how you would close the capability gap the third regional manager revealed, and how you would confirm the carrier vendor and regional managers now have the same correct date.
subParts: Identify the communication gap and fix it in the plan
Run the accuracy check against governance guidelines
Close the dashboard access gap and confirm alignment
modelAnswer: The gap is that the newsletter audience, especially regional managers and the external carrier vendor, received a date that the governance board had already changed. The most reliable source is the approved governance minutes, because the board is the body with authority over date changes, and a draft slide is not an approved record. The plan change is to add a rule that every roadmap date published externally or to regional managers must be checked against the latest governance minutes before release, and to add a short same-week 'date change notice' method so that approved changes reach recipients quickly instead of waiting for the next monthly newsletter. Recipients should be split so that vendors receive only items cleared for external sharing. The lesson is that a communication plan must name the authoritative source for each message, not just the channel. Common mistake: fixing only the newsletter text and not the process, so the same error repeats next month.

Start by treating the governance minutes as the reference. Compare every date, budget figure, and project status in the draft against the minutes, and mark anything that differs. Check consistency by confirming that the same date appears everywhere the project is mentioned in the newsletter, not only in the headline. Check completeness by confirming that the newsletter states that the date is pending a budget review, because omitting that condition would make a deferred item look settled. Correct the Warehouse Automation entry to Q4, pending budget review, and note the date of the board decision. Also check the vendor-facing paragraph separately, since it is the most consequential. Consequence: if the Q3 date stands, carrier scheduling and scanner deliveries may be booked for a period when the rollout cannot start, creating cost and rework for the vendor and the regional sites.

Ask the portfolio office to provide the third regional manager with read access to the dashboard, and confirm the access request is logged in the tool's access record with an owner and a completion date. Until access is granted, send him a written copy of the current approved dates from the minutes so he is not working from memory. To confirm alignment, send a short written confirmation to the carrier vendor and all regional managers stating the approved Q4 date and the pending budget review, ask each recipient to reply acknowledging the date, and track the replies against the distribution list. Follow up with anyone who has not replied within three working days, and record any remaining differences as open items for the next governance review. Common mistake: assuming that because a message was sent, the stakeholder understood it. The acknowledgment step is what verifies understanding.
